The owner or occupier of the dominant heritage is entitled to enjoy the easement without disturbance by any other person.

The owner of any interest in the dominant heritage, or the occupier of such heritage, may institute a suit for compensation for the disturbance of the easement or of any right accessory thereto; provided that the disturbance has actually caused substantial damage to the plaintiff.

The removal of the means of support to which a dominant owner is entitled does not give rise to a right to recover compensation unless and until substantial damage is actually sustained.

Subject to the provisions of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, an injunction may be granted to restrain the disturbance of an easement: if the easement is actually disturbed when compensation for such disturbance might be recovered under this Chapter; or if the disturbance is only threatened or intended, when the act threatened or intended must necessarily, if performed, disturb the easement.

When, from a cause which preceded the imposition of an easement, the person by whom it was imposed ceases to have any right in the servient heritage, the easement is extinguished.

An easement is extinguished when the dominant owner releases it, expressly or impliedly, to the servient owner. Such release can be made only in the circumstances and to the extent in and to which the dominant owner can alienate the dominant heritage. An easement may be released as to part only of the servient heritage.

An easement is extinguished when the servient heritage is by superior force so permanently altered that the dominent owner can no longer enjoy such easement.

An easement is extinguished where it has been imposed for a limited period, or acquired on condition that it shall become void on the performance or non-performance of a specified act, and the period expires or the condition is fulfilled.

An easement of necessity is extinguished when the necessity comes to an end.

An easement is extinguished when it becomes incapable of being at any time under any circumstances beneficial to the dominant owner.

An easement is extinguished where the servient heritage is by superior force so permanently altered that the dominent owner can no longer enjoy such easement.

An easement is extinguished when either the dominant or the servient heritage is completely destroyed.

The Act defines "appropriate Government" as, in the case of advocates admitted on the roll of a Bar Council of a State, the State Government; and in the case of advocates admitted on the roll of a Bar Council of a Union territory, the Central Government. The Act establishes a Trustee Committee, which is a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal, with power to acquire, hold and dispose of property. The Trustee Committee shall consist of the Advocate-General of a State, the Secretary to the appropriate Government in the Law Department or Ministry, the Secretary to the appropriate Government in the Home Department or Ministry, the Chairman of the State Bar Council, the Government Pleader or the Public Prosecutor, as may be nominated by the appropriate Government, and two advocates to be nominated by the State Bar Council. The Trustee Committee shall administer the Fund, which shall be held and applied by the Trustee Committee subject to the provisions of this Act. The Trustee Committee shall receive applications for admission or re-admission as members to the Fund, and dispose of such applications within ninety days from the date of receipt thereof. The Trustee Committee shall record in the minutes book of the Trustee Committee, its decisions on the applications. The Trustee Committee shall pay to the members of the Fund or their nominees or legal heirs, as the case may be, the amounts at the rates specified in Schedule I. The Trustee Committee shall send such periodical and annual reports as may be prescribed, to the appropriate Government and the State Bar Council. The Trustee Committee shall communicate to the applicants, by registered post with acknowledgment due or through electronic mode, the decisions of the Trustee Committee in respect of applications for admission or re-admission as members to the Fund or claims to the benefit of the Fund. The Trustee Committee shall do such other acts as are or may be directed by the State Bar Council and the appropriate Government. The Trustee Committee may borrow, from time to time, any sum required for carrying out the purposes of this Act, with the prior approval of the appropriate Government and the State Bar Council. The Trustee Committee shall deposit all monies and receipts forming part of the Fund in any scheduled bank or invest the same in debt instruments of any corporation owned or controlled by the appropriate Government or in loans floated by the appropriate Government or in any other manner as the State Bar Council may, from time to time, direct with the prior approval of the appropriate Government. The accounts of the Trustee Committee shall be audited annually by a chartered accountant appointed by the State Bar Council. The Trustee Committee shall comply with the directions issued by the State Bar Council under sub-section (3). The Trustee Committee shall pay from the Fund the charges for the audit as may be fixed by the State Bar Council. The Secretary of the Trustee Committee shall be the chief executive authority of the Trustee Committee and responsible for carrying out its decisions. The Secretary of the Trustee Committee shall represent the Trustee Committee in all suits and proceedings for and against the Trustee Committee. The Secretary of the Trustee Committee shall authenticate by his signature all decisions and instruments of the Trustee Committee. The Secretary of the Trustee Committee shall operate bank account of the Trustee Committee jointly with the Chairperson. The Secretary of the Trustee Committee shall convene meetings of the Trustee Committee and prepare minutes of such meetings. The Secretary of the Trustee Committee shall attend meetings of the Trustee Committee with all the necessary records and information. The Secretary of the Trustee Committee shall maintain such forms, registers and other records as may be prescribed from time to time and do all correspondence relating to the Trustee Committee. The Secretary of the Trustee Committee shall prepare an annual statement of business transacted by the Trustee Committee during a financial year. The Secretary of the Trustee Committee shall do such other acts as are or may be directed by the Trustee Committee and the State Bar Council. The decision of the State Bar Council on any matter regarding recognition of an association under sub-section (4) shall be final. The Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen. A contingent contract cannot be enforced by law unless and until the event on which it is contingent has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if a specified uncertain event happens within a fixed time become void if, at the expiration of the time fixed, such event has not happened, or if, before the time fixed, such event becomes impossible. Contingent agreements to do or not to do anything, if an impossible event happens, are void, whether the impossibility of the event is known or not to the parties to the agreement at the time when it is made. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law. Promises bind the representatives of the promisors in case of the death of such promisors before performance, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If a promisor has made an offer of performance to the promisee, and the offer has not been accepted, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance, nor does he thereby lose his rights under the contract. THE EQUAL REMUNERATION ACT, 1976 (ACT NO. 25 OF 1976) came into force on the 11th of February, 1976, with the main objective of providing for the payment of equal remuneration to men and women workers and for the prevention of discrimination against women in matters of employment. The Act applies to the whole of India and has overriding effect over any other law or instrument that is inconsistent with its provisions.

Chapter I of the Act deals with preliminary matters and defines key terms used throughout the Act. The term "appropriate Government" refers to the Central Government in cases where the employment is carried out by or under the authority of the Central Government, a railway administration, a banking company, a mine, oilfield, or major port, or any corporation established by or under a Central Act. In all other cases, the "appropriate Government" refers to the State Government. The term "employer" is defined as any person who employs one or more workers in an establishment or employment in which this Act has come into force. "Man" and "woman" are defined as male and female human beings, respectively, of any age. "Remuneration" includes basic wage or salary and any additional emoluments payable in cash or kind to a person employed in respect of employment or work done in such employment. "Same work or work of a similar nature" means work in respect of which the skill, effort, and responsibility required are the same when performed under similar working conditions by a man or a woman.

Chapter II of the Act focuses on the payment of remuneration at equal rates to men and women workers and other matters. Section 4 states that no employer shall pay to any worker remuneration at rates less favorable than those at which remuneration is paid by him to workers of the opposite sex in the same establishment or employment for performing the same work or work of a similar nature. Section 5 prohibits discrimination in recruitment and other conditions of service, such as promotions, training, or transfer, based on sex. However, this provision does not affect any priority or reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, ex-servicemen, retrenched employees, or any other class or category of persons in the matter of recruitment to the posts in an establishment or employment.

Chapter III of the Act contains miscellaneous provisions. Section 8 mandates employers to maintain registers and other documents in relation to the workers employed by them. Section 9 empowers the appropriate Government to appoint Inspectors for the purpose of making investigations as to whether the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder are being complied with by employers. Section 10 lays down penalties for non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, including failure to maintain registers or other documents, making recruitment in contravention of the provisions of the Act, making payment of remuneration at unequal rates, and making discrimination between men and women workers.

* Unlawful assembly: An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly” if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is to overawe by criminal force or show of criminal force, resist the execution of any law or of any legal process, commit any mischief or criminal trespass or other offence, by means of criminal force or show of criminal force to any person, take or obtain possession of any property, deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, use of water or other incorporeal right of which he is in possession or enjoyment, or to enforce any right or supposed right, or by means of criminal force or show of criminal force, compel any person to do what he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do.

* Joining unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapon: Whoever, being armed with any deadly weapon or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, is a member of an unlawful assembly, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the consequences of breaching a contract in Chapter VI, specifically in Section 73. According to this section, when a contract is broken, the party who suffers as a result is entitled to receive compensation from the party who breached the contract for any loss or damage caused by the breach. This compensation is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The same compensation is also applicable when an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged.

The section further explains that in estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Illustrations are provided to further explain the application of this section. For example, if A contracts to sell and deliver 50 maunds of saltpetre to B, at a certain price to be paid on delivery, and A breaks his promise, B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the sum, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which B might have obtained 50 maunds of saltpetre of like quality at the time when the saltpetre ought to have been delivered.

Another illustration explains that if A hires B‟s ship to go to Bombay, and there take on board, on the first of January, a cargo, which A is to provide, and to bring it to Calcutta, the freight to be paid when earned. B’s ship does not go to Bombay, but A has opportunities of procuring suitable conveyance for the cargo upon terms as advantageous as those on which he had chartered the ship. A avails himself of those opportunities, but is put to trouble and expense in doing so. A is entitled to receive compensation from B in respect of such trouble and expense.

Overall, this section of the Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the compensation that the party who suffers from a breach of contract is entitled to receive from the party who breached the contract. The compensation is for any loss or damage caused by the breach, and it is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account while estimating the loss or damage.

THE USURIOUS LOANS ACT, 1918 (Act No. 10 OF 1918)

The Usurious Loans Act, 1918, is an Act that aims to give additional powers to Courts to deal with usurious loans of money or in kind. The Act, which came into force on 22nd March 1918, extends to the whole of India except the territories which were comprised in Part B States before 1st November 1956. The State Government may specify any area, class of persons, or class of transactions to which the Act shall not apply.

The Act defines "interest" as the rate of interest and includes the return to be made over and above what was actually lent, whether the same is charged or sought to be recovered specifically by way of interest or otherwise. "Loan" means a loan whether of money or in kind and includes any transaction which is, in the opinion of the Court, in substance a loan. "Suit to which this Act applies" means any suit for the recovery of a loan made after the commencement of this Act or for the enforcement of any security taken or any agreement, whether by way of settlement of account or otherwise, made, after the commencement of this Act, in respect of any loan made either before or after the commencement of this Act or for the redemption of any security given after the commencement of this Act in respect of any loan made either before or after the commencement of this Act.

Under Section 3 of the Act, the Court may exercise powers to re-open the transaction, take an account between the parties, and relieve the debtor of all liability in respect of any excessive interest. The Court may also re-open any account already taken between the parties and relieve the debtor of all liability in respect of any excessive interest. The Court may set aside any security given or agreement made in respect of any loan, and if the creditor has parted with the security, order him to indemnify the debtor in such manner and to such extent as it may deem just. However, the Court shall not re-open any agreement purporting to close previous dealings and to create a new obligation which has been entered into by the parties or any persons from whom they claim at a date more than twelve years from the date of the transaction or do anything which affects any decree of a Court.

Under Section 4, on any application relating to the admission or amount of a proof of a loan in any insolvency proceedings, the Court may exercise the like powers as may be exercised under Section 3 by a Court in a suit to which this Act applies.

The Act applies to any suit, whatever its form may be, if such suit is substantially one for the recovery of a loan or for the enforcement of any agreement or security in respect of a loan or for the redemption of any such security. The Act does not affect the rights of any transferee for value who satisfies the Court that the transfer to him was bona fide, and that he had at the time of such transfer no notice of any fact which would have entitled the debtor as against the lender to relief under this section. The Act does not derogate from the existing powers or jurisdiction of any Court.

The Act has been amended in several states, including Uttar Pradesh, the Central Provinces, Madras, East Punjab, Andhra Pradesh, and Himachal Pradesh. The Act has been extended to the whole of Madhya Pradesh and the Union territory of Pondicherry. The Act has been repealed in its application to Bellary District by Mysore Act 14 of 1955.

In this summary, we will explain the key provisions of Sections 24 and 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which deal with the power of transfer and withdrawal of suits, appeals, and other proceedings.

Section 24: General power of transfer and withdrawal

Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for the transfer and withdrawal of suits, appeals, and other proceedings. The section gives the High Court or the District Court the power to transfer or withdraw any suit, appeal, or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same. Where any suit or proceeding has been transferred or withdrawn under sub-section (1), the Court which is thereafter to try or dispose of such suit or proceeding may, subject to any special directions in the case of an order of transfer, either retry it or proceed from the point at which it was transferred or withdrawn.

The Indian Evidence Act of 1872 outlines the relevance of various types of evidence in legal proceedings. This summary will focus on sections of the Act that relate to Indian laws, including Acts, Articles, or other legal terms.

Section 34 discusses the relevance of entries in books of account, including those maintained electronically, in the course of business. Section 35 states that an entry in any public or official book, register, or record, or an electronic record, made by a public servant in the discharge of his official duty, is a relevant fact.

Section 36 states that statements of facts in issue or relevant facts, made in published maps or charts generally offered for public sale, or in maps or plans made under the authority of the Central Government or any State Government, are themselves relevant facts.

Section 37 states that when the court has to form an opinion as to the existence of any fact of a public nature, any statement of it made in a recital contained in any Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom or in any Central Act, Provincial Act, or State Act, or in a Government notification or notification by the Crown Representative appearing in the Official Gazette, is a relevant fact.

Section 38 states that when the court has to form an opinion as to a law of any country, any statement of such law contained in a book purporting to be printed or published under the authority of the Government of such country and to contain any such law, is relevant.

Section 250 deals with the evidence of medical witnesses in cases of rape. According to this section, when a person is accused of an offence under section 376, section 376A, section 376AB, section 376B, section 376C, section 376D, section 376DA, section 376DB or section 376E of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), the Court shall take evidence of medical witnesses, if any, as to the age of the woman, as to whether she was, in the opinion of the medical witness, a virgin or not, and as to the nature of the injuries, if any, on her person, and the evidence of the medical witness shall be taken in the presence of the accused, or, if the accused is not produced in Court, in the presence of his pleader, if any.

Section 251 deals with the evidence of persons of unsound mind. According to this section, no witness who appears to be of unsound mind shall be tendered for examination, unless the Court, after examination of the witness, is of opinion that he is capable of giving evidence, and, if the witness is a person of unsound mind, the Court shall record a finding to that effect.

Section 252 deals with the examination of persons accused of offences. According to this section, any person accused of an offence before a Criminal Court shall be examined as a witness, unless he is exempted from personal appearance under any law for the time being in force, or the Court considers that he is unable to give evidence by reason of his state of health or other cause, or that it is not expedient to examine him.

Section 253 deals with the examination of persons present in Court. According to this section, any person present in Court when a witness is examined may be examined, although he is not called as a witness, and any person present in Court when a deposition is taken may be allowed to cross-examine the deponent, although he is not examined as a witness.

Section 254 deals with the examination of persons in the custody of the Court. According to this section, any person in the custody of the Court may be examined as a witness, whether he is a party to the case or not, and whether he is named in the list of witnesses or not, and any such person, when so examined, shall be deemed to be a competent witness.

Section 255 deals with the examination of children. According to this section, a child under the age of twelve years may be examined, but his evidence shall not be recorded by the Court unless the Court is satisfied that he is possessed of sufficient intelligence to justify his examination, and understands the nature of an oath; and when a child is so examined, his evidence shall be recorded in the presence of his parent or guardian, or some other person in whom he has confidence.

Section 258 deals with the examination of persons who cannot hear. Section 259 deals with the examination of persons who cannot read or write. A charge must state the offence with which the accused is charged, and if the law that creates the offence gives it a specific name, the offence may be described in the charge by that name only. If the law does not give the offence a specific name, so much of the definition of the offence must be stated as to give the accused notice of the matter with which they are charged. The law and section of the law against which the offence is said to have been committed must be mentioned in the charge. The charge must be written in the language of the Court. If the accused is liable to enhanced punishment or a different kind of punishment for a subsequent offence due to a previous conviction, the fact, date, and place of the previous conviction must be stated in the charge. When the nature of the case is such that the particulars mentioned in sections 211 and 212 do not give the accused sufficient notice of the matter with which they are charged, the charge shall also contain such particulars of the manner in which the alleged offence was committed as will be sufficient for that purpose. In every charge, words used in describing an offence shall be deemed to have been used in the sense attached to them respectively by the law under which such offence is punishable. No error in stating either the offence or the particulars required to be stated in the charge, and no omission to state the offence or those particulars, shall be regarded at any stage of the case as material, unless the accused was in fact misled by such error or omission, and it has occasioned a failure of justice. Any Court may alter or add to any charge at any time before judgment is pronounced. If the alteration or addition to a charge is such that proceeding immediately with the trial is not likely, in the opinion of the Court, to prejudice the accused in his defence or the prosecutor in the conduct of the case, the Court may, in its discretion, after such alteration or addition has been made, proceed with the trial as if the altered or added charge had been the original charge. If the alteration or addition is such that proceeding immediately with the trial is likely, in the opinion of the Court, to prejudice the accused or the prosecutor as aforesaid, the Court may either direct a new trial or adjourn the trial for such period as may be necessary. If the offence stated in the altered or added charge is one for the prosecution of which previous sanction is necessary, the case shall not be proceeded with until such sanction is obtained, unless sanction has been already obtained for a prosecution on the same facts as those on which the altered or added charge is founded. Whenever a charge is altered or added to by the Court after the commencement of the trial, the prosecutor and the accused shall be allowed—to recall or re-summon and cross-examine any witness who has been examined.

The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 (MGNREGA) is a social welfare legislation enacted by the Parliament of India to provide at least one hundred days of guaranteed wage employment in every financial year to every household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work in rural areas. The Act aims to enhance the livelihood security of the rural population and promote rural development.

The Act defines various terms used in the legislation, including "adult", "applicant", "Block", "Central Council", "District Programme Coordinator", "household", "implementing agency", "minimum wage", "National Fund", "notification", "preferred work", "prescribed", "Programme Officer", "project", "rural area", "Scheme", "State Council", "unskilled manual work", and "wage rate".

The Act is divided into six chapters. Chapter I, titled "Preliminary", deals with the short title, extent, and commencement of the Act. Chapter II, titled "Guarantee of Employment in Rural Areas", provides for the guarantee of employment to rural households and the payment of wages. Chapter III, titled "Employment Guarantee Schemes and Unemployment Allowance", deals with the Schemes made by the State Government for providing employment and the payment of unemployment allowance. Chapter IV, titled "Implementing and Monitoring Authorities", establishes the Central Employment Guarantee Council and the State Employment Guarantee Council to discharge the functions and perform the duties assigned to them. Chapter V, titled "Establishment of National and State Employment Guarantee Funds and Audit", provides for the establishment of the National Employment Guarantee Fund and the State Employment Guarantee Fund to meet the cost of the Schemes. Chapter VI, titled "Miscellaneous", deals with various miscellaneous provisions, including penalty for non-compliance, power to delegate, power of the Central Government to give directions, and protection of action taken in good faith.

The Act also contains two schedules. Schedule I lays down the minimum features of a rural employment guarantee scheme, and Schedule II lays down the conditions for guaranteed rural employment under a scheme and the minimum entitlements of laborers.

The Act has been amended twice, first by the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee (Amendment) Act, 2009, and then by the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee (Amendment) Act, 2013. The amendments have made various changes to the Act, including the change of name from the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act to the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, the extension of the Act to the Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, and the increase in the wage rate from sixty rupees per day to one hundred rupees per day.

Overall, the MGNREGA is a landmark legislation that aims to provide employment opportunities to the rural population, promote rural development, and enhance the livelihood security of rural households.

Summary:

The Indian Information Technology Act of 2000 includes several provisions related to the protection of electronic records, personal information, and electronic signatures. Section 72 of the Act makes it a punishable offense to access or disclose any electronic record, book, register, correspondence, information, document, or other material without consent. Section 72A increases the penalty for disclosing personal information in breach of a lawful contract. Section 73 prohibits the publication of electronic signature certificates with false information and imposes penalties for violations. Section 74 makes it a criminal offense to create, publish, or make available an electronic signature certificate for fraudulent or unlawful purposes.

Section 75 extends the provisions of the Act to offenses committed outside India if the act or conduct involves a computer, computer system, or computer network located in India. Section 76 authorizes the confiscation of any computer, computer system, or related accessories used in the commission of an offense under the Act. Section 77 states that compensation, penalties, or confiscation under the Act shall not interfere with other punishments under other laws. Section 77A allows for the compounding of offenses under the Act, except for offenses punishable by life imprisonment or imprisonment for a term exceeding three years.

Section 77B makes offenses punishable by three years of imprisonment bailable. Section 78 grants police officers the power to investigate offenses under the Act. Section 79 provides exemptions from liability for intermediaries under certain circumstances. Summary:

The Indian Information Technology Act, 2000, contains various provisions related to electronic governance, digital signatures, and penalties for cybercrimes. Summary:
* Digital signature: A digital signature is created using an asymmetric cryptosystem and hash function, which envelops and transforms the initial electronic record into another electronic record. The authentication of the electronic record is effected by the use of a private key, and the electronic record can be verified by anyone using the subscriber's public key.
* Electronic signature: A subscriber may authenticate any electronic record by such electronic signature or electronic authentication technique, which is considered reliable and specified in the Second Schedule. The electronic signature or authentication technique is considered reliable if certain conditions are met, such as the signature creation data or authentication data being linked to the signatory, under the signatory's control at the time of signing, and any alteration to the electronic signature or information being detectable. The Central Government may prescribe the procedure for ascertaining whether an electronic signature is that of the person by whom it is purported to have been affixed or authenticated.
* Legal recognition of electronic records: Where any law provides that information or any other matter shall be in writing or in the typewritten or printed form, then, notwithstanding anything contained in such law, such requirement shall be deemed to have been satisfied if such information or matter is rendered or made available in an electronic form and accessible so as to be usable for a subsequent reference.
* Legal recognition of electronic signatures: Where any law provides that information or any other matter shall be authenticated by affixing the signature or any document shall be signed or bear the signature of any person, then, notwithstanding anything contained in such law, such requirement shall be deemed to have been satisfied if such information or matter is authenticated by means of an electronic signature affixed in such manner as may be prescribed by the Central Government.
* Use of electronic records and electronic signatures in Government and its agencies: Any filing, issue, grant, receipt, or payment required by law to be made in a particular manner can be satisfied by means of an electronic form as prescribed by the appropriate Government. The appropriate Government may prescribe the manner and format in which such electronic records shall be filed, created, or issued and the manner or method of payment of any fee or charges for filing, creation, or issue of any electronic record.
* Delivery of services by service provider: The appropriate Government may authorize any service provider to set up, maintain and upgrade computerized facilities and perform other services as specified by the notification in the Official Gazette. The appropriate Government may also authorize the service provider to collect, retain and appropriate such service charges as may be prescribed by the appropriate Government for the purpose of providing such services. The appropriate Government shall specify the scale of service charges which may be charged and collected by the service providers under this section.
* Retention of electronic records: Where any law provides that documents, records, or information shall be retained for any specific period, then, that requirement shall be deemed to have been satisfied if such documents, records, or information are retained in the electronic form, if the information contained therein remains accessible so as to be usable for a subsequent reference, the electronic record is retained in the format in which it was originally generated, sent or received or in a format which can be demonstrated to represent accurately the information originally generated, sent or received, and the details which will facilitate the identification of the origin, destination, date and time of despatch or receipt of such electronic record are available in the electronic record.

No court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which the Tribunal is empowered to determine, and no injunction shall be granted by any court or other authority in respect of any action taken or to be taken in pursuance of any power conferred by or under this Act. Any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Tribunal may file an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the decision or order of the Tribunal. The document provided is a part of Order XXIII of the Indian Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). This Order deals with discontinuance, compromise, and abuse of the process of the court.

Rule 1 of Order XXIII outlines the consequences of abandoning or withdrawing from a suit or part of a claim without permission. If a plaintiff abandons a suit or part of a claim, they will be liable for costs and will be precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of the same subject matter or part of the claim. Similarly, if a plaintiff withdraws from a suit or part of a claim without permission, they will be liable for costs and will be precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of the same subject matter or part of the claim. However, the court cannot permit one of several plaintiffs to abandon a suit or part of a claim without the consent of the other plaintiff.

Rule 1A permits the transposition of defendants as plaintiffs in certain circumstances. Where a suit is withdrawn or abandoned by a plaintiff under Rule 1, and a defendant applies to be transposed as a plaintiff under Rule 10 of Order I, the court shall consider such application, having due regard to the question of whether the applicant has a substantial question to be decided as against any of the other defendants.

Rule 2 provides that the law of limitation is not affected by a first suit. In any fresh suit instituted on permission granted under the last preceding rule, the plaintiff shall be bound by the law of limitation in the same manner as if the first suit had not been instituted.

Rule 3 deals with the compromise of a suit. Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise in writing and signed by the parties, or where the defendant satisfies the plaintiff in respect to the whole or any part of the subject matter of the suit, the court shall order such agreement, compromise, or satisfaction to be recorded and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith, so far as it relates to the parties to the suit, whether or not the subject matter of the agreement, compromise, or satisfaction is the same as the subject matter of the suit.

Rule 3A bars a suit from being set aside on the ground that the compromise on which the decree is based was not lawful.

Rule 3B provides that no agreement or compromise can be entered into in a representative suit without the leave of the court. Any such agreement or compromise entered into without the leave of the court shall be void.

Rule 3B(2) states that before granting such leave, the court shall give notice to such persons as may appear to it to be interested in the suit.

Rule 3B has an explanation that defines a representative suit as a suit under Section 91 or Section 92, a suit under Rule 8 of Order I, a suit in which the manager of an undivided Hindu family sues or is sued as representing the other members of the family, or any other suit in which the decree passed may, by virtue of the provisions of this Code or of any other law for the time being in force, bind any person who is not named as a party to the suit.

Rule 4 states that nothing in this Order shall apply to any proceedings in execution of a decree or order.

Order XXIV deals with payment into court. It outlines the procedure for deposit of money by a defendant in satisfaction of a claim, notice of the deposit, interest on the deposit, and procedure where the plaintiff accepts the deposit as satisfaction in part or in full.

Order XXV deals with security for costs. It outlines the circumstances under which a court may require a plaintiff to give security for the payment of costs, the effect of failure to furnish security, and the procedure for setting aside a dismissal for non-compliance with the security for costs order.

Section 40 states that the existence of any judgment, order or decree which by law prevents any court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial, is a relevant fact when the question is whether such court ought to take cognizance of such suit or to hold such trial.

Section 41 states that a final judgment, order or decree of a competent court, in the exercise of probate, matrimonial, admiralty or insolvency jurisdiction, which confers upon or takes away from any person any legal character, or which declares any person to be entitled to any such character, or to be entitled to any specific thing, not as against any specified person but absolutely, is relevant when the existence of any such legal character, or the title of any such person to any such thing, is relevant. Such judgment, order or decree is conclusive proof that any legal character which it confers accrued at the time when such judgment, order or decree came into operation, and that anything to which it declares any person to be so entitled was the property of that person at the time from which such judgment, order or decree declares that it had been or should be his property.

Section 42 states that judgments, orders or decrees other than those mentioned in section 41 are relevant if they relate to matters of a public nature relevant to the enquiry, but such judgments, orders or decrees are not conclusive proof of that which they state.

Section 43 states that judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in sections 40, 41, and 42, are irrelevant, unless the existence of such judgment, order or decree is a fact in issue, or is relevant under some other provision of this Act.

Section 44 states that any party to a suit or other proceeding may show that any judgment, order, or decree which is relevant under section 40, 41, or 42, and which has been proved by the adverse party, was delivered by a court not competent to deliver it, or was obtained by fraud or collusion.

Section 45 states that when the court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law or of science, or art, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions upon that point of persons specially skilled in such foreign law, science, or art, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, are relevant facts.

Section 46 states that facts bearing upon the question whether an expert is competent to express an opinion, and facts calculated to affect the weight of his opinion, are relevant, whether they are or are not themselves proved by other evidence.

The document summarizes various Indian laws related to contracts. Section 21 states that a contract is not void due to a mistake in law, but a mistake in a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact. Section 22 states that a contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by a mistake of one party as to a matter of fact. Section 23 outlines the lawfulness of the consideration or object of an agreement, which is unlawful if it is forbidden by law, defeats the provisions of any law, is fraudulent, involves injury to the person or property of another, or is immoral or opposed to public policy. Section 24 states that if any part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any one or any part of any one of several considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void. Section 25 states that an agreement made without consideration is void, unless it is expressed in writing and registered, or is a promise to compensate for something done, or is a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation law. Section 26 states that every agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person, other than a minor, is void. Section 27 states that every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void. Section 28 states that every agreement, by which any party thereto is restricted absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any contract, by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or which limits the time within which he may thus enforce his rights, is void to that extent. However, this section does not render illegal a contract to refer to arbitration any dispute that may arise or any question between them which has already arisen.
The Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen. A contingent contract cannot be enforced by law unless and until the event on which it is contingent has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event does not happen can be enforced when the happening of that event becomes impossible, and not before. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if a specified uncertain event happens within a fixed time become void if, at the expiration of the time fixed, such event has not happened, or if, before the time fixed, such event becomes impossible. Contingent agreements to do or not to do anything, if an impossible event happens, are void, whether the impossibility of the event is known or not to the parties to the agreement at the time when it is made. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law. Promises bind the representatives of the promisors in case of the death of such promisors before performance, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If a promisor has made an offer of performance to the promisee, and the offer has not been accepted, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance, nor does he thereby lose his rights under the contract. Every such offer must fulfill certain conditions, such as being unconditional, made at a proper time and place, and under such circumstances that the person to whom it is made may have a reasonable opportunity of ascertaining that the person by whom it is made is able and willing there and then to do the whole of what he is bound by his promise to do. If the offer is an offer to deliver anything to the promisee, the promisee must have a reasonable opportunity of seeing that the thing offered is the thing which the promisor is bound by his promise to deliver.
Summary:

The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the legal framework for contracts in India. The act defines a contract as an agreement that is enforceable by law, and it specifies the essential elements of a contract, including offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity to contract, and free consent.

Section 29 of the act states that a promise to perform an impossible act is void. If a promisor makes a promise without the intention of performing it, or if he has no means of performing it, the promise is void. Similarly, if the act promised becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made, the contract becomes void.

Section 39 of the act states that when a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract. However, if the promisee has signified his acquiescence in its continuance, he cannot put an end to the contract.

Summary:

The Advocates Act, 1961, is an Act to amend and consolidate the law relating to legal practitioners and to provide for the constitution of Bar Councils and an All-India Bar. The Act is divided into several chapters, with Chapter I containing preliminary provisions such as the short title, extent, and commencement of the Act, as well as definitions of key terms used throughout the Act.

Chapter II of the Act deals with Bar Councils, which are established at both the state and national levels. The State Bar Councils are responsible for maintaining the roll of advocates in their respective states and for regulating the practice of law within the state. The Bar Council of India, on the other hand, is responsible for regulating the legal profession throughout the country.

Under the Act, each State Bar Council is required to consist of a certain number of members, including the Advocate-General of the state ex officio and a number of elected members. The elected members must possess certain qualifications or satisfy certain conditions as prescribed by the Bar Council of India. The Bar Council of India, in turn, is required to consist of the Attorney-General and Solicitor-General of India ex officio, as well as one member elected by each State Bar Council.

The Act also establishes procedures for the election and term of office of members of the Bar Councils, as well as provisions for the preparation and revision of electoral rolls. The Bar Council of India is granted the power to make rules regarding the election and term of office of its members, as well as the preparation and revision of electoral rolls.

Overall, the Advocates Act, 1961, provides a framework for the regulation of the legal profession in India, with Bar Councils at both the state and national levels responsible for maintaining the roll of advocates and regulating the practice of law.
Summary:

The Advocates Act, 1961 outlines the functions and powers of State Bar Councils and the Bar Council of India in India. A State Bar Council is a body corporate with perpetual succession and the power to hold property, contract, and sue and be sued. The functions of a State Bar Council include admitting persons as advocates, preparing and maintaining a roll of advocates, entertaining and determining cases of misconduct against advocates, safeguarding the rights and interests of advocates, promoting law reform, conducting seminars and organizing talks on legal topics, providing legal aid to the poor, managing and investing funds, and performing other functions conferred on it by the Act. A State Bar Council may constitute one or more funds for the purpose of giving financial assistance to organize welfare schemes, giving legal aid or advice, and establishing law libraries. The Bar Council of India has similar functions, including laying down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for advocates, safeguarding the rights and interests of advocates, promoting and supporting law reform, dealing with matters arising under the Act, exercising general supervision and control over State Bar Councils, promoting legal education, recognizing Universities, conducting seminars and organizing talks, organizing legal aid to the poor, managing and investing funds, providing for the election of its members, and doing all other things necessary for discharging its functions. The Bar Council of India may also become a member of international legal bodies, contribute sums to such bodies, and authorize expenditure on the participation of its representatives in international legal conferences or seminars. The term of office of an elected member of a State Bar Council is five years, which may be extended by the Bar Council of India for a period not exceeding six months in the event of a failure to provide for the election of members before the expiry of the term. The Bar Council of India may constitute a Special Committee to discharge the functions of the State Bar Council until it is constituted. A Bar Council shall constitute one or more disciplinary committees, each of which shall consist of three persons. A Bar Council may also constitute one or more legal aid committees, each of which shall consist of such number of members as may be prescribed. A State Bar Council and the Bar Council of India may constitute other committees as deemed necessary for carrying out the provisions of the Act. The transaction of business by Bar Councils and committees thereof shall be in accordance with the rules made under the Act.

The appeal must be made within sixty days of the date of the communication of the order to the aggrieved person. The disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India may pass such order, including varying the punishment awarded by the disciplinary committee of the State Bar Council, as it deems fit. However, no order of the disciplinary committee of the State Bar Council shall be varied so as to prejudicially affect the person aggrieved without giving him reasonable opportunity of being heard.

The appeal must be made within sixty days of the date on which the order is communicated to the aggrieved person. The Supreme Court may pass such order, including varying the punishment awarded by the disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India, as it deems fit. However, no order of the disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India shall be varied so as to prejudicially affect the person aggrieved without giving him a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

Section 39 states that the provisions of sections 5 and 12 of the Limitation Act, 1963, shall apply to appeals under Section 37 and Section 38.

However, the disciplinary committee shall not have the right to require the attendance of any presiding officer of a court except with the previous sanction of the High Court to which such court is subordinate or any officer of a revenue court except with the previous sanction of the State Government.

 B) He must be an Indian Citizen

context:
Under Section 9, the Bar Council of India is responsible for constituting disciplinary committees to investigate and punish misconduct by advocates. These committees can meet at any time and place, and must observe rules of procedure prescribed by the Bar Council of India.

Section 10B outlines the disqualification of members of a Bar Council. A member can be disqualified if they are absent without sufficient excuse from three consecutive meetings, if their name is removed from the roll of advocates, or if they are otherwise disqualified under any rule made by the Bar Council of India.

Section 11 allows every Bar Council to appoint a secretary, an accountant, and such other persons on its staff as it deems necessary. The secretary and accountant must possess qualifications prescribed by the Bar Council of India.

Under Section 12, every Bar Council must maintain books of accounts and other books in the form and manner prescribed. The accounts of a Bar Council must be audited by auditors qualified to act as auditors of companies under the Companies Act, 1956. The audited accounts must be sent to the Bar Council of India and published in the official Gazette.

Section 13 states that no act done by a Bar Council or any committee thereof shall be called in question on the ground merely of the existence of any vacancy in, or any defect in the constitution of, the Council or committee.

Section 14 states that no election of a member to a Bar Council shall be called in question on the ground merely that due notice thereof has not been given to any person entitled to vote thereat, if notice of the date has, not less than thirty days before that date, been published in the Official Gazette.

Finally, Section 15 gives the Bar Council the power to make rules to carry out the purposes of this Chapter. These rules may provide for the election of members of the Bar Council, the manner of election of the Chairman and Vice-Chairman, the filling of casual vacancies, the powers and duties of the Chairman and Vice-Chairman, the constitution of funds, the summoning and holding of meetings, the conduct of business, the qualifications and conditions of service of the secretary, the accountant and other employees, the maintenance of books of accounts, the appointment of auditors, and the management and investment of the funds of the Bar Council. No rules made under this section by a State Bar Council shall have effect unless they have been approved by the Bar Council of India.
Summary:

The Bar Council of India has the authority to transfer the name of a person from one State Bar Council roll to another, without requiring any fee. This transfer does not affect the seniority of the person in the new roll. Every State Bar Council must send an authenticated copy of their roll of advocates to the Bar Council of India and inform them of any alterations or additions made. To be admitted as an advocate on a State roll, a person must be a citizen of India, have completed the age of 21 years, hold a law degree from a recognized university or be a barrister called to the Bar before December 31, 1976, fulfill any other conditions specified by the State Bar Council, and pay the required enrolment fee. A vakil or pleader who is a law graduate can be admitted as an advocate on a State roll if they make an application within two years of the appointed day and fulfill the specified conditions. The condition must not be invalid, and the event to which it relates must be one that could legally constitute the condition of the creation of an interest.

Section 32: This section deals with transfers conditional on the performance of an act, with no time being specified for performance. The condition is broken when the person renders impossible, permanently or for an indefinite period, the performance of the act.

If the performance of the act is prevented by the fraud of a person who would be directly benefited by non-fulfilment of the condition, such further time shall be allowed for performing the act as shall be requisite to make up for the delay caused by such fraud.

Section 35: This section deals with election when necessary. Where a person professes to transfer property which he has no right to transfer, and as part of the same transaction confers any benefit on the owner of the property, such owner must elect either to confirm such transfer or to dissent from it.

Section 36: This section deals with election must be made within a reasonable time. An election made under section 35 must be made within a reasonable time.

Section 37: This section deals with the effect of dissent from transfer. Where a person dissents from a transfer made under section 35, the benefit conferred on him by such transfer becomes void.

Section 38: This section deals with the effect of confirmation of transfer. Where a person confirms a transfer made under section 35, he shall be entitled to the benefit so conferred.

Section 39: This section deals with property transferred not liable for transferor’s debts. Where a person transfers property and dies before the transferee has elected under section 35, the property shall not be liable for the transferor's debts.

Section 40: This section deals with property transferred not liable for transferee’s debts. Where a person transfers property and dies after the transferee has elected under section 35, the property shall not be liable for the transferee's debts, if the transfer was for consideration.

* Being member of unlawful assembly: A person who is aware of facts which render any assembly an unlawful assembly and intentionally joins that assembly or continues in it is said to be a member of an unlawful assembly.
* Punishment: Whoever is a member of an unlawful assembly shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.
* Joining unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapon: Whoever, being armed with any deadly weapon or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, is a member of an unlawful assembly, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

* Rioting: Whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, or by any member thereof, in prosecution of the common object of such assembly, every member of such assembly is guilty of the offence of rioting.
* Punishment for rioting: Whoever is guilty of rioting, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
* Rioting, armed with deadly weapon: Whoever is guilty of rioting, being armed with a deadly weapon or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.
* Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object: If an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object of that assembly, or such as the members of such assembly knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object, every person who, at the time of the committing of that offence, is a member of the same assembly, is guilty of that offence.

The Constitution (Thirty-Sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, removed Article 2A, forming Sikkim as a State within the Indian Union.

Article 3 of the Constitution allows Parliament to form a new State by separating territory from any State or by uniting two or more States or parts of States or by uniting any territory to a part of any State. It can increase, diminish, or alter the boundaries or name of any State, provided that no Bill for the purpose shall be introduced in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President and after the expression of views by the State Legislature, if the proposal affects the area, boundaries, or name of any of the States.

The Constitution (Fifth Amendment) Act, 1955, modified Article 3 to provide a time limit within which the State has to express their views on State reorganization laws. Personal laws (Hindu Law, Muslim Law, and Christian Law) are not part of the definition of Law under Article 13. The Bye-Laws made by the Cooperative Societies are also not part of the definition of Law. The Right to Information Act, 2005, is a law passed by the Parliament of India which gives citizens the right to access information held by public authorities. The Act defines 'public authority' as any authority or body or institution of self-government established or constituted by or under the Constitution; by any other law made by Parliament; by any other law made by State Legislature; by notification issued or order made by the appropriate Government, and includes any body owned, controlled or substantially financed; non-Government organization substantially financed, directly or indirectly by funds provided by the appropriate Government.

Under this Act, all citizens have the right to request information from any public authority, and the public authority is required to provide the information within 30 days, or within 48 hours if the information sought is related to the life or liberty of a person. However, there are certain exemptions to this right, including information that would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security, strategic, scientific or economic interests of the State, relation with foreign State or lead to incitement of an offence, information which has been expressly forbidden to be published by any Court of law or tribunal or the disclosure of which may constitute contempt of Court, information, the disclosure of which would cause a breach of privilege of Parliament or the State Legislature, information including commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property, the disclosure of which would harm the competitive position of a third party, unless the competent authority is satisfied that larger public interest warrants the disclosure of such information, information available to a person in his fiduciary relationship, unless the competent authority is satisfied that the larger public interest warrants the disclosure of such information, information received in confidence from foreign Government, information, the disclosure of which would endanger the life or physical safety of any person or identify the source of information or assistance given in confidence for law enforcement or security purposes, information which would impede the process of investigation or apprehension or prosecution of offenders, cabinet papers including records of deliberations of the Council of Ministers, Secretaries and other officers, and information which relates to personal information the disclosure of which has no relationship to any public activity or interest, or which would cause unwarranted invasion of the privacy of the individual unless the Central Public Information Officer or the State Public Information Officer or the appellate authority, as the case may be, is satisfied that the larger public interest justifies the disclosure of such information.

The Act also provides for the designation of Public Information Officers and Assistant Public Information Officers in all administrative units or offices under a public authority, who are responsible for receiving and responding to requests for information. If a request for information is transferred from one public authority to another, the period for response is extended by 5 days.

If a request for information is rejected, the public authority is required to provide reasons for the rejection, the period within which an appeal can be filed, and the particulars of the appellate authority.

The Act also provides for the establishment of a Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions, which are responsible for hearing appeals against the decisions of public authorities and for ensuring compliance with the provisions of the Act. The Commissioners are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister.

The Act also provides for penalties for non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, including fines and disciplinary action against officers who fail to provide information or who provide false or misleading information.

In summary, the Right to Information Act, 2005 is a landmark law that gives citizens the right to access information held by public authorities, subject to certain exemptions. The Act establishes a framework for the designation of Public Information Officers and Assistant Public Information Officers, and provides for the establishment of Central and State Information Commissions to hear appeals and ensure compliance with the provisions of the Act. The Act also provides for penalties for non-compliance, and seeks to promote transparency and accountability in the functioning of public authorities.

The Order lays down the rules for the attendance of parties in court on the day fixed for the defendant to appear and answer, and the consequences of non-appearance by either party.

Rule 1 states that parties to a suit must appear in court on the day fixed for the defendant to appear and answer. Failure to appear may result in the dismissal of the suit.

Rule 4 provides that where a suit is dismissed under Rule 2 or Rule 3, the plaintiff may (subject to the law of limitation) bring a fresh suit or apply for an order to set aside the dismissal. If the plaintiff satisfies the court that there was sufficient cause for his non-appearance, the court shall set aside the dismissal and appoint a day for proceeding with the suit.

The Securities Contracts (Regulation) (Procedure for Holding Inquiry and Imposing Penalties) Rules, 2005, provide the procedure for holding an inquiry and imposing penalties under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956. These rules apply to the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and any officer appointed by SEBI as an adjudicating officer for holding an inquiry.

Under these rules, SEBI may initiate an inquiry against any person who has committed contraventions under sections 23-A, 23-B, 23-C, 23-D, 23-E, 23-F, 23-G, and 23-H of the Act. The inquiry process begins with the issuance of a show-cause notice to the person, requiring them to show cause why an inquiry should not be held against them. The notice must indicate the nature of the offence alleged to have been committed by the person.

If, after considering the cause shown by the person, SEBI or the adjudicating officer is of the opinion that an inquiry should be held, a notice fixing a date for the appearance of the person either personally or through their lawyer or authorized representative is issued. On the date fixed, the adjudicating officer explains the offence alleged to have been committed by the person and gives them an opportunity to produce documents or evidence relevant to the inquiry. The adjudicating officer is not bound to observe the provisions of the Evidence Act, 1872, while taking evidence.

While holding an inquiry under these rules, the adjudicating officer has the power to summon and enforce the attendance of any person acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case to give evidence or to produce any document which may be useful for or relevant to the subject-matter of the inquiry. If any person fails to appear before the adjudicating officer, the inquiry may proceed in their absence after recording the reasons for doing so.

Upon consideration of the evidence produced before the adjudicating officer, if SEBI or the adjudicating officer is satisfied that the person has become liable to penalty under any of the sections specified in sub-section (1) of section 23-I of the Act, they may impose such penalty as they think fit in accordance with the provisions of the relevant section or sections specified in section 23-I of the Act.

While adjudging the quantum of penalty, the adjudicating officer shall have due regard to the amount of disproportionate gain or unfair advantage, wherever quantifiable, made as a result of the default, the amount of loss caused to an investor or group of investors as a result of the default, and the repetitive nature of the default. The order imposing penalty shall specify the provisions of the Act in respect of which default has taken place and shall contain brief reasons for such decision.

A notice or an order issued under these rules shall be served on the person in the manner specified in rule 7, which includes delivering or tendering it to the person or their duly authorized agent, sending it by fax or electronic mail or by courier or speed post with acknowledge due or registered post with acknowledgement due to the address of their place of residence or their last known place of residence or the place where they carried on, or last carried on, business or personally works, or last worked, for gain. If it cannot be served in any of these ways, it may be affixed on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the premises in which the person resides or is known to have last resided, or carried on business or personally works or last worked for gain, and a written report thereof should be witnessed by two persons. If it cannot be affixed on the outer door, it may be published in at least two newspapers, one in an English daily newspaper having nationwide circulation, and another in a newspaper having wide circulation published in the language of the region where the person was last known to have resided or carried on business or personally worked for gain.

Under Section 101, if a will purports to make two bequests to the same person, and a question arises whether the testator intended to make the second bequest instead of or in addition to the first, the following rules shall have effect in determining the construction to be put upon the will: (a) If the same specific thing is bequeathed twice to the same legatee in the same will or in the will and again in the codicil, he is entitled to receive that specific thing only; (b) Where one and the same will or one and the same codicil purports to make, in two places, a bequest to the same person of the same quantity or amount of anything, he shall be entitled to one such legacy only; (c) Where two legacies of unequal amount are given to the same person in the same will, or in the same codicil, the legatee is entitled to both; (d) Where two legacies, whether equal or unequal in amount, are given to the same legatee, one by a will and the other by a codicil, or each by a different codicil, the legatee is entitled to both legacies.

Under Section 102, a residuary legatee may be constituted by any words that show an intention on the part of the testator that the person designated shall take the surplus or residue of his property.

Under Section 103, under a residuary bequest, the legatee is entitled to all property belonging to the testator at the time of his death, of which he has not made any other testamentary disposition which is capable of taking effect.

Under Section 104, if a legacy is given in general terms, without specifying the time when it is to be paid, the legatee has a vested interest in it from the day of the death of the testator, and, if he dies without having received it, it shall pass to his representatives.

Under Section 105, if the legatee does not survive the testator, the legacy cannot take effect, but shall lapse and form part of the residue of the testator’s property, unless it appears by the Will that the testator intended that it should go to some other person.

Under Section 106, if a legacy is given to two persons jointly, and one of them dies before the testator, the other legatee takes the whole.

Under Section 107, if a legacy is given to legatees in words which show that the testator intended to give them distinct shares of it, then, if any legatee dies before the testator, so much of the legacy as was intended for him shall fall into the residue of the testator's property.

The document summarizes various sections of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, specifically focusing on laws related to lapsed shares, void bequests, and the rule against perpetuity.

Section 106 explains that a lapsed share in a Will goes as undisposed of, meaning it becomes part of the general residue bequeathed by the Will. This applies to shares that lapse and are part of the general residue.

Section 107 states that a bequest to a child or lineal descendant of the testator does not lapse if the legatee dies in the testator's lifetime, as long as a lineal descendant of the legatee survives the testator and no contrary intention appears in the Will.

Section 108 explains that when a share which lapses is a part of the general residue bequeathed by the Will, it shall go as undisposed of.

Section 109 states that a bequest to a person for the benefit of another does not lapse by the death, in the testator’s lifetime, of the person to whom the bequest is made.

Section 110 explains the survivorship rule in case of a bequest to a described class. If a bequest is made simply to a described class of persons, the thing bequeathed shall go only to such as are alive at the testator’s death. However, if property is bequeathed to a class of persons described as standing in a particular degree of kindred to a specified individual, but their possession of it is deferred until a time later than the death of the testator, the property shall at that time go to such of them as are then alive, and to the representatives of any of them who have died since the death of the testator.

Section 112 states that where a bequest is made to a person by a particular description, and there is no person in existence at the testator's death who answers the description, the bequest is void.

Section 113 explains that where a bequest is made to a person not in existence at the time of the testator's death, subject to a prior bequest contained in the will, the later bequest shall be void, unless it comprises the whole of the remaining interest of the testator in the thing bequeathed.

Section 114 explains the rule against perpetuity, which states that no interest is good unless it must vest, if at all, not later than twenty-one years after some life in being at the creation of the interest.

Chapter VI, titled "Product Liability," details the rules for product liability actions. This chapter applies to any claim for compensation for harm caused by a defective product manufactured by a product manufacturer, serviced by a product service provider, or sold by a product seller (Section 82). A product liability action can be brought by a complainant against any of these parties for harm caused by a defective product (Section 83).

A product manufacturer can be held liable for a product liability action if the product contains a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, has a deviation from manufacturing specifications, does not conform to the express warranty, or fails to contain adequate instructions or correct usage to prevent harm (Section 84). A product seller who is not a product manufacturer can be held liable for a product liability action if they exercised substantial control over the design, testing, manufacturing, packaging, or labeling of a product that caused harm, altered or modified the product and such alteration or modification was the substantial factor in causing the harm, made an express warranty of a product independent of any express warranty made by a manufacturer and such product failed to conform to the express warranty made by the product seller which caused the harm, sold the product and the identity of the product manufacturer is not known, or if known, the service of notice or process or warrant cannot be effected on them or they are not subject to the law in force in India, or the order passed or to be passed cannot be enforced against them, or failed to exercise reasonable care in assembling, inspecting, or maintaining such product or they did not pass on the warnings or instructions of the product manufacturer regarding the dangers involved or proper usage of the product while selling such product and such failure was the proximate cause of the harm (Section 86).
