context:
The Indian Evidence Act of 1872 outlines the rules for the admission of evidence in legal proceedings in India. The Act defines an admission as a statement made by a party or their agent that suggests any inference as to a fact in issue or a relevant fact. Admissions can be made orally, in writing, or electronically. Admissions made by parties to a proceeding, or their agents, are admissible as evidence. Admissions made by parties in a representative capacity, such as a suitor, are admissible if made while they held that character. Admissions made by parties interested in the subject matter or persons from whom they have derived their interest are admissible if made during the continuance of their interest. Statements made by persons whose position or liability must be proved in the suit are admissions if made while they occupy that position or are subject to that liability. Statements made by persons to whom a party has expressly referred for information are also admissions. Admissions can be proved by or on behalf of the person making them in certain circumstances, such as if the statement is of a nature that would be relevant if the person were dead, or if it is relevant otherwise than as an admission. Oral admissions as to the contents of a document are not relevant unless the party proposing to prove them shows that they are entitled to give secondary evidence of the contents of the document or if the genuineness of the document is in question. In civil cases, no admission is relevant if it is made on the condition that evidence of it is not to be given or if the parties agreed that evidence of it should not be given. Confessions caused by inducement, threat, or promise are irrelevant in criminal proceedings. Confessions made to a police officer cannot be proved as against a person accused of an offense. Confessions made while a person is in the custody of a police officer, unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, are not admissible as evidence against them. However, if a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of an offense, so much of such information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered may be proved. A confession made after the removal of the impression caused by any such inducement, threat, or promise is relevant. A confession is not rendered inadmissible merely because it was made under a promise of secrecy or in consequence of a deception practiced on the accused.

Section 27: Confessions made to a police officer not to be proved

Under Section 27, confessions made to a police officer are not admissible as evidence against the person making the confession. This provision is meant to protect individuals from being coerced into confessing to a crime by the police.

Section 28: Confessions made by accused in presence of police officer

Similarly, confessions made by an accused person in the presence of a police officer, but not in the immediate presence of a magistrate, are also not admissible as evidence. This provision is intended to ensure that confessions are made voluntarily and without any pressure from the police.

Section 29: Confessions to be proved by persons who heard them made

However, if a confession is made in the immediate presence of a magistrate, it can be used as evidence against the person making the confession. Such confessions must be proved by the persons who heard them made.

Section 30: Consideration of proved confession affecting person making it and others jointly under trial for same offence

Under Section 30, if more than one person is being tried jointly for the same offence, and a confession made by one of them affects both themselves and the other accused, the court may take the confession into consideration as evidence against the other accused as well.

Section 31: Admissions not conclusive proof, but may estop

Under Section 31, admissions made by a person are not conclusive proof of the facts admitted, but they may be used to prevent the person from denying those facts in a later proceeding. This provision is intended to prevent people from making inconsistent statements in different proceedings.

Section 280 deals with record in absence of accused. Whenever any evidence is given in the absence of the accused, it shall be taken down in writing and shall, at the commencement of the next sitting of the Court, be read over to the accused and shall be open to correction by him.

Section 281 deals with record in absence of pleader. Whenever any evidence is given in the absence of the pleader of the accused, it shall be taken down in writing and shall, at the commencement of the next sitting of the Court, be read over to such pleader and shall be open to correction by him.

Section 282 deals with record of statements under section 164. Whenever any person makes a statement under section 164, the Magistrate shall record it in the manner provided in that section and shall furnish a copy thereof to the person making the statement and to the accused.

Section 283 deals with record of confessions and statements. Any confession or statement made by any person to a police officer or any person in authority shall be recorded in the manner provided in sections 164 and 281 and shall be open to correction by the person making the confession or statement.

Section 284 deals with commission for examination of witness in prison. The provisions of this Chapter shall be without prejudice to the power of the Court to issue, under this section, a commission for the examination, as a witness, of any person confined or detained in a prison. The provisions of Part B of Chapter XXIII shall apply in relation to the examination on commission of any such person in the prison as they apply in relation to the examination on commission of any other person.

Section 285 deals with evidence on commission to be given orally. Any person examined on commission shall, if so required by the Court, give his evidence orally in open Court.

Section 286 deals with evidence on commission to be reduced to writing. Any person examined on commission may, if he so desires, give his evidence in writing, and the Court may, if it thinks fit, permit him to dictate his evidence.

Section 287 deals with deposit of commission. The commission shall be deposited in the office of the Court which issued it, within the time mentioned in the warrant for its issue, or within such further time as the Court may, for sufficient reasons, allow.

Section 288 deals with failure to comply with commission. If any person to whom a commission is issued does not attend to comply with the terms of the commission, he shall be deemed to have committed a contempt of the Court which issued the commission.

Section 289 deals with evidence taken in pursuance of commission. Any evidence taken in pursuance of a commission shall be reduced to writing and shall be authenticated by the person appointed to take the same, and shall be filed with the record of the case.

Section 290 deals with evidence taken in pursuance of commission to be read in open Court. Any evidence taken in pursuance of a commission shall, at the trial, be read in open Court, unless the Court, for sufficient reasons, directs otherwise.

Section 291 deals with evidence taken in pursuance of commission to be open to inspection. Any evidence taken in pursuance of a commission shall be open to inspection by the parties, and such inspection shall be given in the presence of the Judge.

Section 292 deals with evidence taken in pursuance of commission to be filed. Any evidence taken in pursuance of a commission shall be filed with the record of the case, unless the Court, for sufficient reasons, directs otherwise.

Section 293 deals with evidence taken in pursuance of commission to be evidence in the case. Any evidence taken in pursuance of a commission shall be evidence in the case in which the commission was issued.

Section 294 deals with evidence taken in pursuance of commission to be conclusive proof. Any evidence taken in pursuance of a commission shall be conclusive proof of the facts which it states, unless the Court, for sufficient reasons, directs otherwise.

Section 295 deals with evidence taken in pursuance of commission to be conclusive proof of documents. Any document purporting to be a copy of any evidence taken in pursuance of a commission shall be admitted in evidence and shall, unless the Court, for sufficient reasons, directs otherwise, be deemed to be a true copy of such evidence.

Section 296 deals with evidence taken in pursuance of commission to be conclusive proof of signature. Any document purporting to bear the signature or seal of any person examined in pursuance of a commission shall be admitted in evidence and shall, unless the Court, for sufficient reasons, directs otherwise, be deemed to have been signed or sealed by such person.

The Act defines various terms related to the handling of hazardous substances, including "accident," "handling," "hazardous substance," "insurance," "notification," "owner," "prescribed," "Relief Fund," "rules," and "vehicle."

The Act imposes a liability on the owner to give relief in certain cases on the principle of no fault in case of death or injury to any person or damage to any property resulting from an accident involving a hazardous substance. The owner is not required to plead and establish that the death, injury, or damage was due to any wrongful act, neglect, or default of any person. The amount of relief is specified in the Schedule and is payable by the insurer, up to a maximum amount of fifty crore rupees, and the insurer is also required to pay a further amount, not exceeding the sum equivalent to the amount of premium, to the Relief Fund established under section 7A.

Every owner is required to take out one or more insurance policies providing for contracts of insurance whereby he is insured against liability to give relief under sub-section (1) of section 3. The insurance policy must be renewed from time to time before the expiry of the period of validity and the liability of the insurer under one assurance policy shall not exceed the amount specified in the terms of the contract of insurance in that insurance policy. The Central Government may exempt certain owners from the operation of sub-section (1) if a fund has been established and is maintained by that owner for meeting any liability under sub-section (1) of section 3.

The Collector is required to verify the occurrence of an accident and cause publicity to be given for inviting applications for claim for relief. The Collector is required to hold an inquiry into the claim and make an award determining the amount of relief which appears to him to be just and specifying the person or persons to whom such amount of relief shall be paid. The Collector shall arrange to deliver copies of the award to the parties concerned expeditiously and in any case within a period of fifteen days from the date of the award.

THE DISTURBED AREAS (SPECIAL COURTS) ACT, 1976, is an Act that aims to provide for the speedy trial of certain offences committed in disturbed areas. The Act defines key terms such as "Code," "disturbed area," "period of disturbance," "scheduled offence," "Special Court," and refers to the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for the meaning of other undefined terms.

Under Section 3, the State Government may declare an area as a disturbed area if there is extensive disturbance of public peace and tranquility due to differences or disputes between members of different religious, racial, language, regional groups, castes, or communities. The State Government may specify the period during which the area shall be a disturbed area, and such period may be extended if necessary.

Section 4 deals with the constitution of Special Courts, which may be constituted by the State Government for the purpose of providing speedy trial of scheduled offences committed in disturbed areas. A Special Court shall consist of a single judge appointed by the High Court upon a request made by the State Government. A person shall not be qualified for appointment as a judge of a Special Court unless they are qualified for appointment as a judge of a High Court or have been a Sessions Judge or an Additional Sessions Judge for at least one year.

Section 5 states that a scheduled offence committed in any disturbed area during the period of disturbance shall be triable only by the Special Court constituted in or in relation to the disturbed area in which the offence has been committed. When trying any scheduled offence, a Special Court may also try any offence other than the scheduled offence with which the accused may be charged at the same trial if the offence is connected with the scheduled offence.

Section 6 deals with the procedure and powers of Special Courts. Every scheduled offence shall be cognizable, and a Special Court may take cognizance of any scheduled offence upon its being committed to it under section 209 of the Code or upon a police report of the facts together with a certificate from the public prosecutor. Where a scheduled offence is an offence triable exclusively by a Court of Session under the Code, a Special Court shall have all the powers of a Court of Session and shall try such offence as if it were a Court of Session.

Section 7 deals with the power to transfer cases to regular courts. Where, after taking cognizance of any offence, a Special Court is of opinion that the offence is not a scheduled offence, it shall transfer the case for trial to any court having jurisdiction under the Code.

Section 8 deals with appeal and revision, and the High Court may exercise all the powers conferred by Chapters XXIX and XXX of the Code on a High Court, as if a Special Court is a Court of Session trying cases within the local limits of the jurisdiction of the High Court.

Section 9 states that the provisions of this Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in the Code or any other law, but save as expressly provided in this Act, the provisions of the Code shall apply to the proceedings before a Special Court.

The Schedule to the Act lists the scheduled offences under various provisions of the Indian Penal Code, the Arms Act, and the Indian Explosives Act.

The Act applies to the whole of India, except the State of Jammu and Kashmir, and came into force on 15th August 1976.

The Indian Workmen's Compensation Act of 1923 outlines the responsibilities of employers and contractors in the event of an employee's injury or death. Under the Act, an employer is liable to pay compensation to an employee who suffers an injury in the course of their employment, with the amount of compensation determined by the employee's wages. If the principal is liable to pay compensation, they may be indemnified by the contractor or any other person from whom the employee could have recovered compensation. An employee may also recover compensation from the contractor instead of the principal. This section does not apply if the accident occurred elsewhere than on, in or about the premises on which the principal has undertaken or usually undertakes to execute the work.

If an employee has recovered compensation in respect of any injury caused under circumstances creating a legal liability of some person other than the person by whom the compensation was paid to pay damages in respect thereof, the person by whom the compensation was paid and any person who has been called on to pay an indemnity under section 12 shall be entitled to be indemnified by the person so liable to pay damages as aforesaid.

If an employer has entered into a contract with insurers in respect of any liability under this Act to any employee and becomes insolvent, the rights of the employer against the insurers as respects that liability shall be transferred to and vest in the employee. The insurers shall have the same rights and remedies and be subject to the same liabilities as if they were the employer, so, however, that the insurers shall not be under any greater liability to the employee than they would have been under to the employer.

Where an employer transfers his assets before any amount due in respect of any compensation, the liability where for accrued before the date of the transfer, has been paid, such amount shall be a first charge on that part of the assets so transferred as consists of immovable property.

This Act shall apply in the case of employees who are masters of ships or seamen subject to certain modifications. The notice of the accident and the claim for compensation may be served on the master of the ship as if he were the employer, but where the accident happened and the disablement commenced on board the ship it shall not be necessary for any seaman to give any notice of the accident. In the case of the death of a master or seaman, the claim for compensation shall be made within one year after the news of the death has been received by the claimant or, where the ship has been or is deemed to have been lost with all hands, within eighteen months of the date on which the ship was, or is deemed to have been, so lost.

The Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923, applies to employees who are captains or other members of the crew of aircrafts, with certain modifications. Notice of an accident and claim for compensation may be served on the captain of the aircraft as if he were the employer, but where the accident happened and the disablement commenced on board the aircraft, it is not necessary for any member of the crew to give notice of the accident. In the case of the death of the captain or other member of the crew, the claim for compensation must be made within one year after the news of the death has been received by the claimant. Where an injured captain or other member of the crew is discharged or left behind in any part of India or in any other country, any depositions taken by any Judge or Magistrate in that part, or by any Consular Officer in the foreign country, and transmitted by the person by whom they are taken to the Central Government or any State Government, shall be admissible in evidence.

The Act also applies to employees who are persons recruited by companies registered in India and working as such abroad, and persons sent for work abroad along with motor vehicles registered under the Motor Vehicles, Act, 1988 as drivers, helpers, mechanics, cleaners or other employees. The notice of the accident and the claim for compensation may be served on the local agent of the company, or the local agent of the owner of the motor vehicle, in the country of accident. In the case of death of the employee in respect of whom the provisions of this section shall apply, the claim for compensation shall be made within one year after the news of the death has been received by the claimant. THE CIVIL LIABILITY FOR NUCLEAR DAMAGE ACT, 2010

This Act establishes a no-fault liability regime for nuclear damage, with the operator being liable for compensation to victims. The Act applies to nuclear incidents occurring in or over the maritime areas beyond the territorial waters of India, in the exclusive economic zone of India, on board or by a ship or aircraft registered in India, or on or by an artificial island, installation, or structure under the jurisdiction of India. The Act applies only to nuclear installations owned or controlled by the Central Government.

The Act defines various terms, including "nuclear damage," "nuclear fuel," "nuclear reactor," "operator," and "preventive measures." The operator is liable for nuclear damage caused by a nuclear incident occurring in or involving nuclear material coming from the nuclear installation. The liability of the operator is strict and based on the principle of no-fault liability.

The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board is required to notify a nuclear incident within 15 days of its occurrence. The operator is liable for nuclear damage caused by a nuclear incident directly due to a grave natural disaster or an act of armed conflict, hostility, civil war, insurrection, or terrorism. The operator is not liable for nuclear damage caused to the nuclear installation itself, to property on the same site used in connection with the installation, or to the means of transport upon which the nuclear material involved was carried at the time of the nuclear incident.

The maximum amount of liability for each nuclear incident is the rupee equivalent of three hundred million Special Drawing Rights or such higher amount as the Central Government may specify by notification. The liability of an operator for each nuclear incident is rupees one thousand five hundred crores in respect of nuclear reactors having thermal power equal to or above ten MW, rupees three hundred crores in respect of spent fuel reprocessing plants, and rupees one hundred crores in respect of the research reactors having thermal power below ten MW, fuel cycle facilities other than spent fuel reprocessing plants, and transportation of nuclear materials. The Central Government may review the amount of operator's liability from time to time and specify a higher amount.

The Central Government may establish a fund called the Nuclear Liability Fund to meet part of its liability under clause (a) or clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 7. The operator is required to take out insurance policy or such other financial security or combination of both, covering his liability under sub-section (2) of section 6.

For the purposes of adjudicating upon claims for compensation, the Central Government shall appoint one or more Claims Commissioners for such area as may be specified in that notification. A person is not qualified for appointment as a Claims Commissioner unless he is, or has been, a District Judge or in the service of the Central Government and has held the post not below the rank of Additional Secretary to the Government of India or any other equivalent post in the Central Government. The salary and allowances payable to and other terms and conditions of service of Claims Commissioner shall be such as may be prescribed.

An application for compensation may be made by a person who has sustained injury, the owner of the property to which damage has been caused, the legal representatives of the deceased, or any agent duly authorized by such person or owner or legal representatives. Every application for compensation before the Claims Commissioner shall be made in such form, containing such particulars and accompanied by such documents, as may be prescribed. The Claims Commissioner shall, after giving notice of such application to the operator and affording an opportunity of being heard to the parties, dispose of the application within a period of three months from the date of such receipt and make an award accordingly. The Claims Commissioner shall not take into consideration any benefit, reimbursement, or amount received by the applicant in pursuance of contract of insurance taken by him or for members of his family or otherwise.

The operator has a right of recourse where such right is expressly provided for in a contract in writing, the nuclear incident has resulted as a consequence of an act of supplier or his employee, or the nuclear incident has resulted from the act of commission or omission of an individual done with the intent to cause nuclear damage.

The right to claim compensation for nuclear damage shall extinguish if such claim is not made within a period of ten years in the case of damage to property or twenty years in the case of personal injury to any person from the date of occurrence of the incident notified under sub-section (1) of section 3.

The Act removed property as a fundamental right, making it only a legal right. It also strengthened the provisions related to the proclamation of an emergency, requiring the approval of Parliament and a majority of the electorate in a referendum for certain changes to the Constitution. Additionally, the Act provided safeguards against the misuse of emergency provisions, ensured the right to life and liberty, and guaranteed the right of the media to report freely and without censorship the proceedings in Parliament and the State Legislatures. The Act also aimed to remove or correct the distortions that came into the Constitution during the period of the Internal Emergency.

* Unlawful assembly: An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly” if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is to overawe by criminal force or show of criminal force, resist the execution of any law or of any legal process, commit any mischief or criminal trespass or other offence, by means of criminal force or show of criminal force to any person, take or obtain possession of any property, deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, use of water or other incorporeal right of which he is in possession or enjoyment, or to enforce any right or supposed right, or by means of criminal force or show of criminal force, compel any person to do what he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do.
* Being member of unlawful assembly: A person who is aware of facts which render any assembly an unlawful assembly and intentionally joins that assembly or continues in it is said to be a member of an unlawful assembly.
* Punishment: Whoever is a member of an unlawful assembly shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.
* Joining unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapon: Whoever, being armed with any deadly weapon or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, is a member of an unlawful assembly, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, is an Act that defines and limits the powers of certain courts in punishing contempts of courts and regulates their procedure in relation thereto. The Act extends to the whole of India. Contempt of court is defined as civil contempt or criminal contempt, with civil contempt meaning wilful disobedience to any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ or other process of a court or wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court. Criminal contempt includes the publication (whether by words, spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representations, or otherwise) of any matter or the doing of any other act whatsoever which scandalises or tends to scandalise, or lowers or tends to lower the authority of, any court; prejudices, or interferes or tends to interfere with, the due course of any judicial proceeding; or interferes or tends to interfere with, or obstructs or tends to obstruct, the administration of justice in any other manner. A person shall not be guilty of contempt of court on the ground that he has published (whether by words, spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representations, or otherwise) any matter which interferes or tends to interfere with, or obstructs or tends to obstruct, the course of justice in connection with any civil or criminal proceeding pending at that time of publication, if at that time he had no reasonable grounds for believing that the proceeding was pending. The publication of any such matter in connection with any civil or criminal proceeding which is not pending at the time of publication shall not be deemed to constitute contempt of court. A person shall not be guilty of contempt of court on the ground that he has distributed a publication containing any such matter as is mentioned in sub-section (1), if at the time of distribution he had no reasonable grounds for believing that it contained or was likely to contain any such matter as aforesaid. The Act also includes provisions for the punishment of contempt of court, with the punishment for contempt being simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to two thousand rupees, or with both. Under Section 104, if a legacy is given in general terms, without specifying the time when it is to be paid, the legatee has a vested interest in it from the day of the death of the testator, and, if he dies without having received it, it shall pass to his representatives.

Under Section 106, if a legacy is given to two persons jointly, and one of them dies before the testator, the other legatee takes the whole.

Under Section 107, if a legacy is given to legatees in words which show that the testator intended to give them distinct shares of it, then, if any legatee dies before the testator, so much of the legacy as was intended for him shall fall into the residue of the testator's property.

The Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen. Promises bind the representatives of the promisors in case of the death of such promisors before performance, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If a promisor has made an offer of performance to the promisee, and the offer has not been accepted, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance, nor does he thereby lose his rights under the contract. Every such offer must fulfill certain conditions, such as being unconditional, made at a proper time and place, and under such circumstances that the person to whom it is made may have a reasonable opportunity of ascertaining that the person by whom it is made is able and willing there and then to do the whole of what he is bound by his promise to do. Under Part II, Chapter V on cancellation of instruments, the Act states that any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, and who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable, and the court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled.

The Indian Evidence Act of 1872 outlines the rules for the admission of evidence in legal proceedings in India. The Act defines an admission as a statement made by a party or their agent that suggests any inference as to a fact in issue or a relevant fact. Admissions can be made orally, in writing, or electronically. Admissions made by parties to a proceeding, or their agents, are admissible as evidence. Admissions made by parties in a representative capacity, such as a suitor, are admissible if made while they held that character. Admissions made by parties interested in the subject matter or persons from whom they have derived their interest are admissible if made during the continuance of their interest. Statements made by persons whose position or liability must be proved in the suit are admissions if made while they occupy that position or are subject to that liability. Statements made by persons to whom a party has expressly referred for information are also admissions. Admissions can be proved by or on behalf of the person making them in certain circumstances, such as if the statement is of a nature that would be relevant if the person were dead, or if it is relevant otherwise than as an admission. Oral admissions as to the contents of a document are not relevant unless the party proposing to prove them shows that they are entitled to give secondary evidence of the contents of the document or if the genuineness of the document is in question. In civil cases, no admission is relevant if it is made on the condition that evidence of it is not to be given or if the parties agreed that evidence of it should not be given. Confessions caused by inducement, threat, or promise are irrelevant in criminal proceedings. Confessions made to a police officer cannot be proved as against a person accused of an offense. Confessions made while a person is in the custody of a police officer, unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, are not admissible as evidence against them. However, if a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of an offense, so much of such information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered may be proved. A confession made after the removal of the impression caused by any such inducement, threat, or promise is relevant. A confession is not rendered inadmissible merely because it was made under a promise of secrecy or in consequence of a deception practiced on the accused.

In relation to offenses against public tranquility, the following offenses are described:

* Unlawful assembly: An assembly of five or more persons is designated an “unlawful assembly” if the common object of the persons composing that assembly is to overawe by criminal force or show of criminal force, resist the execution of any law or of any legal process, commit any mischief or criminal trespass or other offence, by means of criminal force or show of criminal force to any person, take or obtain possession of any property, deprive any person of the enjoyment of a right of way, use of water or other incorporeal right of which he is in possession or enjoyment, or to enforce any right or supposed right, or by means of criminal force or show of criminal force, compel any person to do what he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do what he is legally entitled to do.
* Being member of unlawful assembly: A person who is aware of facts which render any assembly an unlawful assembly and intentionally joins that assembly or continues in it is said to be a member of an unlawful assembly.
* Punishment: Whoever is a member of an unlawful assembly shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.
* Joining unlawful assembly armed with deadly weapon: Whoever, being armed with any deadly weapon or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death, is a member of an unlawful assembly, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
* Joining or continuing in unlawful assembly, knowing it has been commanded to disperse: Whoever joins or continues in an unlawful assembly, knowing that such unlawful assembly has been commanded in the manner prescribed by law to disperse, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
* Rioting: Whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly, or by any member thereof, in prosecution of the common object of such assembly, every member of such assembly is guilty of the offence of rioting.

Prisoners of war accused of an offence against discipline shall not be kept in confinement pending the hearing unless a member of the armed forces of the Detaining Power would be so kept if he were accused of a similar offence, or if it is essential in the interests of camp order and discipline. Any period spent by a prisoner of war in confinement awaiting the disposal of an offence against discipline shall be reduced to an absolute minimum and shall not exceed fourteen days.

Acts which constitute offences against discipline shall be investigated immediately. Disciplinary punishment may be ordered only by an officer having disciplinary powers in his capacity as camp commander, or by a responsible officer who replaces him or to whom he has delegated his disciplinary powers. In no case may such powers be delegated to a prisoner of war or be exercised by a prisoner of war.

Before any disciplinary award is pronounced, the accused shall be given precise information regarding the offences of which he is accused, and given an opportunity of explaining his conduct and of defending himself. He shall be permitted, in particular, to call witnesses and to have recourse, if necessary, to the services of a qualified interpreter. The decision shall be announced to the accused prisoner of war and to the prisoners' representative.

A record of disciplinary punishments shall be maintained by the camp commander and shall be open to inspection by representatives of the Protecting Power. Prisoners of war undergoing confinement as a disciplinary punishment shall continue to enjoy the benefits of the provisions of this Convention except in so far as these are necessarily rendered inapplicable by the mere fact that he is confined. In no case may he be deprived of the benefits of the provisions of Articles 78 and 126.

Prisoners of war awarded disciplinary punishment may not be deprived of the prerogatives attached to his rank. Prisoners of war awarded disciplinary punishment shall be allowed to exercise and to stay in the open air at least two hours daily. They shall be allowed, on their request, to be present at the daily medical inspections. They shall receive the attention which their state of health requires and, if necessary, shall be removed to the camp infirmary or to a hospital. They shall have permission to read and write, likewise to send and receive letters. Parcels and remittances of money however, may be withheld from them until the completion of the punishment; they shall meanwhile be entrusted to the prisoners' representative, who will hand over to the infirmary the perishable goods contained in such parcels.

Prisoners of war who have served disciplinary or judicial sentences may not be treated differently from other prisoners of war. Women prisoners of war undergoing disciplinary punishment shall be confined in separate quarters from male prisoners of war and shall be under the immediate supervision of women.

No moral or physical coercion may be exerted on a POW to admit guilt, and a POW cannot be convicted without having had an opportunity to present their defense and the assistance of a qualified advocate or counsel.

THE COMMISSIONS OF INQUIRY ACT, 1952 is an Act that provides for the appointment of Commissions of Inquiry and vests them with certain powers. The Act is applicable to the whole of India and came into force on a date appointed by the Central Government. The Act defines "appropriate Government" as the Central Government for matters related to List I, II, or III in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, and the State Government for matters related to List II or III in the Seventh Schedule.

The Act empowers the appropriate Government to appoint a Commission of Inquiry for the purpose of making an inquiry into any definite matter of public importance. The Commission may consist of one or more members, with one member appointed as the Chairman. The appropriate Government may fill any vacancy that may arise in the office of a member of the Commission. The appropriate Government shall cause to be laid before each House of Parliament or the Legislature of the State, the report of the Commission on the inquiry made by the Commission together with a memorandum of the action taken thereon, within a period of six months of the submission of the report by the Commission to the appropriate Government.

The Commission has the powers of a civil court while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, in respect of summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person, requiring the discovery and production of any document, receiving evidence on affidavits, requisitioning any public record or copy thereof from any court or office, issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents, and any other matter which may be prescribed.

The appropriate Government may direct that all or any of the provisions of sections 5(2), 5(3), 5(4), or 5(5) should be made applicable to a Commission. The Commission has the power to require any person to furnish information on points or matters relevant to the subject matter of the inquiry, and any person so required is deemed to be legally bound to furnish such information.

The Commission or any officer authorized by the Commission may enter any building or place where the Commission has reason to believe that any books of account or other documents relating to the subject matter of the inquiry may be found, and may seize any books of account or documents or take extracts or copies therefrom.

The Commission is deemed to be a civil court, and when any offence is committed in the view or presence of the Commission, the Commission may forward the case to a magistrate having jurisdiction to try the same. Any proceeding before the Commission is deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860).

The Commission may utilize the services of any officer or investigation agency of the Central Government or any State Government for conducting any investigation pertaining to the inquiry. The officer or agency whose services are utilized shall investigate into any matter pertaining to the inquiry and submit a report thereon to the Commission within a period specified by the Commission.

The Commission may appoint persons having special knowledge of any matter connected with the inquiry as assessors to assist and advise the Commission in the inquiry. No statement made by a person in the course of giving evidence before the Commission shall subject him to, or be used against him in, any civil or criminal proceeding except a prosecution for giving false evidence by such statement.

Except in cases where a Commission is expressly required to inquire into the process of manufacture of any goods, nothing in this Act shall be deemed to compel any person giving evidence before the Commission to disclose any secret process of manufacture thereof.

The appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare that a Commission shall cease to exist if it is of opinion that the continued existence of the Commission is unnecessary. If a resolution for the discontinuance of the Commission is passed by each House of Parliament or the Legislature of the State, the Commission shall cease to exist. Every notification issued under sub-section (1) shall specify the date from which the Commission shall cease to exist.

The Commission shall have power to regulate its own procedure, including the fixing of places and times of its sittings and deciding whether to sit in public or in private. If, at any stage of the inquiry, the Commission considers it necessary to inquire into the conduct of any person or is of opinion that the reputation of any person is likely to be prejudicially affected by the inquiry, the Commission shall give to that person a reasonable opportunity of being heard in the inquiry and to produce evidence in his defense.
The State Commission consists of a President and not less than four or not more than such number of members as may be prescribed in consultation with the Central Government. The Central Government is responsible for making rules regarding the qualifications, method of recruitment, procedure of appointment, term of office, resignation, and removal of the President and members of the State Commission. Similarly, the State Government is responsible for making rules regarding the salaries, allowances, and other terms and conditions of service of the President and members of the State Commission.

The officers and employees required to assist the State Commission in the discharge of its functions are determined and provided by the State Government. The officers and employees of the State Commission discharge their functions under the general superintendence of the President.

The State Commission has the power to review any of its orders if there is an error apparent on the face of the record, either of its own motion or on an application made by any of the parties within thirty days of such order. Any person aggrieved by an order made by the State Commission may prefer an appeal to the National Commission within a period of thirty days from the date of the order.

The National Commission is responsible for hearing appeals from orders passed by the State Commission. It consists of a President and not less than four and not more than such number of members as may be prescribed. The National Commission may formulate a substantial question of law involved in any case and hear the appeal on that question. An appeal may lie to the National Commission under this section from an order passed ex parte by the State Commission.

The National Commission shall ordinarily function at the National Capital Region and perform its functions at such other places as the Central Government may in consultation with the National Commission notify in the Official Gazette. The Central Government may, by notification, establish regional Benches of the National Commission, at such places, as it deems fit.

The National Commission has jurisdiction over consumer disputes involving a consideration of at least ten crore rupees, unfair contracts with a consideration of at least ten crore rupees, appeals against orders of State Commissions or the Central Authority, and cases where a State Commission has exercised jurisdiction not vested in it or has failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it. The case of Ors. vs State of Punjab and Anrs. (1967) established that an amendment of the Constitution is a legislative process and that any amendment under article 368 is "law" within the meaning of article 13 of the Constitution. This means that if an amendment "takes away or abridges" a Fundamental Right conferred by Part III, it is void. The Court also held that Fundamental Rights included in Part III of the Constitution are given a "transcendental position" under the Constitution and are kept beyond the reach of Parliament.

The document also discusses the concept of equality before law as outlined in Article 14 of the Constitution of India. This article guarantees equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. It is divided into two parts: Equality before the law, which indicates that all are to be treated equally in the eyes of the law, and equal protection of the laws, which means that the same law will be applied to all the people equally across the society.

The doctrine of Anti-Arbitrariness is also discussed in the document. This doctrine ensures equality of treatment and protects against the arbitrariness of State action. It was first recognized in the case of S.G. Jaisinghani v. Union of India (1967) and has been further developed through subsequent cases.

Natural Justice is also an integral part of Article 14. This means that the principles of natural justice, which include the rule against bias and the right to a fair hearing, are essential to ensuring that the right to equality is upheld.

The document also discusses the classification test, which is used to determine whether differential treatment is permitted under Article 14. This test requires that any classification must be founded on intelligible differentia and have a rational nexus with the objective sought to be achieved by the classification.

The Act applies to the whole of India and has overriding effect over any other law or instrument that is inconsistent with its provisions.

Chapter I of the Act deals with preliminary matters and defines key terms used throughout the Act. The term "employer" is defined as any person who employs one or more workers in an establishment or employment in which this Act has come into force. "Man" and "woman" are defined as male and female human beings, respectively, of any age. "Remuneration" includes basic wage or salary and any additional emoluments payable in cash or kind to a person employed in respect of employment or work done in such employment. "Same work or work of a similar nature" means work in respect of which the skill, effort, and responsibility required are the same when performed under similar working conditions by a man or a woman.

Section 5 prohibits discrimination in recruitment and other conditions of service, such as promotions, training, or transfer, based on sex. However, this provision does not affect any priority or reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, ex-servicemen, retrenched employees, or any other class or category of persons in the matter of recruitment to the posts in an establishment or employment.

Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for the transfer and withdrawal of suits, appeals, and other proceedings. The Act defines a child as a person who, if a male, has not completed 21 years of age, and if a female, has not completed 18 years of age. The Act considers any marriage to which either of the contracting parties is a child as a child marriage.

Key provisions of the Act include:

1. Section 3: Every child marriage is voidable at the option of the contracting party who was a child at the time of the marriage. A petition for annulling a child marriage by a decree of nullity may be filed in the district court only by a contracting party to the marriage who was a child at the time of the marriage.
2. Section 4: The district court may make an interim or final order directing the male contracting party to the child marriage, and in case the male contracting party to such marriage is a minor, his parent or guardian to pay maintenance to the female contracting party to the marriage until her remarriage.
3. Section 5: Where there are children born of the child marriage, the district court shall make an appropriate order for the custody of such children. While making an order for the custody of a child under this section, the welfare and best interests of the child shall be the paramount consideration to be given by the district court.
4. Section 6: Notwithstanding that a child marriage has been annulled by a decree of nullity under section 3, every child begotten or conceived of such marriage before the decree is made, whether born before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be deemed to be a legitimate child for all purposes.
5. Section 9: Whoever, being a male adult above eighteen years of age, contracts a child marriage shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment which may extend to two years or with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees or with both.
6. 7. The Indian Transfer of Property Act, 1882, contains various sections that govern the conditions and rules for transferring property. Here are some of the key sections:

Section 23: This section deals with transfers that are contingent on the happening of a specified uncertain event. The interest in the property fails unless the event occurs before or at the same time as the intermediate or precedent interest ceases to exist.

Section 27: This section deals with conditional transfers coupled with a transfer to another person on the failure of the prior disposition. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Second Amendment) Act, 2018, introduces a new Chapter II, Fresh Start Process, for individuals who are unable to pay their debts. The Fresh Start Process is designed to provide a debtor with a fresh start by discharging their qualifying debts.

To be eligible for the Fresh Start Process, the debtor must meet certain conditions, including having a gross annual income of less than 60,000 rupees, owning assets worth less than 20,000 rupees, and having qualifying debts of less than 35,000 rupees. The debtor must also not be an undischarged bankrupt, own a dwelling unit, have a subsisting fresh start, insolvency resolution, or bankruptcy process, or have received a fresh start order under this Chapter in the preceding twelve months.

To apply for a fresh start order, the debtor must file an application with the Adjudicating Authority, accompanied by a fee, and provide certain information, including a list of all debts, interest payable, security held, financial information, personal details, reasons for making the application, and details of any legal proceedings.

Upon receiving the application, the Adjudicating Authority will direct the Board to nominate a resolution professional for the fresh start process. The resolution professional will examine the application and submit a report to the Adjudicating Authority, recommending acceptance or rejection of the application.

The Adjudicating Authority may admit or reject the application within fourteen days of receiving the report. If the application is accepted, the moratorium period will commence, during which no legal action or proceedings can be initiated by the creditors. The debtor must not act as a director of any company, dispose of or alienate any of their assets, or enter into any financial or commercial transaction without informing the creditors. The debtor must also disclose the name under which they enter into business transactions, if it is different from the name in the application.

In summary, the Fresh Start Process under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Second Amendment) Act, 2018, provides a debtor with a fresh start by discharging their qualifying debts, subject to certain conditions and eligibility criteria. The Public Debt Act, 1944, is an Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to Government securities and to the management by the Reserve Bank of India of the public debt of the Government. The Act applies to Government securities created and issued by the Central Government or a State Government, whether before or after the commencement of the Act. The Act defines "Government security" to include securities created and issued by the Government for the purpose of raising a public loan, and having one of the following forms: stock transferable by registration in the books of the Bank; a promissory note payable to order; a bearer bond payable to bearer; or a form prescribed in this behalf.

The Act regulates the transfer of Government securities and provides that a transfer of a Government security shall be made only in the manner prescribed for the making of transfers of securities of the class to which it belongs. The Act also provides that no transfer of a Government security which is made after certain specified dates, depending on the issuing authority, shall be valid if it does not purport to convey the full title to the security or is of such a nature as to affect the manner in which the security was expressed by the Government to be held.

The Act also provides that a person shall not, by reason only of his having transferred a Government security, be liable to pay any money due either as principal or as interest thereunder. The Act also regulates the holding of Government securities by holders of public offices and provides that when a Government security is held in the name of an office, it shall be deemed to be transferred without any further endorsement or transfer deed from each holder of the office to the succeeding holder of the office on and from the date on which the latter takes charge of the office.

The Act also provides that no notice of any trust in respect of any Government security shall be receivable by the Government, nor shall the Government be bound by any such notice even though expressly given, nor shall the Government be regarded as a trustee in respect of any Government security. However, the Bank may, as an act of grace and without any liability to the Bank or to the Government, record in its books such directions by the holder of stock for the payment of interest on, or of the maturity value of, or the transfer of, or such other matters relating to, the stock as the Bank thinks fit.

The Act also provides for the recognition by the Bank of the manager or the sole surviving male member of a Hindu undivided family governed by the Mitakshara Law as having a title to a Government security, when the security appears to the Bank to stand in the name of a deceased member of the family and an application is made by such manager or sole surviving male member for recognition of his title.

The Act also provides for the right of survivors of joint holders or several payees of Government securities and provides that when a Government security is held by two or more persons jointly and either or any of them dies, the title to the security shall vest in the survivor or survivors of those persons.

The Act also provides for a summary procedure for the determination of title to a Government security in case of dispute and provides that the Bank may proceed to determine the person who shall for the purposes of the Bank be deemed to be the person entitled to the security.

The Act also provides that the rights of all persons in relation to Government securities shall be determined in connection with all such questions as are dealt with by this Act by the law and in the Courts of India.

The Act also provides that the Bank may make such order as it thinks fit for the vesting of a Government security in a person when it belongs to a minor or a person who is insane and incapable of managing his affairs and the face value of the security or securities does not in the aggregate exceed five thousand rupees.

The Act also provides for the issue of duplicate securities and of new securities on conversion, consolidation, sub-division or renewal and provides that if the person entitled to a Government security applies to the Bank alleging that the security has been lost, stolen or destroyed, or has been defaced or mutilated, the Bank may, on proof to its satisfaction of the loss, theft, destruction, defacement or mutilation of the security, subject to such conditions and on payment of such fees as may be prescribed, order the issue of a duplicate security payable to the applicant.

Summary:
The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is an Act of the Parliament of India that consolidates and amends the law relating to domestic arbitration, international commercial arbitration, and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards. It also defines the law relating to conciliation and matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The Act is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985) and the UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules (1980). The Act applies to the whole of India and came into force on a date appointed by the Central Government. The Act is divided into two parts: Part I - Arbitration and Part II - Conciliation. Part I of the Act contains general provisions, arbitration agreement, composition and jurisdiction of arbitral tribunal, conduct of arbitral proceedings, making of arbitral award and terms of settlement, recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards, and appeals. Part II of the Act deals with conciliation, including provisions for the commencement of conciliation proceedings, the conduct of the conciliation proceedings, the termination of conciliation proceedings, and the effects of conciliation agreements. The Act provides for extensive judicial intervention in arbitration proceedings, but also allows for parties to agree to derogate from certain provisions of the Act. The Act applies to every arbitration under any other enactment for the time being in force, as if the arbitration were pursuant to an arbitration agreement and as if that other enactment were an arbitration agreement. However, the provisions of this Part are inconsistent with that other enactment or with any rules made thereunder. The Act also provides for administrative assistance in the conduct of arbitral proceedings.
Summary:

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is a law in India that governs domestic and international commercial arbitration and conciliation. The Act applies to any arbitration agreement, whether it is in the form of an arbitration clause in a contract or a separate agreement.

Section 7 defines an arbitration agreement as a written agreement between two or more parties to submit to arbitration all or certain disputes that have arisen or may arise between them in respect of a defined legal relationship, whether contractual or not.

Section 8 empowers a judicial authority to refer parties to arbitration where there is an arbitration agreement, provided that a party to the agreement or any person claiming through or under him applies for it not later than the date of submitting his first statement on the substance of the dispute.

Section 9 allows a party to apply to a court for the appointment of a guardian for a minor or person of unsound mind for the purposes of arbitral proceedings, or for an interim measure of protection in respect of certain matters, such as the preservation, interim custody or sale of goods, securing the amount in dispute, and interim injunction or the appointment of a receiver.

Section 10 provides that the parties are free to determine the number of arbitrators, provided that such number shall not be an even number. Failing the determination, the arbitral tribunal shall consist of a sole arbitrator.

Section 11 states that a person of any nationality may be an arbitrator, unless otherwise agreed by the parties. The parties are free to agree on a procedure for appointing the arbitrator or arbitrators. If there is no agreement, in an arbitration with three arbitrators, each party shall appoint one arbitrator, and the two appointed arbitrators shall appoint the third arbitrator who shall act as the presiding arbitrator.
Summary:
Chapter X of the Act deals with miscellaneous provisions. Upon termination of the arbitral proceedings, the arbitral tribunal shall render an accounting to the parties of the deposits received and shall return any unexpended balance to the party or parties, as the case may be. Section 39 states that the arbitral tribunal shall have a lien on the arbitral award for any unpaid costs of the arbitration. If the arbitral tribunal refuses to deliver its award except on payment of the costs demanded by it, the Court may order that the arbitral tribunal shall deliver the arbitral award to the applicant on payment into Court by the applicant of the costs demanded. The Court may further order that out of the money so paid into Court there shall be paid to the arbitral tribunal by way of costs such sum as the Court may consider reasonable and that the balance of the money, if any, shall be refunded to the applicant. An application under sub-section (2) may be made by any party unless the fees demanded have been fixed by written agreement between him and the arbitral tribunal, and the arbitral tribunal shall be entitled to appear and be heard on any such application. The Court may make such orders as it thinks fit respecting the costs of the arbitration where any question arises respecting such costs and the arbitral award contains no sufficient provision concerning them.

Section 40 states that an arbitration agreement shall not be discharged by the death of any party thereto either as respects the deceased or as respects any other party, but shall in such event be enforceable by or against the legal representative of the deceased. The mandate of an arbitrator shall not be terminated by the death of any party by whom he was appointed. Section 41 deals with provisions in case of insolvency. Where a person who has been adjudged an insolvent had, before the commencement of the insolvency proceedings, become a party to an arbitration agreement, and any matter to which the agreement applies is required to be determined in connection with, or for the purposes of, the insolvency proceedings, then, if the case is one to which sub-section (1) does not apply, any other party or the receiver may apply to the judicial authority having jurisdiction in the insolvency proceedings for an order directing that the matter in question shall be submitted to arbitration in accordance with the arbitration agreement, and the judicial authority may, if it is of opinion that, having regard to all the circumstances of the case, the matter ought to be determined by arbitration, make an order accordingly.

Section 42 states that notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Part or in any other law for the time being in force, where with respect to an arbitration agreement any application under this Part has been made in a Court, that Court alone shall have jurisdiction over the arbitral proceedings and all subsequent applications arising out of that agreement and the arbitral proceedings shall be made in that Court and in no other Court.

Section 42A states that notwithstanding anything contained by any other law for the time being in force, the arbitrator, the arbitral institution and the parties to the arbitration agreement shall maintain confidentiality of all arbitral proceedings except award where its disclosure is necessary for the purpose of implementation and enforcement of award.

Section 42B states that no suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against the arbitrator for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done under this Act or the rules or regulations made thereunder.

The application for correction or additional award shall be made within thirty days of the receipt of the award, and the arbitral tribunal may correct any error or make an additional award within thirty days from the date of receipt of the application.

Under Section 34, an application for the setting aside of an arbitral award may be made to the court by a party to the arbitration within three months from the date on which the party making the application received the arbitral award. Under Section 35, the court shall, on an application made by any party to the arbitration, order the arbitral tribunal to make an award within a time specified by the court.

The Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen. A contingent contract cannot be enforced by law unless and until the event on which it is contingent has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event does not happen can be enforced when the happening of that event becomes impossible, and not before. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if a specified uncertain event happens within a fixed time become void if, at the expiration of the time fixed, such event has not happened, or if, before the time fixed, such event becomes impossible. Contingent agreements to do or not to do anything, if an impossible event happens, are void, whether the impossibility of the event is known or not to the parties to the agreement at the time when it is made. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law. Promises bind the representatives of the promisors in case of the death of such promisors before performance, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If a promisor has made an offer of performance to the promisee, and the offer has not been accepted, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance, nor does he thereby lose his rights under the contract. Every such offer must fulfill certain conditions, such as being unconditional, made at a proper time and place, and under such circumstances that the person to whom it is made may have a reasonable opportunity of ascertaining that the person by whom it is made is able and willing there and then to do the whole of what he is bound by his promise to do. If the offer is an offer to deliver anything to the promisee, the promisee must have a reasonable opportunity of seeing that the thing offered is the thing which the promisor is bound by his promise to deliver.

The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the legal framework for contracts in India. The act defines a contract as an agreement that is enforceable by law, and it specifies the essential elements of a contract, including offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity to contract, and free consent.

Section 29 of the act states that a promise to perform an impossible act is void. Section 103 discusses the burden of proof as to any particular fact. The burden of proof as to any particular fact lies on that person who wishes the court to believe in its existence, unless it is provided by any law that the proof of that fact shall lie on any particular person. In this summary, we will explain the key provisions of Sections 24 and 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which deal with the power of transfer and withdrawal of suits, appeals, and other proceedings.

Section 24: General power of transfer and withdrawal

Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for the transfer and withdrawal of suits, appeals, and other proceedings. The section gives the High Court or the District Court the power to transfer or withdraw any suit, appeal, or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same. This power can be exercised on the application of any of the parties or of its own motion without notice.

The section also provides for the transfer of a suit, appeal, or other proceeding pending in any Court subordinate to the High Court or District Court to any Court subordinate to the same High Court or District Court and competent to try or dispose of the same. This power can be exercised by the High Court or District Court on its own motion or on the application of any of the parties after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desired to be heard.

Where any suit or proceeding has been transferred or withdrawn under sub-section (1), the Court which is thereafter to try or dispose of such suit or proceeding may, subject to any special directions in the case of an order of transfer, either retry it or proceed from the point at which it was transferred or withdrawn.

Section 25: Power of Supreme Court to transfer suits, etc.

Section 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for the transfer of suits, appeals, and other proceedings by the Supreme Court. The section empowers the Supreme Court, on the application of a party and after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desire to be heard, to direct that any suit, appeal, or other proceeding be transferred from a High Court or other Civil Court in one State to a High Court or other Civil Court in any other State.

The Partition Act, 1893, also known as Act No. 4 of 1893, was enacted on the 9th of March, 1893, with the purpose of amending the law relating to partition. The Act applies to the whole of India, except the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The Act does not affect any local law that provides for the partition of immoveable property that pays revenue to the government.

The Act gives the court the power to order a sale instead of division in partition suits if the nature of the property, the number of shareholders, or any other special circumstances make a division unreasonable or inconvenient. The court may direct a sale if requested by any shareholder interested individually or collectively to the extent of one moiety or upwards. If another shareholder applies for leave to buy the share or shares of the party or parties asking for a sale, the court shall order a valuation of the share or shares and offer to sell the same to the shareholder at the price so ascertained.

If two or more shareholders apply for leave to buy, the court shall direct a sale of the share or shares to the shareholder who offers to pay the highest price above the valuation made by the court. If no shareholder is willing to buy the share or shares at the price so ascertained, the applicant or applicants shall be liable to pay all costs of or incident to the application or applications.

If a share of a dwelling-house belonging to an undivided family has been transferred to a person who is not a member of such family, and such transferee sues for partition, the court shall, if any member of the family being a shareholder shall undertake to buy the share of such transferee, make a valuation of such share and direct the sale of such share to such shareholder.

In any suit for partition, a request for sale may be made or an undertaking or application to buy may be given or made on behalf of any party under disability by any person authorized to act on behalf of such party in such suit. The court shall not be bound to comply with any such request, undertaking, or application unless it is of opinion that the sale or purchase will be for the benefit of the party under such disability.

Every sale under section 2 shall be subject to a reserved bidding, and the amount of such bidding shall be fixed by the court in such manner as it may think fit and may be varied from time to time. On any such sale, any of the shareholders shall be at liberty to bid at the sale on such terms as to non-payment of deposit or as to setting off or accounting for the purchase-money or any part thereof instead of paying the same as to the court may seem reasonable.

When any property is directed to be sold under this Act, the following procedure shall, as far as practicable, be adopted: (a) if the property be sold under a decree or order of the High Court of Calcutta, Madras, or Bombay, in the exercise of its original jurisdiction, the procedure of such court in its original civil jurisdiction for the sale of property by the Registrar; (b) if the property be sold under a decree or order of any other court, such procedure as the High Court may from time to time by rules prescribe in this behalf, and until such rules are made, the procedure prescribed in the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of sales in execution of decrees.

Any order for sale made by the court under section 2, 3, or 4 shall be deemed to be a decree within the meaning of section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (14 of 1882). In any suit for partition, the court may, if it shall think fit, make a decree for a partition of part of the property to which the suit relates and a sale of the remainder under this Act.

This Act shall apply to suits instituted before the commencement thereof, in which no scheme for the partition of the property has been finally approved by the court. The Act has been extended to Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Pondicherry, and Sikkim.

* The Company Liquidator must deposit all monies received in a special bank account opened in a scheduled bank.

The Indian Succession Act of 1925 outlines the rules for inheritance and succession in India. In this summary, we will focus on the sections related to contingent and onerous bequests.

A contingent bequest is a bequest that is dependent on the happening of a specified uncertain event. According to Section 120 of the Act, a legacy bequeathed in case a specified uncertain event shall happen does not vest until that event happens. A legacy bequeathed in case a specified uncertain event shall not happen does not vest until the happening of that event becomes impossible. The interest of the legatee is called contingent until the condition has been fulfilled.

An onerous bequest is a bequest that imposes an obligation on the legatee. According to Section 122 of the Act, where a bequest imposes an obligation on the legatee, he can take nothing by it unless he accepts it fully. If the legatee refuses to accept the onerous bequest, he forfeits the beneficial bequest as well.

There are exceptions to these rules. For example, according to Section 121 of the Act, where a bequest is made only to such members of a class as shall have attained a particular age, a person who has not attained that age cannot have a vested interest in the legacy. A fund bequeathed to such of the children of A as shall attain the age of 18, with a direction that, while any child of A shall be under the age of 18, the income of the share, to which it may be presumed he will be eventually entitled, shall be applied for his maintenance and education. No child of A who is under the age of 18 has a vested interest in the bequest.

Similarly, Section 124 of the Act states that where a legacy is given if a specified uncertain event shall happen and no time is mentioned in the will for the occurrence of that event, the legacy cannot take effect, unless such event happens before the period when the fund bequeathed is payable or distributable.

In conclusion, the Indian Succession Act of 1925 lays down the rules for contingent and onerous bequests. A contingent bequest is dependent on the happening of a specified uncertain event, and an onerous bequest imposes an obligation on the legatee.
