THE CIVIL LIABILITY FOR NUCLEAR DAMAGE ACT, 2010

This Act establishes a no-fault liability regime for nuclear damage, with the operator being liable for compensation to victims. The Act applies to nuclear incidents occurring in or over the maritime areas beyond the territorial waters of India, in the exclusive economic zone of India, on board or by a ship or aircraft registered in India, or on or by an artificial island, installation, or structure under the jurisdiction of India. The Act applies only to nuclear installations owned or controlled by the Central Government.

The Act defines various terms, including "nuclear damage," "nuclear fuel," "nuclear reactor," "operator," and "preventive measures." The operator is liable for nuclear damage caused by a nuclear incident occurring in or involving nuclear material coming from the nuclear installation. The liability of the operator is strict and based on the principle of no-fault liability.

The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board is required to notify a nuclear incident within 15 days of its occurrence. The operator is liable for nuclear damage caused by a nuclear incident directly due to a grave natural disaster or an act of armed conflict, hostility, civil war, insurrection, or terrorism. The operator is not liable for nuclear damage caused to the nuclear installation itself, to property on the same site used in connection with the installation, or to the means of transport upon which the nuclear material involved was carried at the time of the nuclear incident.

The maximum amount of liability for each nuclear incident is the rupee equivalent of three hundred million Special Drawing Rights or such higher amount as the Central Government may specify by notification. The liability of an operator for each nuclear incident is rupees one thousand five hundred crores in respect of nuclear reactors having thermal power equal to or above ten MW, rupees three hundred crores in respect of spent fuel reprocessing plants, and rupees one hundred crores in respect of the research reactors having thermal power below ten MW, fuel cycle facilities other than spent fuel reprocessing plants, and transportation of nuclear materials. The Central Government may review the amount of operator's liability from time to time and specify a higher amount.

The Central Government may establish a fund called the Nuclear Liability Fund to meet part of its liability under clause (a) or clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 7. The operator is required to take out insurance policy or such other financial security or combination of both, covering his liability under sub-section (2) of section 6.

For the purposes of adjudicating upon claims for compensation, the Central Government shall appoint one or more Claims Commissioners for such area as may be specified in that notification. A person is not qualified for appointment as a Claims Commissioner unless he is, or has been, a District Judge or in the service of the Central Government and has held the post not below the rank of Additional Secretary to the Government of India or any other equivalent post in the Central Government. The salary and allowances payable to and other terms and conditions of service of Claims Commissioner shall be such as may be prescribed.

An application for compensation may be made by a person who has sustained injury, the owner of the property to which damage has been caused, the legal representatives of the deceased, or any agent duly authorized by such person or owner or legal representatives. Every application for compensation before the Claims Commissioner shall be made in such form, containing such particulars and accompanied by such documents, as may be prescribed. The Claims Commissioner shall, after giving notice of such application to the operator and affording an opportunity of being heard to the parties, dispose of the application within a period of three months from the date of such receipt and make an award accordingly. The Claims Commissioner shall not take into consideration any benefit, reimbursement, or amount received by the applicant in pursuance of contract of insurance taken by him or for members of his family or otherwise.

The operator has a right of recourse where such right is expressly provided for in a contract in writing, the nuclear incident has resulted as a consequence of an act of supplier or his employee, or the nuclear incident has resulted from the act of commission or omission of an individual done with the intent to cause nuclear damage.

The right to claim compensation for nuclear damage shall extinguish if such claim is not made within a period of ten years in the case of damage to property or twenty years in the case of personal injury to any person from the date of occurrence of the incident notified under sub-section (1) of section 3.

Where one person grants to another, or to a definite number of other persons, a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the grantor, something which would, in the absence of such right, be unlawful, and such right does not amount to an easement or an interest in the property, the right is called a license.

A license may be granted by any one in the circumstances, and to the extent in and to which he may transfer his interests in the property affected by the license.

The grant of a license may be express or implied from the conduct of the grantor, and an agreement which purports to create an easement, but is ineffectual for that purpose, may operate to create a license.

All licenses necessary for the enjoyment of any interest, or the exercise of any right, are implied in the constitution of such interest or right. Such licenses are called accessory licenses.

The grantor of a license is bound to disclose to the licensee any defect in the property affected by the license, likely to be dangerous to the person or property of the licensee, of which the grantor is, and the licensee is not, aware.

The grantor of a license is bound not to do anything likely to render the property affected by the license dangerous to the person or property of the licensee.

When the grantor of the license transfers the property affected thereby, the transferee is not as such bound by the license.

A license may be revoked by the grantor, unless it is coupled with a transfer of property and such transfer is in force; or the licensee, acting upon the license, has executed a work of a permanent character and incurred expenses in the execution.

The revocation of a license may be express or implied.

A license is deemed to be revoked when, from a cause preceding the grant of it, the grantor ceases to have any interest in the property affected by the license; or when the licensee releases it, expressly or impliedly, to the grantor or his representative; or where it has been granted for a limited period, or acquired on condition that it shall become void on the performance or non-performance of a specified act, and the period expires, or the condition is fulfilled; or where the property affected by the license is destroyed or by superior force so permanently altered that the licensee can no longer exercise his right; or where the licensee becomes entitled to the absolute ownership of the property affected by the license; or where the license is granted for a specified purpose and the purpose is attained, or abandoned, or becomes impracticable; or where the license is granted to the licensee as holding a particular office, employment or character, and such office, employment or character ceases to exist; or where the license totally ceases to be used as such for an unbroken period of twenty years, and such cessation is not in pursuance of a contract between the grantor and the licensee; or in the case of an accessory license, when the interest or right to which it is accessory ceases to exist.

Where a license is revoked, the licensee is entitled to a reasonable time to leave the property affected thereby and to remove any goods which he has been allowed to place on such property.

Where a license has been granted for a consideration, and the licensee, without any fault of his own, is evicted by the grantor before he has fully enjoyed, under the license, the right for which he contracted, he is entitled to recover compensation from the grantor.

The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is an Act to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumer councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers’ disputes and for matters connected therewith. The Act establishes three tiers of consumer dispute redressal agencies, namely, the District Forum, the State Commission, and the National Commission. The District Forum has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed does not exceed rupees twenty lakhs. The State Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed exceeds rupees twenty lakhs but does not exceed rupees one crore, and appeals against the orders of any District Forum within the State. The National Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed exceeds rupees one crore, and appeals against the orders of any State Commission. The Act also provides for the appointment of members to these forums, their qualifications, terms of office, salaries and allowances, resignation, removal, and other terms and conditions of service. The Act also lays down the procedure for filing and disposing of complaints and appeals, and the powers and functions of the consumer dispute redressal agencies. The Act also provides for penalties for non-compliance with the orders of the consumer dispute redressal agencies, and protection of action taken in good faith. The Act also empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act, and the State Governments to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act in relation to the State Commissions and District Fora. The officers and employees required to assist the State Commission in the discharge of its functions are determined and provided by the State Government. The officers and employees of the State Commission discharge their functions under the general superintendence of the President.

The State Commission has the power to review any of its orders if there is an error apparent on the face of the record, either of its own motion or on an application made by any of the parties within thirty days of such order. Any person aggrieved by an order made by the State Commission may prefer an appeal to the National Commission within a period of thirty days from the date of the order.

The National Commission is responsible for hearing appeals from orders passed by the State Commission. It consists of a President and not less than four and not more than such number of members as may be prescribed. The National Commission may formulate a substantial question of law involved in any case and hear the appeal on that question. The Right to Information Act, 2005, is a law passed by the Parliament of India which gives citizens the right to access information held by public authorities. The Act defines 'public authority' as any authority or body or institution of self-government established or constituted by or under the Constitution; by any other law made by Parliament; by any other law made by State Legislature; by notification issued or order made by the appropriate Government, and includes any body owned, controlled or substantially financed; non-Government organization substantially financed, directly or indirectly by funds provided by the appropriate Government.

Under this Act, all citizens have the right to request information from any public authority, and the public authority is required to provide the information within 30 days, or within 48 hours if the information sought is related to the life or liberty of a person. However, there are certain exemptions to this right, including information that would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security, strategic, scientific or economic interests of the State, relation with foreign State or lead to incitement of an offence, information which has been expressly forbidden to be published by any Court of law or tribunal or the disclosure of which may constitute contempt of Court, information, the disclosure of which would cause a breach of privilege of Parliament or the State Legislature, information including commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property, the disclosure of which would harm the competitive position of a third party, unless the competent authority is satisfied that larger public interest warrants the disclosure of such information, information available to a person in his fiduciary relationship, unless the competent authority is satisfied that the larger public interest warrants the disclosure of such information, information received in confidence from foreign Government, information, the disclosure of which would endanger the life or physical safety of any person or identify the source of information or assistance given in confidence for law enforcement or security purposes, information which would impede the process of investigation or apprehension or prosecution of offenders, cabinet papers including records of deliberations of the Council of Ministers, Secretaries and other officers, and information which relates to personal information the disclosure of which has no relationship to any public activity or interest, or which would cause unwarranted invasion of the privacy of the individual unless the Central Public Information Officer or the State Public Information Officer or the appellate authority, as the case may be, is satisfied that the larger public interest justifies the disclosure of such information.

The Act also provides for the designation of Public Information Officers and Assistant Public Information Officers in all administrative units or offices under a public authority, who are responsible for receiving and responding to requests for information. If a request for information is transferred from one public authority to another, the period for response is extended by 5 days.

If a request for information is rejected, the public authority is required to provide reasons for the rejection, the period within which an appeal can be filed, and the particulars of the appellate authority.

The Act also provides for the establishment of a Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions, which are responsible for hearing appeals against the decisions of public authorities and for ensuring compliance with the provisions of the Act. The Commissioners are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee consisting of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister.

The Act also provides for penalties for non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, including fines and disciplinary action against officers who fail to provide information or who provide false or misleading information.

In summary, the Right to Information Act, 2005 is a landmark law that gives citizens the right to access information held by public authorities, subject to certain exemptions. The Act establishes a framework for the designation of Public Information Officers and Assistant Public Information Officers, and provides for the establishment of Central and State Information Commissions to hear appeals and ensure compliance with the provisions of the Act. The Act also provides for penalties for non-compliance, and seeks to promote transparency and accountability in the functioning of public authorities.

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 29A, 29B, 30, 31, 31A, and 32, pertains to the time limit for making an arbitral award, fast track procedure, settlement, form and contents of arbitral award, regime for costs, and termination of proceedings.

Under Section 29A, the award shall be made within a period of twelve months from the date the arbitral tribunal enters upon the reference. If the award is not made within the specified period, the parties may apply to the court for termination of the mandate of the arbitrator. The court may impose actual or exemplary costs upon any of the parties. An application filed under this sub-section shall be disposed of by the court as expeditiously as possible and endeavor shall be made to dispose of the matter within a period of sixty days from the date of service of notice on the opposite party. In the case of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh (UTs), the period for making an arbitral award is six months from the date the arbitral tribunal enters upon the reference.

Under Section 29B, the parties to an arbitration agreement may agree in writing to have their dispute resolved by fast track procedure. The arbitral tribunal shall decide the dispute on the basis of written pleadings, documents, and submissions filed by the parties without any oral hearing. The arbitral award shall be made within a period of six months from the date the arbitral tribunal enters upon the reference. If the award is not made within the specified period, the provisions of sub-sections (3) to (9) of Section 29A shall apply to the proceedings.

Under Section 30, it is not incompatible with an arbitration agreement for an arbitral tribunal to encourage settlement of the dispute. If the parties settle the dispute during the arbitral proceedings, the arbitral tribunal shall terminate the proceedings and, if requested by the parties and not objected to by the arbitral tribunal, record the settlement in the form of an arbitral award on agreed terms. The arbitral award on agreed terms shall have the same status and effect as any other arbitral award on the substance of the dispute.

Under Section 31, the arbitral award shall be made in writing and shall be signed by the members of the arbitral tribunal. The arbitral award shall state the reasons upon which it is based, unless the parties have agreed that no reasons are to be given. The arbitral award shall state its date and the place of arbitration. After the arbitral award is made, a signed copy shall be delivered to each party. The arbitral tribunal may make an interim arbitral award on any matter with respect to which it may make a final arbitral award.

Under Section 31A, the Court or arbitral tribunal shall have the discretion to determine the costs of the arbitration proceedings. The general rule is that the unsuccessful party shall be ordered to pay the costs of the successful party. The Court or arbitral tribunal may make a different order for reasons to be recorded in writing.

Under Section 32, the arbitral proceedings shall be terminated by the final arbitral award or by an order of the arbitral tribunal under sub-section (2). The arbitral tribunal shall issue an order for the termination of the arbitral proceedings if the claimant withdraws his claim, if the parties agree on the termination of the proceedings, or if the arbitral tribunal finds that the continuation of the proceedings has for any other reason become unnecessary or impossible.

(1)A Banking Ombudsman may, on receipt of a complaint, make an award against the bank directing it to pay such compensation to the customer not exceeding one lakh rupees, as he thinks fit, for any loss suffered by the customer as a result of deficiency in banking services by the bank.(2)A Banking Ombudsman may also direct the bank to do any other act or thing as he thinks fit in the circumstances of the case for redressal of the deficiency in banking services by the bank.(3)A Banking Ombudsman may not award any compensation or make any direction against a bank in respect of any matter which is the subject matter of any suit or other legal proceedings instituted or pending before any court, or which is in the nature of a criminal offence, or which is in respect of matters which have been resolved by the bank through its internal grievance redressal mechanism, or which are beyond the scope of the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006.


Procedure for making a complaint.

(1)A customer may make a complaint to the Banking Ombudsman in writing in English or in the official language of the area in which the branch or office of the bank against which the complaint is made is situated.(2)The complaint shall be accompanied by copies of such documents as are necessary to establish the claim of the customer and to substantiate the grounds of the complaint.(3)The Banking Ombudsman may, if he thinks fit, call for any other documents or information from the bank or the customer as he may deem necessary for the disposal of the complaint.(4)No fees shall be charged from the customer for making a complaint to the Banking Ombudsman.


Time limit for making a complaint.

(1)A complaint shall be made to the Banking Ombudsman within one year from the date on which the cause of action has arisen, provided that the Banking Ombudsman may, if he is satisfied that the complainant had sufficient cause for not making the complaint within the time limit, entertain the complaint even after the expiry of the said period of one year.(2)The Banking Ombudsman may, if he thinks fit, extend the time limit for making a complaint by such further period as he thinks fit.


Procedure for disposal of complaint.

(1)On receipt of a complaint, the Banking Ombudsman shall within fourteen days of the receipt of the complaint, send a copy of the complaint to the bank against which the complaint is made, calling upon it to give its version of the case within thirty days from the date of receipt of the complaint.(2)The bank shall send its version of the case to the Banking Ombudsman within the time limit specified in sub-section (1).(3)The Banking Ombudsman may, before making an award, call upon the parties to the dispute to submit such further evidence or to make such further statement as he may consider necessary.(4)The Banking Ombudsman may, after considering the evidence and the facts of the case, make such award as he thinks fit and send a copy of the award to each of the parties to the dispute.

The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Rules, 2012, outlines the procedures for implementing the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. The rules define key terms, including District Child Protection Unit (DCPU), expert, special educator, support person, and person familiar with the manner of communication of the child. The rules also specify the qualifications and experience required for interpreters, translators, special educators, and experts.

The rules require that the DCPU maintain a register of interpreters, translators, and special educators for the purposes of the Act. The rules also outline the procedures for engaging interpreters, translators, special educators, and experts. The rules specify that interpreters, translators, and special educators should be unbiased and impartial and should disclose any real or perceived conflict of interest.

The rules also outline the procedures for providing care and protection to children who are victims of sexual offences. The rules require that the SJPU or local police disclose certain details to the person making the report, including their name and designation, address and telephone number, and the name and contact details of the officer who supervises the officer receiving the information. The rules also specify the procedures for recording and registering a First Information Report, providing emergency medical care, taking the child to the hospital for medical examination, and ensuring that samples collected for forensic tests are sent to the forensic laboratory at the earliest.

The rules also require that the SJPU or local police inform the child and his parent or guardian or other person in whom the child has trust and confidence of the availability of support services, including counselling, and assist them in contacting the persons who are responsible for providing these services and relief.

The rules also outline the procedures for producing the child before the Child Welfare Committee (CWC) and determining whether the child is in need of care and protection. The rules specify the factors that the CWC must take into account in making this determination, including the capacity of the parents or guardian to provide for the immediate care and protection needs of the child, the need for the child to remain in the care of his parent, family and extended family, and the child's age, level of maturity, gender, and social and economic background.

The rules also provide for the assignment of a support person to render assistance to the child through the process of investigation and trial. The support person may be a person or organization working in the field of child rights or child protection, or an official of a children's home or shelter home having custody of the child, or a person employed by the DCPU.

The rules also outline the procedures for monitoring the implementation of the Act by the National Commission for the Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) or the State Commission for the Protection of Child Rights (SCPCR). The NCPCR or SCPCR may call for a report on any specific case of child sexual abuse falling within the jurisdiction of a CWC and may collect information and data on reported cases of sexual abuse and their disposal under the processes established under the Act.

The rules also provide for the payment of compensation to the victim in appropriate cases. The compensation may be awarded at any stage after registration of the First Information Report and may be paid by the State Government from the Victims Compensation Fund or other scheme or fund established by it for the purposes of compensating and rehabilitating victims.

question_text: Under Section 3 of the Commission of Inquiry Act 1952, an Inquiry Commission is appointed by
options:
A) Central government or State government 
 B) Union Public Service Commission 
 C) State Public commission 
 D) Supreme Court of India
context:
Summary:

THE COMMISSIONS OF INQUIRY ACT, 1952 is an Act that provides for the appointment of Commissions of Inquiry and vests them with certain powers. The Act is applicable to the whole of India and came into force on a date appointed by the Central Government. The Act defines "appropriate Government" as the Central Government for matters related to List I, II, or III in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, and the State Government for matters related to List II or III in the Seventh Schedule.

The Act empowers the appropriate Government to appoint a Commission of Inquiry for the purpose of making an inquiry into any definite matter of public importance. The Commission may consist of one or more members, with one member appointed as the Chairman. The appropriate Government may fill any vacancy that may arise in the office of a member of the Commission. The appropriate Government shall cause to be laid before each House of Parliament or the Legislature of the State, the report of the Commission on the inquiry made by the Commission together with a memorandum of the action taken thereon, within a period of six months of the submission of the report by the Commission to the appropriate Government.

The Commission has the powers of a civil court while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, in respect of summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person, requiring the discovery and production of any document, receiving evidence on affidavits, requisitioning any public record or copy thereof from any court or office, issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents, and any other matter which may be prescribed.

The appropriate Government may direct that all or any of the provisions of sections 5(2), 5(3), 5(4), or 5(5) should be made applicable to a Commission. The Commission has the power to require any person to furnish information on points or matters relevant to the subject matter of the inquiry, and any person so required is deemed to be legally bound to furnish such information.

The Commission or any officer authorized by the Commission may enter any building or place where the Commission has reason to believe that any books of account or other documents relating to the subject matter of the inquiry may be found, and may seize any books of account or documents or take extracts or copies therefrom.

The Commission is deemed to be a civil court, and when any offence is committed in the view or presence of the Commission, the Commission may forward the case to a magistrate having jurisdiction to try the same. Any proceeding before the Commission is deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860).

The Commission may utilize the services of any officer or investigation agency of the Central Government or any State Government for conducting any investigation pertaining to the inquiry. The officer or agency whose services are utilized shall investigate into any matter pertaining to the inquiry and submit a report thereon to the Commission within a period specified by the Commission.

The Commission may appoint persons having special knowledge of any matter connected with the inquiry as assessors to assist and advise the Commission in the inquiry. No statement made by a person in the course of giving evidence before the Commission shall subject him to, or be used against him in, any civil or criminal proceeding except a prosecution for giving false evidence by such statement.

Except in cases where a Commission is expressly required to inquire into the process of manufacture of any goods, nothing in this Act shall be deemed to compel any person giving evidence before the Commission to disclose any secret process of manufacture thereof.

The appropriate Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare that a Commission shall cease to exist if it is of opinion that the continued existence of the Commission is unnecessary. If a resolution for the discontinuance of the Commission is passed by each House of Parliament or the Legislature of the State, the Commission shall cease to exist. Every notification issued under sub-section (1) shall specify the date from which the Commission shall cease to exist.

The Commission shall have power to regulate its own procedure, including the fixing of places and times of its sittings and deciding whether to sit in public or in private. If, at any stage of the inquiry, the Commission considers it necessary to inquire into the conduct of any person or is of opinion that the reputation of any person is likely to be prejudicially affected by the inquiry, the Commission shall give to that person a reasonable opportunity of being heard in the inquiry and to produce evidence in his defense.
Where the Central Government, having regard to the injury or damage caused by a nuclear incident, is of the opinion that it is expedient in public interest that such claims for such damage be adjudicated by the Commission instead of a Claims Commissioner, it may, by notification, establish a Commission for the purpose of this Act. The Commission shall consist of a Chairperson and such other Members, not exceeding six, as the Central Government may, by notification, appoint.

The Chairperson and other Members of the Commission shall be appointed on the recommendation of a Selection Committee consisting of three experts from amongst the persons having at least thirty years of experience in nuclear science and a retired Supreme Court Judge. The salary and allowances payable to and other terms and conditions of service of the Chairperson and other Members shall be such as may be prescribed.

A person shall not be qualified for appointment as the Chairperson of the Commission unless he has attained the age of fifty-five years and is or has been or qualified to be a Judge of a High Court. A person shall not be qualified for appointment as a Member unless he has attained the age of fifty-five years and has held or is holding or qualified to hold, the post of Additional Secretary to the Government of India or any other equivalent post in the Central Government and possesses special knowledge in law relating to nuclear liability arising out of nuclear incident or has been a Claims Commissioner for five years.

The Chairperson or a Member may, by a notice in writing under his hand addressed to the Central Government, resign his office. The Central Government shall remove from office the Chairperson or a Member who has been adjudged an insolvent, has been convicted of an offence which, in the opinion of the Central Government, involves moral turpitude, has become physically or mentally incapable of acting as a Member, has acquired such financial or other interest as is likely to affect prejudicially his functions as a Member, or has so abused his position as to render his continuance in office detrimental to the public interest.

A person who, immediately before the date of assuming office as a Chairperson or a Member, was in service of the Government, shall be deemed to have retired from service on the date on which he enters upon office as such.

The Chairperson shall have the power of superintendence in the general administration of the Commission and exercise such powers as may be prescribed. The Commission shall have original jurisdiction to adjudicate upon every application for compensation filed before it under sub-section (1) of section 31 or transferred to it under section 33. The Commission shall not be bound by the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but shall be guided by the principles of natural justice and subject to the other provisions of this Act and of any rules made thereunder, the Commission shall have the power to regulate its own procedure including the places and the times at which it shall have its sittings.

Every proceeding before the Claims Commissioner or the Commission under this Act shall be deemed to be judicial proceeding within the meaning of sections 193, 219, and 228 of, and for the purposes of section 196 of, the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860). No civil court (except the Supreme Court and a High Court exercising jurisdiction under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution) shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceedings in respect of any matter which the Claims Commissioner or the Commission, as the case may be, is empowered to adjudicate under this Act and no injunction shall be granted by any court or other authority in respect of any action taken or to be taken in pursuance of any power conferred by or under this Act.

When an award is made under sub-section (1) of section 16 or under sub-section (6) of section 32, the insurer or any person, as the case may be, who under the contract of insurance or financial security under section 8 is required to pay any amount in terms of such award and to the extent of his liability under such contract, shall deposit that amount within such time and in such manner as the Claims Commissioner or the Commission, as the case may be, may direct. The operator shall, subject to the maximum liability specified under sub-section (2) of section 6, deposit the remaining amount by which such award exceeds the amount deposited under clause (a). Where any person fails to deposit the amount of award within the period specified in the award, such amount shall be recoverable from such person as arrears of land revenue.

The Commission shall prepare, in such form and at such time in each financial year, as may be prescribed, an annual report giving full account of its activities during that financial year and submit a copy thereof to the Central Government which shall cause the same to be laid before each House of Parliament.

The Identification of Prisoners Act, 1920 (Act No. 33 of 1920) is a law in India that authorizes the taking of measurements and photographs of convicts and others. The Act extends to the whole of India except for the territories that were formerly part of Part B States.

The Act defines "measurements" to include finger impressions and foot-print impressions, and "police officer" as an officer in-charge of a police-station, a police officer making an investigation under Chapter XIV of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, or any other police officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector.

The Act requires every person who has been convicted of any offence punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term of one year or upwards, or of any offence which would render him liable to enhanced punishment on a subsequent conviction, to allow his measurements and photograph to be taken by a police officer in the prescribed manner.

Any person who has been arrested in connection with an offence punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term of one year or upwards shall, if so required by a police officer, allow his measurements to be taken in the prescribed manner.

A Magistrate may order any person to allow his measurements or photograph to be taken if it is expedient for the purposes of any investigation or proceeding under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. However, no order shall be made directing any person to be photographed except by a magistrate of the first class, and only if the person has at some time been arrested in connection with such investigation or proceeding.

Resistance to or refusal to allow the taking of measurements or photographs under this Act is an offence under section 186 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

Where any person who, not having been previously convicted of an offence punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term of one year or upwards, has had his measurements taken or has been photographed in accordance with the provisions of this Act is released without trial or discharged or acquitted by any court, all measurements and all photographs (both negatives and copies) so taken shall, unless the court or (in a case where such person is released without trial) the District Magistrate or Sub-Divisional Officer for reasons to be recorded in writing otherwise directs, be destroyed or made over to him.

The State Government may make rules for the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions of this Act, including restrictions on the taking of photographs, the places at which measurements and photographs may be taken, the nature of the measurements that may be taken, the method in which any class or classes of measurements shall be taken, the dress to be worn by a person when being photographed, and the preservation, safe custody, destruction and disposal of records of measurements and photographs.

No suit or other proceeding shall lie against any person for anything done, or intended to be done, in good faith under this Act or under any rule made thereunder.

THE SPECIAL COURT (TRIAL OF OFFENCES RELATING TO TRANSACTIONS IN SECURITIES) ACT, 1992 is an Act to provide for the establishment of a Special Court for the trial of offences relating to transactions in securities and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The Act defines "securities" to include shares, scrips, stocks, bonds, debentures, debenture stock, units of the Unit Trust of India or any other mutual fund or other marketable securities of a like nature in or of any incorporated company or other body corporate, Government securities, and rights or interests in securities.

The Act establishes a Special Court for the trial of offences relating to transactions in securities. The Special Court shall consist of one or more sitting Judges of the High Court nominated by the Chief Justice of the High Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the Special Court is situated, with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India. When the office of a Judge of the Special Court is vacant by reason of absence or leave, the duties of the office shall be performed by such Judge of the High Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the Special Court is situated as the Chief Justice of that High Court may, with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India, nominate for the purpose.

The Act provides that any prosecution in respect of any offence referred to in sub-section (2) of section 3 shall be instituted only in the Special Court and any prosecution in respect of such offence pending in any court shall stand transferred to the Special Court. The Special Court shall have jurisdiction to try any person concerned in the offence referred to in sub-section (2) of section 3 either as a principal, conspirator or abettor and all other offences and accused persons as can be jointly tried therewith at one trial in accordance with the Code.

The Act empowers the Special Court to pass upon any person convicted by it any sentence authorized by law for the punishment of the offence of which such person is convicted. While dealing with any other matter brought before it, the Special Court may adopt such procedure as it may deem fit consistent with the principles of natural justice.

The Act also confers jurisdiction, powers, authority and procedure of Special Court in civil matters. On and from the commencement of the Special Court (Trial of Offences Relating to Transactions in Securities) Amendment Act, 1994, the Special Court shall exercise all such jurisdiction, powers and authority as were exercisable, immediately before such commencement, by any civil court in relation to any matter or claim relating to any property standing attached under sub-section(3) of section 3 and arising out of transactions in securities entered into after the 1st day of April, 1991, and on or before the 6th day of June, 1992, in which a person notified under sub-section (2) of section 3 is involved as a party, broker, intermediary or in any other manner.

An appeal shall lie from any judgment, decree, sentence or order, not being interlocutory order, of the Special Court to the Supreme Court both on facts and on law. The Magistrates and Proceedings Before Magistrates document outlines various sections related to the appointment, jurisdiction, and powers of municipal magistrates in Delhi, India.

Section 469 specifies the appointment and jurisdiction of municipal magistrates. It states that the state government may appoint one or more Metropolitan Magistrates for the trial of offenses against this Act and any rule, regulation, or bye-law made thereunder. These magistrates shall be called municipal magistrates and shall exercise all other powers and discharge all other functions of a magistrate as provided in this Act or any rule, regulation, or bye-law made thereunder. They shall be paid a salary, pension, leave, and other allowances as fixed by the state government, and the Corporation shall pay the amounts of the salary, pension, leave, and other allowances together with all other incidental charges in connection with the establishments of the said magistrates. Each such magistrate shall have jurisdiction over the whole of Delhi. For the purposes of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, all municipal magistrates appointed under this Act shall be deemed to be magistrates appointed under section 16 of the said Code. Nothing in this section shall be deemed to preclude any magistrate appointed hereunder from trying any offence under any other law.

Section 470 states that all offenses against this Act or any rule, regulation, or bye-law made thereunder, whether committed within or without the limits of Delhi, shall be cognizable by a municipal magistrate. Such magistrate shall not be deemed to be incapable of taking cognizance of any such offence or of any offence under any enactment which is repealed by, or which ceases to have effect under, this Act by reason only of his being liable to pay any municipal tax or rate or benefited out of the Municipal Fund.

Section 471 specifies the limitation of time for prosecution. No person shall be liable to punishment for any offence against this Act or any rule, regulation or bye-law made thereunder, unless complaint of such offence is made before a municipal magistrate within six months next after— (a) the date of the commission of such offence, or (b) the date on which the commission or existence of such offence was first brought to the notice of the complainant.

Section 472 states that if any person summoned to appear before a magistrate to answer a charge of an offence against this Act or any rule, regulation or bye-law made thereunder fails to appear at the time and place mentioned in the summons, or on any date to which the hearing of case is adjourned, the magistrate may hear and determine the case in his absence, if— (a) service of the summons is proved to his satisfaction, and (b) no sufficient cause is shown for the non-appearance of such person.

Section 473 specifies the complaints concerning nuisances and procedure therefor. The Commissioner, or any municipal officer or other municipal employee authorized by him in this behalf or any person who resides or owns property in Delhi, may complain to a municipal magistrate of the existence of any nuisance. Upon the receipt of any such complaint the magistrate, after making such inquiry as he thinks necessary, may by written order direct the person responsible for the nuisance or the owner of the land or building on which the nuisance has taken place, to take such measures as to such magistrate may seem practicable and reasonable, and within such period as may be specified in the order, for abating, preventing, removing or remedying such nuisance and may direct the Commissioner to put into force any of the provisions of this Act or any bye-law made thereunder. The magistrate may further direct the person found responsible for the nuisance to pay to the complainant such reasonable costs of and relating to the said complaint as he shall determine, inclusive of compensation for the complainant’s loss of time in prosecuting such complaint.

Section 474 specifies the powers and duties of police officers. Any police officer may arrest any person who commits in his view any offence against this Act or against any rule, regulation or bye-law made thereunder, if— (a) the name and address of such person be unknown to him, and (b) such person on demand declines to give his name and address or gives a name and address which such officer has reason to believe to be false. No person so arrested shall be detained in custody after his true name and address are ascertained or, without the order of the nearest magistrate, for a period longer than twenty-four hours from the time of arrest exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of such magistrate.

Summary:
The Specific Relief Act, 1963 (Act No. 47 of 1963) is an Act that defines and amends the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief. The Act is divided into three parts. Part I is the preliminary part, which includes the short title, extent, commencement, definitions, savings, and specific relief to be granted only for enforcing individual civil rights and not for enforcing penal laws. Part II is the specific relief part, which includes Chapter I on recovering possession of property, Chapter II on specific performance of contracts, Chapter III on rectification of instruments, Chapter IV on rescission of contracts, Chapter V on cancellation of instruments, Chapter VI on declaratory decrees, Chapter VII on injunctions generally, and Chapter VIII on perpetual injunctions. Part III is the preventive relief part, which includes Chapter IX on temporary and perpetual injunctions, and Chapter X on perpetual injunctions. The Act also includes a schedule that lists the category of projects and infrastructure sub-sectors.

Under Part II, Chapter II on specific performance of contracts, the Act states that specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14, and section 16. The Act also states that specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favor of a person who has obtained substituted performance of the contract under section 20 or who has become incapable of performing, or violates any essential term of, the contract that remains to be performed, or acts in fraud of the contract, or wilfully acts at variance with or in subversion of the relation intended to be established by the contract. The Act also provides for the circumstances under which specific performance may be enforced, such as when the contract is in writing and signed by the party to be charged, when the party to be charged is able to perform the contract, and when the contract is not a contract for the sale of immovable property or for the supply of goods.

Under Part II, Chapter III on rectification of instruments, the Act states that when, through fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, a contract or other instrument in writing does not express their real intention, either party or his representative in interest may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified. The court may, in its discretion, direct rectification of the instrument so as to express that intention, so far as this can be done without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value.

Under Part II, Chapter IV on rescission of contracts, the Act states that any person interested in a contract may sue to have it rescinded, and such rescission may be adjudged by the court in any of the following cases, namely: (a) where the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff; (b) where the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. The Act also states that the court may refuse to rescind the contract if the plaintiff has expressly or impliedly ratified the contract, or if owing to the change of circumstances which has taken place since the making of the contract, the parties cannot be substantially restored to the position in which they stood when the contract was made, or if third parties have, during the subsistence of the contract, acquired rights in good faith without notice and for value, or if only a part of the contract is sought to be rescinded and such part is not severable from the rest of the contract.

Under Part II, Chapter V on cancellation of instruments, the Act states that any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, and who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable, and the court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled.

Under Part II, Chapter VI on declaratory decrees, the Act states that any person entitled to any legal character or to any right as to any property may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may, in its discretion, make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief.
Section 5: This section saves certain suits. Nothing in section four shall be held to prevent the Civil Courts from entertaining the following suits: suits against the Government to contest the amount claimed, or paid under protest, or recovered, as land-revenue on the ground that such amount is in excess of the amount authorized in that behalf by the Government, or that such amount had previous to such claim, payment, or recovery been satisfied, in whole or in part, or that the plaintiff, or the person whom he represents, is not the person liable for such amount; suits between private parties for the purpose of establishing any private right, although it may be affected by any entry in any record of a revenue survey or settlement or in any village papers; suits between superior holders or occupants and inferior holders or tenants regarding the dues claimed or recovered from the latter; and suits, other than suits against the Government, for possession of any land being a whole survey number or a recognized share of a survey number.

Section 6: This section provides that revenue officers shall not be liable to be sued for damages in any Civil Court for any act bona fide done, or ordered to be done, by them as such in pursuance of the provisions of any law for the time being in force.

Section 7: This section provides that nothing in any law for the time being in force which authorizes the punishment departmentally of any Revenue officer for any offence or breach of duty, or which sanctions his prosecution criminally for such offence or breach, shall be held to bar any remedy which may be had in the Civil Court against such officer.

Section 8: This section, which provided for officers to answer in suits against them for acts done by order of superior authority, has been repealed.

Section 12: This section provides that if in the trial or investigation of any suit, claim or objection, which, but for the passing of this Act, might have been tried or investigated by a Civil Court, there arises any question on which the State Government desires to have the decision of the High Court, the State Government may cause a statement of the question to be prepared, and may refer such question for the decision of the High Court.

Section 13: This section provides that if in any suit instituted, or in any appeal presented, in a Civil Court, the Judge doubts whether he is precluded by this Act from taking cognizance of the suit or appeal, he may refer the matter to the High Court.

Section 14: This section provides that every reference under section twelve or section thirteen shall be heard by a Bench consisting of such number of Judges not less than three, as the Chief Justice from time to time directs.

The Patents Act, 1970 (Act No. 39 of 1970) is an Act to amend and consolidate the law relating to patents in India. The Act defines patents as a patent for any invention granted under this Act. The Act extends to the whole of India and came into force on a date appointed by the Central Government.

The Act defines various terms used in the Act, such as "Appellate Board," "assignee," "Budapest Treaty," "capable of industrial application," "Controller," "convention application," "convention country," "district court," "exclusive licensee," "Government undertaking," "High Court," "international application," "invention," "inventive step," "legal representative," "new invention," "Opposition Board," "patent," "patent agent," "patented article," "patented process," "patentee," "patent of addition," "patent office," "person," "person interested," "pharmaceutical substance," "prescribed," "prescribed manner," "priority date," "register," and "true and first inventor."

The Act specifies what are not inventions, including an invention that is frivolous or obviously contrary to natural laws, an invention whose primary or intended use is contrary to public order or morality, the mere discovery of a scientific principle or the formulation of an abstract theory, and a method of agriculture or horticulture. The Act also specifies that no patent shall be granted in respect of an invention relating to atomic energy falling within sub-section (1) of section 20 of the Atomic Energy Act, 1962.

The Act sets out the procedures for making an application for a patent, including the requirements for the application, the fees to be paid, and the examination of the application by the Controller. The Act also sets out the grounds for refusal of a patent and the procedures for appeal and opposition to the grant of a patent.

The Act also includes provisions for the grant of compulsory licenses, the revocation of patents, and the rights and obligations of patent holders and licensees. The Act also establishes the Patent Office and the Appellate Board to oversee the administration of the Act.

In summary, the Patents Act, 1970 is an Act that governs the grant and enforcement of patents in India. The Act sets out the requirements for obtaining a patent, the grounds for refusal of a patent, and the procedures for appeal and opposition to the grant of a patent. The Act also includes provisions for the grant of compulsory licenses, the revocation of patents, and the rights and obligations of patent holders and licensees. Summary:

This document outlines various provisions related to the filing and processing of patent applications in India. According to Section 5(1) of the Patents Act, 1970, any person claiming to be the true and first inventor of an invention, an assignee of such a person, or the legal representative of a deceased person who was entitled to make an application for a patent can file an application. The application must be made in the prescribed form and filed in the patent office. If the application is made by virtue of an assignment of the right to apply for a patent, proof of the right to make the application must be furnished within a prescribed period after the filing of the application.

Under Section 8, where an applicant for a patent is prosecuting an application for a patent in any country outside India in respect of the same or substantially the same invention, they must file a statement setting out detailed particulars of such application and an undertaking to keep the Controller informed of any other applications relating to the same or substantially the same invention filed in any country outside India.

Section 9 outlines the requirements for provisional and complete specifications. If an application for a patent is accompanied by a provisional specification, a complete specification must be filed within twelve months from the date of filing of the application. If the complete specification is not so filed, the application shall be deemed to be abandoned.
Under Section 4 of the Patents Act, the specification of an application for a patent can be amended before the grant of the patent. This amendment can include an amendment of the priority date of a claim. After the grant of a patent, the patentee can still amend the specification in any proceeding before the Appellate Board or High Court for the revocation of a patent, subject to certain provisions and terms.

Section 58 allows for the amendment of a specification before the Appellate Board or High Court in proceedings for the revocation of a patent. The patentee can amend the specification in such manner and subject to such terms as to costs, advertisement, or otherwise as the Appellate Board or High Court may think fit. If the patent is decided to be invalid, the specification can be amended under this section instead of revoking the patent.

Section 59 outlines the supplementary provisions as to amendment of an application or specification. No amendment of an application for a patent or a complete specification or any document relating thereto shall be made except by way of disclaimer, correction, or explanation. The amendment must be for the purpose of incorporation of actual fact, and no amendment of a complete specification shall be allowed if it would claim or describe matter not in substance disclosed or shown in the specification before the amendment.

Section 60 allows for applications for the restoration of lapsed patents. If a patent has ceased to have effect by reason of failure to pay any renewal fee, the patentee or his legal representative can make an application for the restoration of the patent within 18 months from the date on which the patent ceased to have effect. The application must contain a statement, verified in the prescribed manner, fully setting out the circumstances which led to the failure to pay the prescribed fee.

Under Section 61, if the Controller is prima facie satisfied that the failure to pay the renewal fee was unintentional and that there has been no undue delay in the making of the application, he shall publish the application in the prescribed manner. Within the prescribed period, any person interested may give notice to the Controller of opposition to the restoration on the grounds that the failure to pay the renewal fee was not unintentional or that there has been undue delay in the making of the application.

If notice of opposition is given within the period, the Controller shall notify the applicant and give him and the opponent an opportunity to be heard before he decides the case. If no notice of opposition is given within the period or if in the case of opposition, the decision of the Controller is in favour of the applicant, the Controller shall restore the patent upon payment of any unpaid renewal fee and such additional fee as may be prescribed.

Section 62 outlines the rights of patentees of lapsed patents which have been restored. Where a patent is restored, the rights of the patentee shall be subject to such provisions as may be prescribed and to such other provisions as the Controller thinks fit to impose for the protection or compensation of persons who may have begun to avail themselves of, or have taken definite steps by contract or otherwise to avail themselves of, the patented invention between the date when the patent ceased to have effect and the date of the publication of the application for restoration of the patent under this Chapter.

Section 63 allows for the surrender of patents. A patentee may offer to surrender his patent by giving notice in the prescribed manner to the Controller. If such an offer is made, the Controller shall publish the offer in the prescribed manner and notify every person other than the patentee whose name appears in the register as having an interest in the patent. Any person interested may, within the prescribed period, give notice to the Controller of opposition to the surrender. If the Controller is satisfied after hearing the patentee and any opponent that the patent may properly be surrendered, he may accept the offer and revoke the patent.

context:
Article 321 of the Constitution empowers Parliament or the Legislature of a State to provide for the exercise of additional functions by the Union Public Service Commission or the State Public Service Commission as respects the services of the Union or the State and also as respects the services of any local authority or other body corporate constituted by law or of any public institution.
Summary:

The Constitution of India outlines the expenses, reports, and administrative functions of Public Service Commissions. The expenses of the Union or a State Public Service Commission, including salaries, allowances, and pensions, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India or the Consolidated Fund of the State. The Commissions are required to present annual reports on their work to the President or Governor, who will then lay them before the Legislature, along with a memorandum explaining any cases where the Commission's advice was not accepted. The Constitution also allows for the establishment of administrative tribunals to adjudicate disputes and complaints related to recruitment and conditions of service of public servants. These tribunals have the power to punish for contempt and follow a specified procedure. Their jurisdiction, powers, and authority are determined by law, and their decisions are final and binding, excluding the jurisdiction of all courts except the Supreme Court under Article 136. Additionally, the Constitution provides for the establishment of tribunals for other matters, such as taxation, foreign exchange, labor disputes, land reforms, and elections, among others. These tribunals also have the power to punish for contempt and follow a specified procedure, and their decisions are final and binding, excluding the jurisdiction of all courts except the Supreme Court under Article 136. The Election Commission is responsible for the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of all elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President. The Commission consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may fix. The conditions of service and tenure of office of the Election Commissioners are determined by the President. The President or Governor is required to make available to the Election Commission or a Regional Commissioner such staff as may be necessary for the discharge of the functions conferred on the Election Commission.
The document to summarize is about the Constitution of India, specifically discussing laws related to elections and adult suffrage. It begins by stating that the Constitution of India does not allow for any person to be ineligible for inclusion in an electoral roll on the grounds of religion, race, caste, or sex. The Constitution also mandates that elections to the House of the People and to the Legislative Assemblies of States must be on the basis of adult suffrage, meaning that every person who is a citizen of India and is not less than 18 years of age, and is not otherwise disqualified, is entitled to be registered as a voter.

The document then goes on to discuss the Representation of the People Act of 1951, which was amended by the Constitution (Sixty-first Amendment) Act, 1988, to reduce the voting age for elections for Indian citizens from 21 years to 18 years. The Constitution also grants Parliament the power to make provisions with respect to all matters relating to or in connection with elections to either House of Parliament or to the House or either House of the Legislature of a State. This includes the preparation of electoral rolls, the delimitation of constituencies, and all other matters necessary for securing the due constitution of such Houses or Houses. Similarly, the Legislature of a State may also make provisions with respect to all matters relating to or in connection with the elections to the House or either House of the Legislature of the State.

The document also discusses the bar to interference by courts in electoral matters. It states that the validity of any law relating to the delimitation of constituencies or the allotment of seats to such constituencies made or purporting to be made under Article 327 or Article 328 shall not be called in question in any court. Furthermore, no election to either House of Parliament or to the House or either House of the Legislature of a State shall be called in question except by an election petition presented to such authority and in such manner as may be provided for by or under any law made by the appropriate Legislature.
The document also contains provisions related to the continuance of officers in the same post, power of the Central Government to give directions, and provisions as to State Public Service Commissions. The Public Service Commission for the existing State of Punjab shall cease to exist on and from the appointed day. The person holding office immediately before the appointed day as Chairman of the Public Service Commission for the existing State of Punjab shall become the Chairman of the Public Service Commission for the State of Haryana or Punjab as the President shall specify. Every person who becomes the Chairman or other member of a Public Service Commission on the appointed day shall be entitled to receive from the Government of the State conditions of service not less favourable than those to which he was entitled under the provisions applicable to him immediately before the appointed day.

context:
Under Chapter XXX of the CrPC, provisions related to reference to the High Court are provided. According to Section 395, where any Court is satisfied that a case pending before it involves a question as to the validity of any Act, Ordinance, or Regulation or of any provision contained in an Act, Ordinance, or Regulation, the determination of which is necessary for the disposal of the case, and is of opinion that such Act, Ordinance, Regulation, or provision is invalid or inoperative, but has not been so declared by the High Court to which that Court is Subordinate or by the Supreme Court, the Court shall state a case setting out its opinion and the reasons therefor and refer the same for the decision of the High Court. A Court of Session or a Metropolitan Magistrate may, if it thinks fit in any case pending before it to which the provisions of sub-section (1) do not apply, refer for the decision of the High Court any question of law arising in the hearing of such case.

Under Section 396, when a question has been referred, the High Court shall pass such order thereon as it thinks fit, and shall cause a copy of such order to be sent to the Court by which the reference was made, which shall dispose of the case conformably to the said order. The High Court may direct by whom the costs of such reference shall be paid.

Under Section 397, the High Court or any Sessions Judge may call for and examine the record of any proceeding before any inferior Criminal Court situate within its or his local jurisdiction for the purpose of satisfying itself or himself to the correctness, legality, or propriety of any finding, sentence, or order recorded or passed, and as to the regularity of any proceedings of such inferior Court, and may, when calling for such record, direct that the execution of any sentence or order be suspended, and if the accused is in confinement that he be released on bail or on his own bond pending the examination of the record.

Under Section 398, on examining any record under Section 397 or otherwise, the High Court or the Sessions Judge may direct the Chief Judicial Magistrate by himself or by any of the Magistrates subordinate to him to make, and the Chief Judicial Magistrate may himself make or direct any subordinate Magistrate to make, further inquiry into any complaint which has been dismissed under section 203 or sub-section (4) of section 204, or into the case of any person accused of an offence who has been discharged.

Under Section 399, the Sessions Judge may exercise all or any of the powers which may be exercised by the High Court under sub-section (1) of Section 401. Where any proceeding by way of revision is commenced before a Sessions Judge under sub-section (1), the provisions of sub-sections (2), (3), (4) and (5) of Section 401 shall, so far as may be, apply to such proceeding and references in the said sub-sections to the High Court shall be construed as references to the Sessions Judge.

Under Section 400, an Additional Sessions Judge shall have and may exercise all the powers of a Sessions Judge under this Chapter in respect of any case which may be transferred to him by or under any general or special order of the Sessions Judge.

Under Section 401, the High Court has the power of revision. In the case of any proceeding the record of which has been called for by itself or which otherwise comes to its knowledge, the High Court may, in its discretion, exercise any of the powers conferred on a Court of Appeal by sections 386, 389, 390 and 391 or on a Court of Session by section 307, and, when the Judges composing the Court of Revision are equally divided in opinion, the case shall be disposed of in the manner provided by section 392. No order under this section shall be made to the prejudice of the accused or other person unless he has had an opportunity of being heard either personally or by pleader in his own defence. Nothing in this section shall be deemed to authorise a High Court to convert a finding of acquittal into one conviction. Where under this Code an appeal lies and no appeal is brought, no proceeding by way of revision shall be entertained at the instance of the party who could have appealed. Where under this Code an appeal lies but an application for revision has been made to the High Court by any person and the High Court is satisfied that such application was made under the erroneous belief that no appeal lies thereto and that it is necessary in the interests of Justice so to do, the High Court may treat the application for revision as a petition of appeal and deal with the same accordingly.
It is important to note that the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, the Constitution (Forty-Third Amendment) Act, 1977, the Constitution (Thirtieth Amendment) Act, 1972, and the Constitution (Forty-Fourth Amendment) Act, 1978 have made significant changes to the provisions related to the Supreme Court as summarized in this document.
Summary:

The document summarizes several articles from the Constitution of India that relate to the Supreme Court and its jurisdiction, powers, and procedures. The Forty-Fourth Amendment Act of 1978 repealed Article 19(1)(f) and moved Article 31(1) to a separate Article 300A in Chapter IV of Part XII. This amendment removed the right to property as a fundamental right and made it a legal right under the Constitution, emphasizing the value of socialism and conforming to the doctrine of basic structure of the Constitution.

The document also discusses the Supreme Court's power to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order in any cause or matter passed or made by any court or tribunal in the territory of India. The Court has the power to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it, subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament or any rules made under Article 145. The Supreme Court also has the power to confer on itself further jurisdiction and powers with respect to any of the matters in the Union List as Parliament may by law confer, and with respect to any matter as the Government of India and the Government of any State may by special agreement confer, if Parliament by law provides for the exercise of such jurisdiction and powers by the Supreme Court.

The document highlights the Supreme Court's power to issue directions, orders, or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari, or any of them, for any purposes other than those mentioned in clause (2) of Article 32. The Court may also transfer any case, appeal, or other proceedings pending before any High Court to any other High Court if it deems it expedient for the ends of justice.

The document also discusses the ancillary powers of the Supreme Court, which Parliament may confer upon the Supreme Court for the purpose of enabling the court more effectively to exercise the jurisdiction conferred upon it by or under this Constitution. The law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India. The Supreme Court may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and any decree so passed or order so made shall be enforceable throughout the territory of India.

The document highlights the power of the President to consult the Supreme Court on any question of law or fact of such a nature and of such public importance that it is expedient to obtain the opinion of the Supreme Court upon it. The President may also refer a dispute of the kind mentioned in the proviso to Article 131 to the Supreme Court for opinion. All authorities, civil and judicial, in the territory of India shall act in aid of the Supreme Court.

The document also discusses the rules of court, which the Supreme Court may make from time to time, with the approval of the President, for regulating generally the practice and procedure of the Court. The rules may fix the minimum number of Judges who are to sit for any purpose and may provide for the powers of single Judges and Division Courts. The minimum number of Judges who are to sit for the purpose of deciding any case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this Constitution or for the purpose of hearing any reference under Article 143 shall be five.

The document outlines several provisions related to Indian laws. First, it discusses the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and procedures for hearing cases involving constitutional questions. The Court is required to seek the opinion of the Attorney General of India on such questions and dispose of the appeal in conformity with such opinion. No judgment can be delivered without the concurrence of a majority of the Judges present at the hearing.

Next, the document discusses the appointment, conditions of service, and administrative powers of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India. The Comptroller and Auditor-General is appointed by the President and can only be removed in the same manner as a Judge of the Supreme Court. question_text: What is the punishment for advocates if the established finding of the Bar Council is misappropriation?

context:
Under Section 9, the Bar Council of India is responsible for constituting disciplinary committees to investigate and punish misconduct by advocates. These committees can meet at any time and place, and must observe rules of procedure prescribed by the Bar Council of India.

Section 10B outlines the disqualification of members of a Bar Council. A member can be disqualified if they are absent without sufficient excuse from three consecutive meetings, if their name is removed from the roll of advocates, or if they are otherwise disqualified under any rule made by the Bar Council of India.

Section 11 allows every Bar Council to appoint a secretary, an accountant, and such other persons on its staff as it deems necessary. The secretary and accountant must possess qualifications prescribed by the Bar Council of India.

Under Section 12, every Bar Council must maintain books of accounts and other books in the form and manner prescribed. The accounts of a Bar Council must be audited by auditors qualified to act as auditors of companies under the Companies Act, 1956. The audited accounts must be sent to the Bar Council of India and published in the official Gazette.

Section 13 states that no act done by a Bar Council or any committee thereof shall be called in question on the ground merely of the existence of any vacancy in, or any defect in the constitution of, the Council or committee.

Section 14 states that no election of a member to a Bar Council shall be called in question on the ground merely that due notice thereof has not been given to any person entitled to vote thereat, if notice of the date has, not less than thirty days before that date, been published in the Official Gazette.

Finally, Section 15 gives the Bar Council the power to make rules to carry out the purposes of this Chapter. These rules may provide for the election of members of the Bar Council, the manner of election of the Chairman and Vice-Chairman, the filling of casual vacancies, the powers and duties of the Chairman and Vice-Chairman, the constitution of funds, the summoning and holding of meetings, the conduct of business, the qualifications and conditions of service of the secretary, the accountant and other employees, the maintenance of books of accounts, the appointment of auditors, and the management and investment of the funds of the Bar Council. No rules made under this section by a State Bar Council shall have effect unless they have been approved by the Bar Council of India.
