If the person resists or attempts to evade arrest, the police officer may use all necessary means to effect the arrest (Section 46(2)). Section 46(4) states that a woman shall not be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, except in exceptional circumstances.

Section 22 to 26 of the Act deal with the taxation of income from house property. The annual value of a property is determined based on the rent received or receivable, and certain deductions are allowed, such as a standard deduction of 30% and interest paid on borrowed capital. However, the amount of deduction is limited to Rs. 30,000 in respect of properties referred to in sub-section (2) of section 23. Where the property has been acquired or constructed with borrowed capital, the interest payable on such capital for the period prior to the previous year in which the property has been acquired or constructed is deducted in equal instalments for the previous year and for each of the four immediately succeeding previous years.

Section 25 provides that any interest chargeable under the Act, which is payable outside India, on which tax has not been paid or deducted under Chapter XVII-B, and in respect of which there is no person in India who may be treated as an agent under section 163, shall not be deducted in computing the income chargeable under the head “Income from house property”.

Section 25A deals with the taxation of arrears of rent and unrealised rent received subsequently. The amount of arrears of rent received from a tenant or the unrealised rent realised subsequently from a tenant is deemed to be the income from house property in respect of the financial year in which such rent is received or realised. A sum equal to 30% of the arrears of rent or the unrealised rent is allowed as deduction.

Section 26 provides that where property consisting of buildings or buildings and lands appurtenant thereto is owned by two or more persons and their respective shares are definite and ascertainable, such persons shall not in respect of such property be assessed as an association of persons, but the share of each such person in the income from the property as computed in accordance with sections 22 to 25 shall be included in his total income.

Section 27 defines certain legal terms used in sections 22 to 26. An individual who transfers otherwise than for adequate consideration any house property to his or her spouse, not being a transfer in connection with an agreement to live apart, or to a minor child not being a married daughter, is deemed to be the owner of the house property so transferred. The holder of an impartible estate is deemed to be the individual owner of all the properties comprised in the estate. A member of a co-operative society, company, or other association of persons to whom a building or part thereof is allotted or leased under a house building scheme of the society, company, or association is deemed to be the owner of that building or part thereof.

Section 28 deals with the taxation of profits and gains of business or profession. The profits and gains of any business or profession which was carried on by the assessee at any time during the previous year are chargeable to income-tax under the head “Profits and gains of business or profession”. Any compensation or other payment due to or received by a person, at or in connection with the termination of his management or the modification of the terms and conditions relating thereto, is also chargeable to income-tax under this head.

The section allows the assessee to declare a profit of 8% or 6% of the total turnover or gross receipts, as the case may be, subject to certain conditions. The Indian Evidence Act of 1872 outlines the rules for the admission of evidence in legal proceedings in India. The Act defines an admission as a statement made by a party or their agent that suggests any inference as to a fact in issue or a relevant fact. Admissions can be made orally, in writing, or electronically. Admissions made by parties to a proceeding, or their agents, are admissible as evidence. Admissions made by parties in a representative capacity, such as a suitor, are admissible if made while they held that character. Admissions made by parties interested in the subject matter or persons from whom they have derived their interest are admissible if made during the continuance of their interest. Statements made by persons whose position or liability must be proved in the suit are admissions if made while they occupy that position or are subject to that liability. Statements made by persons to whom a party has expressly referred for information are also admissions. Admissions can be proved by or on behalf of the person making them in certain circumstances, such as if the statement is of a nature that would be relevant if the person were dead, or if it is relevant otherwise than as an admission. Oral admissions as to the contents of a document are not relevant unless the party proposing to prove them shows that they are entitled to give secondary evidence of the contents of the document or if the genuineness of the document is in question. In civil cases, no admission is relevant if it is made on the condition that evidence of it is not to be given or if the parties agreed that evidence of it should not be given. THE INDIAN BAR COUNCILS ACT, 1926, is an Act to provide for the constitution of Bar Councils for certain courts, confer powers and impose duties on such Bar Councils, and consolidate and amend the law relating to legal practitioners entitled to practice in such courts. The Act consists of 20 sections divided into three chapters: Preliminary, Constitution of Bar Councils, and Miscellaneous.

In the Preliminary chapter, Section 1 provides the short title, extent, and application of the Act, while Section 2 explains the interpretation of terms used in the Act. The term "advocate" refers to an advocate entered in the roll of advocates of a High Court under the provisions of this Act; "Advocate-General" includes, where there is no Advocate-General, the Government Advocate and, where there is no Advocate-General or Government Advocate, such officer as the State Government may declare to be the Advocate-General for the purposes of this Act; "High Court" means a High Court to which this Act applies; and "prescribed" means prescribed by rules made under this Act.

The Constitution of Bar Councils chapter includes Sections 3 to 7. Section 3 provides for the constitution and incorporation of Bar Councils, while Section 4 explains the composition of Bar Councils. Every Bar Council shall consist of fifteen members, of whom one shall be the Advocate-General, four shall be persons nominated by the High Court, and ten shall be elected by the advocates of the High Court from amongst their number. Of the elected members of every Bar Council, not less than five shall be persons who have for not less than ten years been entitled as of right to practise in the High Court for which the Bar Council has been constituted.

Section 5 contains special provisions regarding the constitution of the first Bar Councils, while Section 5A provides for the Ad hoc Bar Council for the Gujarat High Court. Section 6 allows for the making of rules regarding the constitution and procedure of Bar Councils, while Section 7 permits the Bar Council to make bye-laws for the appointment of ministerial officers and servants, and the appointment and constitution of Committees of the Council, the procedure of such Committees, and the determination of the powers or duties of the Council which may be delegated to such Committees.

The Miscellaneous chapter includes Sections 8 to 20. Section 8 provides for the enrolment of advocates, while Section 9 explains the qualifications and admission of advocates. The Bar Council may, with the previous sanction of the High Court, make rules to regulate the admission of persons to be advocates of the High Court. Section 10 to 13, which dealt with punishment of advocate for misconduct, tribunal of Bar Council, procedure in inquiries, and powers of the Tribunal and Courts in inquiries, respectively, have been repealed by the Advocates Act, 1961.

Section 14 provides for the right of advocates to practice, while Section 15 allows the Bar Council to make rules consistent with this Act to provide for and regulate any of the following matters, namely: the rights and duties of the advocates of the High Court and their discipline and professional conduct; the conditions subject to which advocates of other High Courts may be permitted to practise in the High Court; the giving of facilities for legal education and training and the holding and conduct of examinations by the Bar Council; the charging of fees payable to the Bar Council in respect of the enjoyment of educational facilities provided, or of the right to appear at examinations held, by the Bar Council; the investment and management of the funds of the Bar Council; and any other matter in respect of which the High Court may require rules to be made under this section.

Section 16 allows for the fixing of fees payable as costs, while Section 17 provides for indemnity against legal proceedings. Section 18 requires the publication of rules, while Section 19 deals with amendment of enactments, etc. When sections 8 to 16 come into force in respect of any High Court, any enactment mentioned in the first column of the Schedule which is in force in any State in which the High Court exercises jurisdiction shall, for the purpose of its application to that State, be amended to the extent and in the manner specified in the second column of the Schedule.

The Act defines "civil rights" as any right accruing to a person by reason of the abolition of "untouchability" under Article 17 of the Constitution. The disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India may pass such order, including varying the punishment awarded by the disciplinary committee of the State Bar Council, as it deems fit. However, no order of the disciplinary committee of the State Bar Council shall be varied so as to prejudicially affect the person aggrieved without giving him reasonable opportunity of being heard.

Section 38 provides for an appeal to the Supreme Court against an order made by the disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India under Section 36 or Section 37 or the Attorney-General of India or the Advocate-General of the State concerned. The appeal must be made within sixty days of the date on which the order is communicated to the aggrieved person. The Supreme Court may pass such order, including varying the punishment awarded by the disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India, as it deems fit. However, no order of the disciplinary committee of the Bar Council of India shall be varied so as to prejudicially affect the person aggrieved without giving him a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

Section 39 states that the provisions of sections 5 and 12 of the Limitation Act, 1963, shall apply to appeals under Section 37 and Section 38.

The Act consists of 20 sections divided into three chapters: Preliminary, Constitution of Bar Councils, and Miscellaneous.

In the Preliminary chapter, Section 1 provides the short title, extent, and application of the Act, while Section 2 explains the interpretation of terms used in the Act. The term "advocate" refers to an advocate entered in the roll of advocates of a High Court under the provisions of this Act; "Advocate-General" includes, where there is no Advocate-General, the Government Advocate and, where there is no Advocate-General or Government Advocate, such officer as the State Government may declare to be the Advocate-General for the purposes of this Act; "High Court" means a High Court to which this Act applies; and "prescribed" means prescribed by rules made under this Act.

The Constitution of Bar Councils chapter includes Sections 3 to 7. Section 3 provides for the constitution and incorporation of Bar Councils, while Section 4 explains the composition of Bar Councils. Every Bar Council shall consist of fifteen members, of whom one shall be the Advocate-General, four shall be persons nominated by the High Court, and ten shall be elected by the advocates of the High Court from amongst their number. Of the elected members of every Bar Council, not less than five shall be persons who have for not less than ten years been entitled as of right to practise in the High Court for which the Bar Council has been constituted.

Section 5 contains special provisions regarding the constitution of the first Bar Councils, while Section 5A provides for the Ad hoc Bar Council for the Gujarat High Court. The Miscellaneous chapter includes Sections 8 to 20. Section 8 provides for the enrolment of advocates, while Section 9 explains the qualifications and admission of advocates. The Bar Council may, with the previous sanction of the High Court, make rules to regulate the admission of persons to be advocates of the High Court. Summary:
The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 establishes a National Green Tribunal for the effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to environmental protection and conservation of forests and other natural resources. The Act defines various terms related to the environment, such as "hazardous substance", "injury", "person", and "substantial question relating to environment". The Tribunal shall consist of a full-time Chairperson, not less than ten but subject to maximum of twenty full-time Judicial Members, and not less than ten but subject to maximum of twenty full-time Expert Members. The Chairperson, Judicial Members and Expert Members shall not hold any other office during their tenure as such. The Act also provides for the appointment, term of office, salaries, allowances and other terms and conditions of service of the Chairperson, Judicial Members and Expert Members. The Tribunal shall have the jurisdiction to settle disputes involving a substantial question relating to environment arising out of the implementation of the enactments specified in Schedule I. The Tribunal may also provide relief and compensation to the victims of pollution and other environmental damage arising under the enactments specified in Schedule I. The Tribunal shall have appellate jurisdiction over certain orders and decisions made under various environmental laws. The Act also provides for the liability to pay relief or compensation in certain cases and sets out the procedure for making an application or appeal to the Tribunal. The Tribunal shall not be bound by the procedure laid down by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but shall be guided by the principles of natural justice. The Tribunal shall have the same powers as a civil court for the purposes of discharging its functions. The Tribunal shall apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle while passing any order or decision or award. The decision of the Tribunal by majority shall be binding. Any person aggrieved by any award, decision or order of the Tribunal may file an appeal to the Supreme Court within ninety days from the date of communication of the award, decision or order of the Tribunal. The Tribunal shall have the power to make rules for carrying out the provisions of this Act. The Act also amends certain enactments, such as the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977, the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 to provide for an appeal to the National Green Tribunal.

The Act also imposes penalties for violations of its provisions.

Key provisions of the Act include:

* The Central Government has the power to take all necessary measures to protect and improve the environment, including laying down standards for the quality of the environment and emission or discharge of environmental pollutants, restricting areas where certain industries, operations, or processes can be carried out, and establishing procedures and safeguards for the prevention of accidents that may cause environmental pollution.
* Persons carrying on any industry, operation, or process are prohibited from discharging or emitting any environmental pollutant in excess of the standards prescribed.
* Persons handling hazardous substances must comply with prescribed procedures and safeguards.
* Persons responsible for the discharge of environmental pollutants in excess of the prescribed standards must take remedial measures to prevent or mitigate environmental pollution and inform the authorities or agencies prescribed.
* The Central Government or any officer empowered by it has the power to take samples of air, water, soil, or other substances for analysis, and the results of such analysis are admissible as evidence in legal proceedings.
* Environmental laboratories are established or recognized by the Central Government to carry out the functions entrusted to them under this Act.

question_text: The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under Consumer Protection Act, 2019 shall have the jurisdiction to complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration exceeds Rs.______.

context:
Summary:
The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is an Act to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumer councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers’ disputes and for matters connected therewith. The Act establishes three tiers of consumer dispute redressal agencies, namely, the District Forum, the State Commission, and the National Commission. The District Forum has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed does not exceed rupees twenty lakhs. The State Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed exceeds rupees twenty lakhs but does not exceed rupees one crore, and appeals against the orders of any District Forum within the State. The National Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed exceeds rupees one crore, and appeals against the orders of any State Commission. The Act also provides for the appointment of members to these forums, their qualifications, terms of office, salaries and allowances, resignation, removal, and other terms and conditions of service. The Act also lays down the procedure for filing and disposing of complaints and appeals, and the powers and functions of the consumer dispute redressal agencies. The Act also provides for penalties for non-compliance with the orders of the consumer dispute redressal agencies, and protection of action taken in good faith. The Act also empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act, and the State Governments to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act in relation to the State Commissions and District Fora. The Act also empowers the National Commission to make regulations not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act for carrying out the provisions of the Act.
Summary:

The Commercial Courts Act, 2015, is an Act to provide for the constitution of Commercial Courts, Commercial Appellate Courts, Commercial Division and Commercial Appellate Division in the High Courts for adjudicating commercial disputes of specified value and matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The Act defines commercial dispute as a dispute arising out of ordinary transactions of merchants, bankers, financiers and traders, export or import of merchandise or services, issues relating to admiralty and maritime law, transactions relating to aircraft, aircraft engines, aircraft equipment and helicopters, including sales, leasing and financing of the same, carriage of goods, construction and infrastructure contracts, including tenders, agreements relating to immovable property used exclusively in trade or commerce, franchising agreements, distribution and licensing agreements, management and consultancy agreements, joint venture agreements, shareholders agreements, subscription and investment agreements pertaining to the services industry including outsourcing services and financial services, mercantile agency and mercantile usage, partnership agreements, technology development agreements, intellectual property rights relating to registered and unregistered trademarks, copyright, patent, design, domain names, geographical indications and semiconductor integrated circuits, agreements for sale of goods or provision of services, exploitation of oil and gas reserves or other natural resources including electromagnetic spectrum, insurance and re-insurance, contracts of agency relating to any of the above, and such other commercial disputes as may be notified by the Central Government.

The Act specifies the jurisdiction of Commercial Courts, Commercial Divisions of High Courts, and Commercial Appellate Divisions of High Courts. It also provides for the transfer of pending suits and applications relating to commercial disputes of a specified value to the Commercial Courts or Commercial Divisions of High Courts. The Act amends the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, in its application to commercial disputes. It also provides for the collection and disclosure of data by Commercial Courts, Commercial Divisions and Commercial Appellate Divisions, the power of High Court to issue directions, the provision of infrastructure facilities, training and continuous education, and the power of the Central Government to make rules. The Act has an overriding effect and repeals and saves the Commercial Courts, Commercial Division and Commercial Appellate Division of High Courts Ordinance, 2015. The Act also contains a Schedule that amends the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

The Act aims to provide a specialized forum for adjudicating commercial disputes and to ensure speedy and efficient disposal of such disputes. It also seeks to promote ease of doing business in India by reducing the time and cost of litigation in commercial matters.

If the complaint relates to services, the District Commission shall refer a copy of the complaint to the opposite party and direct him to give his version of the case within a period of thirty days.

If the President and a member of the Commission differ on a point, it is referred to another member for hearing and the majority opinion is the order of the Commission. question_text: For an individual to be deemed to be resident in India in any previous year one of the condition is:
options:
A) If he is in India for a period of 182 days or more during the previous year. 
 B) If he is in India for a period of 180 days or more during the previous year. 
 C) If he is in India for a period of 181 days or more during the previous year.

context:
1. Previous Year: The previous year is defined as the financial year immediately preceding the assessment year, except in the case of a newly set-up business or profession or a new source of income, where the previous year begins with the date of establishment or commencement of the source of income and ends with the financial year.
2. Charge of Income-tax: Income tax is charged for any assessment year at the specified rate or rates for the total income of the previous year, subject to the provisions of the Act. The tax is deducted at the source or paid in advance where it is deductible or payable under the Act.
3. Scope of Total Income:
a. For a resident individual, the total income includes income received or deemed to be received in India, income accrued or arisen or deemed to accrue or arise in India, and income accrued or arisen outside India if the individual is ordinarily resident and the income is derived from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India.
b. For a non-resident individual, the total income includes income received or deemed to be received in India and income accrued or arisen or deemed to accrue or arise in India.
4. Apportionment of Income between Spouses Governed by Portuguese Civil Code: In the case of spouses governed by the Portuguese Civil Code, their income under any head of income (excluding 'Salaries') is apportioned equally between them. The income so apportioned is included separately in their respective total income.
5. Residence in India: An individual is said to be a resident in India if they are in India for at least 182 days or more in a previous year or have been in India for a period or periods amounting to 365 days or more in the four years preceding that year and are in India for at least 60 days or more in that year. However, certain exceptions apply to this rule for individuals who are citizens of India or persons of Indian origin. They are considered residents if they are in India for at least 182 days or more in a previous year for the purpose of employment outside India or as a member of the crew of an Indian ship.

Under Section 6 of the Act, a Hindu undivided family, firm, or other association of persons is said to be a resident in India in any previous year if the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly in India. A company is said to be a resident in India if it is an Indian company or if its place of effective management is in India. The Explanation to this clause provides that in the case of a non-resident, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from operations which are confined to the purchase of goods in India for the purpose of export, or to a non-resident, being a person engaged in the business of running a news agency or of publishing newspapers, magazines or journals, no income shall be deemed to accrue or arise in India to him through or from activities which are confined to the collection of news and views in India for transmission out of India. Summary of THE INDIAN SUCCESSION ACT, 1925:

The Indian Succession Act, 1925, is an Act that consolidates the law applicable to intestate and testamentary succession. The Act is divided into two parts. The first part, titled "Preliminary," contains the short title, definitions, and power of the State Government to exempt any race, sect, or tribe in the State from the operation of the Act. The second part, titled "Of Domicile," outlines the laws regulating succession to a deceased person's immoveable and moveable property.

Under Part II, the Act states that succession to the immoveable property of a person deceased is regulated by the law of India, wherever the person may have had his domicile at the time of his death. Succession to the moveable property of a person deceased, on the other hand, is regulated by the law of the country in which the person had his domicile at the time of his death. The Act also states that a person can have only one domicile for the purpose of the succession to his moveable property.

The Act also outlines the rules for determining a person's domicile of origin, which is the country in which the person was born. The domicile of origin prevails until a new domicile has been acquired. A man acquires a new domicile by taking up his fixed habitation in a country which is not that of his domicile of origin. The Act provides illustrations of how a new domicile can be acquired, such as by settling as a barrister or a merchant in a new country with the intention of residing there during the remainder of one's life.

The Act also contains provisions for acquiring a domicile in India by making and depositing a declaration in writing under one's hand of his desire to acquire such domicile in an office in India appointed in this behalf by the State Government. Additionally, the Act states that a person who is appointed by the Government of one country to be its ambassador, consul, or other representative in another country does not acquire a domicile in the latter country by reason only of residing there in pursuance of his appointment.

In summary, the Indian Succession Act, 1925, is an Act that consolidates the law applicable to intestate and testamentary succession. The Act outlines the laws regulating succession to a deceased person's immoveable and moveable property, and provides rules for determining a person's domicile of origin and how a new domicile can be acquired. The Act also contains provisions for acquiring a domicile in India and states that a person who is appointed by the Government of one country to be its ambassador, consul, or other representative in another country does not acquire a domicile in the latter country by reason only of residing there in pursuance of his appointment.
The document discusses the concept of domicile in the context of Indian laws. It explains that a person cannot acquire a new domicile during their minority, except in certain circumstances. An insane person can only acquire a new domicile by following the domicile of another person. If a person dies in India and there is no proof of any domicile elsewhere, the succession to their moveable property is regulated by Indian law.

The document also discusses the impact of marriage on a person's property rights in India. It explains that a person does not acquire any interest in the property of the person they marry or become incapable of doing any act in respect of their own property by getting married. This provision does not apply to marriages contracted before January 1, 1866, or to marriages where one or both parties professed the Hindu, Muhammadan, Buddhist, Sikh, or Jaina religion at the time of the marriage.

The document also discusses the concept of consanguinity, which is the connection or relation of persons descended from the same stock or common ancestor. Lineal consanguinity is the connection between two persons where one is descended in a direct line from the other, as between a man and his father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and so on. Collateral consanguinity is the connection between two persons who are descended from the same stock or ancestor, but neither of whom is descended in a direct line from the other.

For the purpose of succession, there is no distinction between those who are related to a person deceased through his father and those who are related to him through his mother, or between those who are related to a person deceased by the full blood and those who are related to him by the half blood.

The property of an intestate devolves upon the wife or husband, or upon those who are of the kindred of the deceased, in the order and according to the rules contained in the document.

The sale of tangible immoveable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or in the case of a reversion or other intangible thing, can only be made by a registered instrument. In the case of tangible immoveable property of a value less than one hundred rupees, such transfer may be made either by a registered instrument or by delivery of the property. Delivery of tangible immoveable property takes place when the seller places the buyer, or such person as he directs, in possession of the property. A contract for the sale of immoveable property is a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between the parties, but it does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on such property.

The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 55, outlines the rights and liabilities of the buyer and seller in the absence of a contract to the contrary. The seller is bound to disclose to the buyer any material defect in the property or in the seller’s title thereto of which the seller is, and the buyer is not, aware, and which the buyer could not with ordinary care discover. The seller is also bound to produce to the buyer on his request for examination all documents of title relating to the property which are in the seller's possession or power, to answer to the best of his information all relevant questions put to him by the buyer in respect to the property or the title thereto, and on payment or tender of the amount due in respect of the price, to execute a proper conveyance of the property when the buyer tenders it to him for execution at a proper time and place. The seller is also entitled to the rents and profits of the property till the ownership thereof passes to the buyer and where the ownership of the property has passed to the buyer, to a charge upon the property in the hands of the buyer for the amount of the purchase-money, or any part thereof remaining unpaid, and for interest on such amount or part from the date on which possession has been delivered.

The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 53A, states that where any person contracts to transfer for consideration any immoveable property by writing signed by him or on his behalf from which the terms necessary to constitute the transfer can be ascertained with reasonable certainty, and the transferee has, in part performance of the contract, taken possession of the property or any part thereof, or the transferee, being already in possession, continues in possession in part performance of the contract and has done some act in furtherance of the contract, and the transferee has performed or is willing to perform his part of the contract, then, notwithstanding that the transfer has not been completed in the manner prescribed therefor by the law for the time being in force, the transferor or any person claiming under him shall be debarred from enforcing against the transferee and persons claiming under him any right in respect of the property of which the transferee has taken or continued in possession, other than a right expressly provided by the terms of the contract.

Section 25 states that an agreement made without consideration is void, unless it is expressed in writing and registered, or is a promise to compensate for something done, or is a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation law. Section 26 states that every agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person, other than a minor, is void. Section 27 states that every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void. Section 28 states that every agreement, by which any party thereto is restricted absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any contract, by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or which limits the time within which he may thus enforce his rights, is void to that extent. However, this section does not render illegal a contract to refer to arbitration any dispute that may arise or any question between them which has already arisen.
The Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen. A contingent contract cannot be enforced by law unless and until the event on which it is contingent has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event does not happen can be enforced when the happening of that event becomes impossible, and not before. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if a specified uncertain event happens within a fixed time become void if, at the expiration of the time fixed, such event has not happened, or if, before the time fixed, such event becomes impossible. Contingent agreements to do or not to do anything, if an impossible event happens, are void, whether the impossibility of the event is known or not to the parties to the agreement at the time when it is made. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law. Promises bind the representatives of the promisors in case of the death of such promisors before performance, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If a promisor has made an offer of performance to the promisee, and the offer has not been accepted, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance, nor does he thereby lose his rights under the contract. Every such offer must fulfill certain conditions, such as being unconditional, made at a proper time and place, and under such circumstances that the person to whom it is made may have a reasonable opportunity of ascertaining that the person by whom it is made is able and willing there and then to do the whole of what he is bound by his promise to do. If the offer is an offer to deliver anything to the promisee, the promisee must have a reasonable opportunity of seeing that the thing offered is the thing which the promisor is bound by his promise to deliver.

The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the legal framework for contracts in India. The act defines a contract as an agreement that is enforceable by law, and it specifies the essential elements of a contract, including offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity to contract, and free consent.

Summary:
The Specific Relief Act, 1963 (Act No. 47 of 1963) is an Act that defines and amends the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief. The Act is divided into three parts. Part I is the preliminary part, which includes the short title, extent, commencement, definitions, savings, and specific relief to be granted only for enforcing individual civil rights and not for enforcing penal laws. Part II is the specific relief part, which includes Chapter I on recovering possession of property, Chapter II on specific performance of contracts, Chapter III on rectification of instruments, Chapter IV on rescission of contracts, Chapter V on cancellation of instruments, Chapter VI on declaratory decrees, Chapter VII on injunctions generally, and Chapter VIII on perpetual injunctions. Part III is the preventive relief part, which includes Chapter IX on temporary and perpetual injunctions, and Chapter X on perpetual injunctions. The Act also includes a schedule that lists the category of projects and infrastructure sub-sectors.

Under Part II, Chapter II on specific performance of contracts, the Act states that specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14, and section 16. The Act also states that specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favor of a person who has obtained substituted performance of the contract under section 20 or who has become incapable of performing, or violates any essential term of, the contract that remains to be performed, or acts in fraud of the contract, or wilfully acts at variance with or in subversion of the relation intended to be established by the contract. The Act also provides for the circumstances under which specific performance may be enforced, such as when the contract is in writing and signed by the party to be charged, when the party to be charged is able to perform the contract, and when the contract is not a contract for the sale of immovable property or for the supply of goods.

Under Part II, Chapter III on rectification of instruments, the Act states that when, through fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, a contract or other instrument in writing does not express their real intention, either party or his representative in interest may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified. The court may, in its discretion, direct rectification of the instrument so as to express that intention, so far as this can be done without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value.

Under Part II, Chapter IV on rescission of contracts, the Act states that any person interested in a contract may sue to have it rescinded, and such rescission may be adjudged by the court in any of the following cases, namely: (a) where the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff; (b) where the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. The Act also states that the court may refuse to rescind the contract if the plaintiff has expressly or impliedly ratified the contract, or if owing to the change of circumstances which has taken place since the making of the contract, the parties cannot be substantially restored to the position in which they stood when the contract was made, or if third parties have, during the subsistence of the contract, acquired rights in good faith without notice and for value, or if only a part of the contract is sought to be rescinded and such part is not severable from the rest of the contract.

Under Part II, Chapter V on cancellation of instruments, the Act states that any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, and who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable, and the court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled.

Under Part II, Chapter VI on declaratory decrees, the Act states that any person entitled to any legal character or to any right as to any property may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may, in its discretion, make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief.

The preliminary decree for foreclosure is issued when the plaintiff has made a claim for foreclosure of the mortgaged property. The decree states the amount due to the plaintiff for principal, interest, costs, charges, and expenses. The defendant is ordered to pay the specified amount into court on or before a certain date. If the defendant fails to make the payment, the plaintiff can apply for a final decree of foreclosure.

The final decree for foreclosure is issued when the payment directed by the preliminary decree has not been made. The defendant is ordered to pay into court such sum as the court shall find due and the costs of the suit awarded to the plaintiff.

question_text: By which of the following Amendment Act of 1985, Anti Defection Law was added in the Constitution of India?

context:
The Constitution (Fifty-second Amendment) Act, 1985 amends the Constitution of India to provide that an elected member of Parliament or a State Legislature, who has been elected as a candidate set up by a political party and a nominated member of Parliament or a State Legislature who is a member of a political party at the time he takes his seat or who becomes a member of a political party within six months after he takes his seat would be disqualified on the ground of defection if he voluntarily relinquishes his membership of such political party or votes or abstains from voting in such House contrary to any direction of such party or is expelled from such party. An independent member of Parliament or a State Legislature shall also be disqualified if he joins any political party after his election. A nominated member of Parliament or a State Legislature who is not a member of a political party at the time of his nomination and who has not become a member of any political party before the expiry of six months from the date on which he takes his seat shall be disqualified if he joins any political party after the expiry of the said period of six months. The Act also makes suitable provisions with respect to splits in, and mergers of, political parties. A special provision has been included in the Act to enable a person who has been elected as the presiding officer of a House to sever his connections with his political party. The question as to whether a member of a House of Parliament or State Legislature has become subject to the proposed disqualification will be determined by the presiding officer of the House; where the question is with reference to the presiding officer himself, it will be decided by a member of the House elected by the House in that behalf. The Act amends articles 101, 102, 190, 191, 361B, 194, and 195 of the Constitution and inserts a new article 102A and a new Tenth Schedule. The Tenth Schedule provides for the disqualification of members of Parliament and State Legislatures on the ground of defection.
Summary:

The Act applies to citizens of India outside India and extends to the whole of India. The Act defines various terms such as certificate, conveyance, dependent, emigrant, emigrant conveyance, employer, employment, notification, prescribed, Protector of Emigrants, recruiting agent, recruitment, registering authority, work, and other related terms.

Chapter II of the Act deals with emigration authorities, including the appointment, duties, and powers of Protectors of Emigrants, the power to authorize persons to exercise functions of a Protector, the setting up of emigration check-posts, the appointment of officers in charge of emigration check-posts, and the appointment of other emigration officers and staff.

Chapter III of the Act deals with the registration of recruiting agents, including the appointment of the registering authority, the requirement of a valid certificate for functioning as a recruiting agent, the application for registration, the terms and conditions of registration, and the renewal of registration.

Chapter IV of the Act deals with permits for recruitment by employers, including the competent authority for issuing permits, the procedure for obtaining permits, the period of validity of permits, the registration of certain permits, and the cancellation or suspension of a permit.

Chapter V of the Act deals with emigration clearance, including the requirement of emigration clearance, the procedure for obtaining emigration clearance, the grounds for rejection of an application for emigration clearance, and the registration of certain permits.

Chapter VI of the Act deals with appeals, including the grounds for preferring an appeal, the period for preferring an appeal, the procedure for disposing of an appeal, and the finality of the order made on an appeal.

Chapter VII of the Act deals with offences and penalties, including the offences and penalties under the Act, the offences to be cognizable, the previous sanction of the Central Government necessary for prosecution, punishment to be without prejudice to any other action, and the determination of question as to whether a person is an emigrant.

Chapter VIII of the Act deals with miscellaneous provisions, including the power to prohibit emigration to any country in the interests of the general public, the power to prohibit emigration due to outbreak of epidemics, civil disturbances, etc., in a country, the power to prohibit emigration of any class or category of persons, provisions as to security, refund of security, power to search, seize and detain persons, conveyance, etc., returns and registers, authorities and officers to have certain powers of civil court, power to give directions, effect of other laws, delegation, power to exempt, and power to make rules.

question_text: In which one of the following cases the Supreme Court decided that, a constitutional amendment is a 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) and therefore if it violates any of the fundamental rights it may be declared void?
options:
A) Sajjan Singh V. State of Rajasthan 
 B) Keshvananda Bharati V. State of Kerala 
 C) Indra Sawhney V. Union of India 
 D) Golak Nath V. State of Punjab
context:
The Constitution (Twenty-Four Amendment) Act, 1971, enables Parliament to dilute Fundamental Rights through Amendments of the Constitution. The 24th Amendment was effected to abrogate the Supreme Court ruling in I.C. Golaknath and Sons v. State of Punjab, which held that Parliament did not have the power to amend Fundamental Rights.
Summary:

The case of Ors. vs State of Punjab and Anrs. (1967) established that an amendment of the Constitution is a legislative process and that any amendment under article 368 is "law" within the meaning of article 13 of the Constitution. This means that if an amendment "takes away or abridges" a Fundamental Right conferred by Part III, it is void. The Court also held that Fundamental Rights included in Part III of the Constitution are given a "transcendental position" under the Constitution and are kept beyond the reach of Parliament.

The document also discusses the concept of equality before law as outlined in Article 14 of the Constitution of India. This article guarantees equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. It is divided into two parts: Equality before the law, which indicates that all are to be treated equally in the eyes of the law, and equal protection of the laws, which means that the same law will be applied to all the people equally across the society.

The doctrine of Anti-Arbitrariness is also discussed in the document. This doctrine ensures equality of treatment and protects against the arbitrariness of State action. It was first recognized in the case of S.G. Jaisinghani v. Union of India (1967) and has been further developed through subsequent cases.

Natural Justice is also an integral part of Article 14. This means that the principles of natural justice, which include the rule against bias and the right to a fair hearing, are essential to ensuring that the right to equality is upheld.

The document also discusses the classification test, which is used to determine whether differential treatment is permitted under Article 14. This test requires that any classification must be founded on intelligible differentia and have a rational nexus with the objective sought to be achieved by the classification.

Finally, the document discusses the expansion of Article 14 in terms of defining gender. This includes the recognition of persons who fall outside the male/female gender binary, including persons who identify as "third gender". This recognition is based on the principle of equality and the right to non-discrimination.
Summary:
The Constitution (Ninety-third Amendment) Act, 2005, added a clause to Article 15 of the Indian Constitution, allowing the state to establish specific provisions for the advancement of economically weaker sections of society, as well as scheduled castes and tribes, in relation to their enrollment in academic institutions, including private institutions whether state-assisted or not, except for minority institutions. Additionally, the Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act, 2019, introduced a 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) of society for admission to Central Government-run educational institutions and private educational institutions (except for minority educational institutions), and for employment in Central Government jobs. This reservation is not mandatory in State Government-run educational institutions or State Government jobs, but some states have chosen to implement it. The quota can be availed by persons with an annual gross household income of up to ₹8 lakh (US$10,000) and families that do not own more than 5 acres of agricultural land, a house over 1,000 square feet, or a plot of over 100 yards in notified municipalities. The validity of this amendment has been challenged in the Supreme Court, with a ruling expected to be delivered in November 2022.

Article 15 of the Indian Constitution protects citizens against various forms of discrimination based on religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. It restricts discrimination in access to public places or policies established by the state. Clause 1 of the Article prohibits the State from discriminating against citizens on these five protected grounds only. Clause 2 gives access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment, wells, tanks, bathing Ghats, roads, and places of public resort to all citizens. Clause 3 provides special preference to Women and Children as a matter of positive discrimination. Clause 4 makes special provisions for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens, Schedule Caste (SC), and Schedule Tribes (ST). Clause 5 discusses Reservation in Educational institutions. Clause 6 lays down the Special Provisions for EWS category. This provision was added by the 103rd Constitutional amendment Act, 2019. This is the latest exception that provides for special provisions for the Economic Weaker Section (EWS).
The Constitution (Thirtieth Amendment) Act, 1972, was enacted to modify Article 133 of the Indian Constitution, which deals with appeals to the Supreme Court in civil cases. The Act substituted the existing clause (1) of Article 133 with a new clause, which states that an appeal can be made to the Supreme Court from the final order or judgment of a High Court in a civil proceeding only if the High Court certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance and that the question needs to be decided by the Supreme Court.

The amendment also includes a special provision for pending proceedings. According to this provision, any appeal under the previous clause (1) of Article 133, which was pending before the Supreme Court at the time of the commencement of this Act, can be heard and disposed of by the Supreme Court as if this Act had not been passed. Similarly, any appeal preferred on or after the commencement of this Act against any judgment, decree, or final order in a civil proceeding of a High Court by virtue of a certificate given by the High Court before the commencement of this Act can also be entertained and disposed of by the Supreme Court.

Furthermore, the amendment states that no appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court under the amended clause (1) of Article 133 from any judgment, decree, or final order arising out of a suit or other civil proceeding which was instituted or commenced in any court before the commencement of this Act, unless such appeal satisfies the provisions of that clause as amended by this Act.

In summary, the Constitution (Thirtieth Amendment) Act, 1972, changed the criteria for appeals in civil cases before the Supreme Court of India from a value criterion to one based on important legal issues. The amendment aims to streamline the process for hearing civil appeals in the Supreme Court and ensure that only cases involving significant legal questions are considered by the Court.

question_text: Uniform Civil Code in India is:
options:
A) Fundamental Rights 
 B) Directive Principles of State Policy 
 C) Government Policy 
 D) Constitutional Right
context:
The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, is a procedural law that governs the filing, hearing, and disposal of civil suits in India. It was enacted in 1908 and has been amended several times since then. The Code applies to the whole of India except for the state of Nagaland and the tribal areas, and the application of the Code to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, and certain agencies in Andhra Pradesh is subject to the application of any rule or regulation for the time being in force in those areas.

The Code defines various legal terms used in civil proceedings, such as "decree," "decree-holder," "district," "foreign Court," "foreign judgment," "Government Pleader," "High Court," "Judge," "judgment," "judgment-debtor," "legal representative," "mesne profits," "movable property," "order," "pleader," "prescribed," "public officer," "rules," "share in a corporation," and "signed."

Under the Code, the District Court is subordinate to the High Court, and every Civil Court of a grade inferior to that of a District Court and every Court of Small Causes is subordinate to the High Court and District Court. The Code also provides for the subordination of Revenue Courts, which are governed by the provisions of this Code in those matters of procedure upon which any special enactment applicable to them is silent.

The Code lays down the pecuniary jurisdiction of Civil Courts, which means that Civil Courts have jurisdiction over suits the amount or value of the subject-matter of which does not exceed the pecuniary limits of their ordinary jurisdiction. The Code also provides for the application of the Code to Revenue Courts, which may be excluded from the application of certain portions of the Code by notification in the Official Gazette by the State Government.

The Code provides for the stay of suits, which means that no Court shall proceed with the trial of any suit in which the matter in issue is also directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title where such suit is pending in the same or any other Court in India having jurisdiction to grant the relief claimed, or in any Court beyond the limits of India established or continued by the Central Government and having like jurisdiction, or before the Supreme Court.

The Code also provides for the doctrine of res judicata, which means that no Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court.

The Code provides for the bar to further suit, which means that where a plaintiff is precluded by rules from instituting a further suit in respect of any particular cause of action, he shall not be entitled to institute a suit in respect of such cause of action in any Court to which this Code applies.

The Code provides for the conclusiveness of foreign judgments, which means that a foreign judgment shall be conclusive as to any matter thereby directly adjudicated upon between the same parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title except in certain circumstances.

The Code provides for the institution of suits, which means that every suit shall be instituted in the Court of the lowest grade competent to try it. The Code also provides for the place of suing, which means that suits for the recovery of immovable property with or without rent or profits, for the partition of immovable property, for foreclosure, sale or redemption in the case of a mortgage of or charge upon immovable property, for the determination of any other right to or interest in immovable property, for compensation for wrong to immovable property, for the recovery of movable property actually under distraint or attachment, shall be instituted in the Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the property is situate.

The Code provides for the transfer of suits, which means that where a suit may be instituted in any one of two or more Courts and is instituted in one of such Courts, any defendant, after notice to the other parties, may, at the earliest possible opportunity and in all cases where issues are settled, at or before such settlement, apply to have the suit transferred to another Court, and the Court to which such application is made, after considering the objections of the other parties (if any), shall determine in which of the several Courts having jurisdiction the suit shall proceed.
Summary:
The Civil Defence Act, 1968, is a law in India that aims to provide for civil defense and related matters. The Act is divided into four chapters. Chapter I, titled "Preliminary," includes the short title, extent, and commencement of the Act, as well as definitions of key terms used throughout the Act. Chapter II, titled "Power of Central Government to Make Rules for Civil Defence," outlines the powers of the Central Government to make rules for civil defense, including preventing the prosecution of any work likely to prejudice civil defense, providing and maintaining commodities and things required for civil defense, and regulating traffic and the use of vessels, buoys, lights, and signals in ports and territorial, tidal, and inland waters. Chapter III, titled "Civil Defence Corps," discusses the constitution of the Civil Defence Corps, the appointment of members and officers, the dismissal of members of the Corps, and the functions of members of the Corps. Chapter IV, titled "Miscellaneous," includes provisions on the application of the Personal Injuries (Emergency Provisions) Act to injuries sustained by members of the Corps, penalties for non-compliance with the Act, the effect of the Act and rules inconsistent with other enactments, the limitation of prosecutions, and the power of the Central Government to delegate. The Act also includes provisions on the protection of action taken in good faith, the status of authorized persons and members of the Corps as public servants, and the laying of rules and regulations before Parliament.

Additionally, the Constitution (One Hundred and Third Amendment) Act, 2019, introduced a 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) of society for admission to Central Government-run educational institutions and private educational institutions (except for minority educational institutions), and for employment in Central Government jobs. This reservation is not mandatory in State Government-run educational institutions or State Government jobs, but some states have chosen to implement it. The quota can be availed by persons with an annual gross household income of up to ₹8 lakh (US$10,000) and families that do not own more than 5 acres of agricultural land, a house over 1,000 square feet, or a plot of over 100 yards in notified municipalities. The validity of this amendment has been challenged in the Supreme Court, with a ruling expected to be delivered in November 2022.

Article 15 of the Indian Constitution protects citizens against various forms of discrimination based on religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. It restricts discrimination in access to public places or policies established by the state. Clause 1 of the Article prohibits the State from discriminating against citizens on these five protected grounds only. Clause 2 gives access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment, wells, tanks, bathing Ghats, roads, and places of public resort to all citizens. Clause 3 provides special preference to Women and Children as a matter of positive discrimination. Clause 4 makes special provisions for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens, Schedule Caste (SC), and Schedule Tribes (ST). Clause 5 discusses Reservation in Educational institutions. Clause 6 lays down the Special Provisions for EWS category. This provision was added by the 103rd Constitutional amendment Act, 2019. This is the latest exception that provides for special provisions for the Economic Weaker Section (EWS).

The document summarizes various Indian laws related to contracts. Section 21 states that a contract is not void due to a mistake in law, but a mistake in a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact. Section 22 states that a contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by a mistake of one party as to a matter of fact. Section 23 outlines the lawfulness of the consideration or object of an agreement, which is unlawful if it is forbidden by law, defeats the provisions of any law, is fraudulent, involves injury to the person or property of another, or is immoral or opposed to public policy. Section 24 states that if any part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any one or any part of any one of several considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void. Section 25 states that an agreement made without consideration is void, unless it is expressed in writing and registered, or is a promise to compensate for something done, or is a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation law. Section 26 states that every agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person, other than a minor, is void. Section 27 states that every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void. Section 28 states that every agreement, by which any party thereto is restricted absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any contract, by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or which limits the time within which he may thus enforce his rights, is void to that extent. However, this section does not render illegal a contract to refer to arbitration any dispute that may arise or any question between them which has already arisen.
The Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen. A contingent contract cannot be enforced by law unless and until the event on which it is contingent has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event does not happen can be enforced when the happening of that event becomes impossible, and not before. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if a specified uncertain event happens within a fixed time become void if, at the expiration of the time fixed, such event has not happened, or if, before the time fixed, such event becomes impossible. Contingent agreements to do or not to do anything, if an impossible event happens, are void, whether the impossibility of the event is known or not to the parties to the agreement at the time when it is made. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law. Promises bind the representatives of the promisors in case of the death of such promisors before performance, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If a promisor has made an offer of performance to the promisee, and the offer has not been accepted, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance, nor does he thereby lose his rights under the contract. Every such offer must fulfill certain conditions, such as being unconditional, made at a proper time and place, and under such circumstances that the person to whom it is made may have a reasonable opportunity of ascertaining that the person by whom it is made is able and willing there and then to do the whole of what he is bound by his promise to do. If the offer is an offer to deliver anything to the promisee, the promisee must have a reasonable opportunity of seeing that the thing offered is the thing which the promisor is bound by his promise to deliver.

The Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, is a law that provides for the regulation of registration of births and deaths in India. The Act applies to the whole of India and came into force on different dates in different parts of a State. Under the Act, it is the duty of certain persons to give information regarding births and deaths to the Registrar. These persons include the head of the house or the oldest adult male person present in the house in the case of a birth or death in a house, the medical officer in charge or any person authorized by him in the case of a birth or death in a hospital, health centre, maternity or nursing home or other like institution, the jailor in charge in the case of a birth or death in a jail, the person in charge in the case of a birth or death in a choultry, chattram, hostel, dharmasala, boarding-house, lodging-house, tavern, barrack, toddy shop or place of public resort, and the headman or other corresponding officer of the village or the officer in charge of the local police station in the case of a new-born child or dead body found deserted in a public place.

The Act also specifies the duties of the Registrar, including entering in the register maintained for the purpose all information given to him under section 8 or section 9, taking steps to inform himself carefully of every birth and of every death which takes place in his jurisdiction, and ascertaining and registering the particulars required to be registered. The Registrar is required to have an office in the local area for which he is appointed and to attend his office for the purpose of registering births and deaths on such days and at such hours as the Chief Registrar may direct. The Registrar may, with the prior approval of the Chief Registrar, appoint Sub-Registrars and assign to them any or all of his powers and duties in relation to specified areas within his jurisdiction.

The Act also specifies the duties of certain persons to notify births and deaths and to certify the cause of death, and provides for the correction or cancellation of entry in the register of births and deaths.

The Act requires the Registrar to keep registers of births and deaths in the prescribed form and to send periodical returns to the Chief Registrar for compilation. The Chief Registrar is required to cause the information in the returns furnished by the Registrars to be compiled and to publish for the information of the public a statistical report on the registered births and deaths during the year at such intervals and in such form as may be prescribed.

The Act provides for penalties for various offences, including failing to give information, giving false information, refusing to write one's name, description, and place of abode in the register, neglecting or refusing to register a birth or death, neglecting or refusing to submit returns, and contravening any provision of the Act for which no penalty is provided. The Act also provides for the compounding of offences and the sanction for prosecution.

The Act provides that Registrars and Sub-Registrars shall be deemed to be public servants within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, and that the State Government may delegate its powers under the Act to any officer or authority subordinate to it. If the opposite party disobeys the injunction, the Court may attach their property or detain them in civil prison. Order XL deals with the appointment of receivers. The Court may remove a receiver if they are not performing their duties or if there is a change in circumstances.

Legal Terms:

The arbitral award shall state the reasons upon which it is based, unless the parties have agreed that no reasons are to be given. The arbitral award shall state its date and the place of arbitration. After the arbitral award is made, a signed copy shall be delivered to each party. The arbitral tribunal may make an interim arbitral award on any matter with respect to which it may make a final arbitral award.

The general rule is that the unsuccessful party shall be ordered to pay the costs of the successful party. The Court or arbitral tribunal may make a different order for reasons to be recorded in writing.

An application under sub-section (2) may be made by any party unless the fees demanded have been fixed by written agreement between him and the arbitral tribunal, and the arbitral tribunal shall be entitled to appear and be heard on any such application. Nothing in this section shall affect the operation of any law by virtue of which any right of action is extinguished by the death of a person.

Section 41 deals with provisions in case of insolvency. Section 42 states that notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Part or in any other law for the time being in force, where with respect to an arbitration agreement any application under this Part has been made in a Court, that Court alone shall have jurisdiction over the arbitral proceedings and all subsequent applications arising out of that agreement and the arbitral proceedings shall be made in that Court and in no other Court.

Section 42A states that notwithstanding anything contained by any other law for the time being in force, the arbitrator, the arbitral institution and the parties to the arbitration agreement shall maintain confidentiality of all arbitral proceedings except award where its disclosure is necessary for the purpose of implementation and enforcement of award.

Section 42B states that no suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against the arbitrator for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done under this Act or the rules or regulations made thereunder.

Under Section 137, a witness can be cross-examined on any matter relevant to the case, even if it was not mentioned during the examination-in-chief. The re-examination should be directed to explaining matters referred to in cross-examination. Leading questions, which suggest the answer the person asking it wishes or expects to receive, are not allowed in examination-in-chief or re-examination without the permission of the court. However, they may be asked in cross-examination.

Section 144 allows a witness to give oral evidence of statements made by other persons about the contents of documents if such statements are in themselves relevant facts. Section 145 permits a witness to be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing or reduced into writing, relevant to matters in question, without the writing being shown to him.

Section 146 outlines the questions that can be asked during cross-examination, including those that test the veracity of the witness, discover who they are and what is their position in life, or to shake their credit by injuring their character. However, in a prosecution for certain offences under the Indian Penal Code, it is not permissible to adduce evidence or to put questions in the cross-examination of the victim as to their general immoral character or previous sexual experience.

The court has the discretion to decide whether a witness should be compelled to answer a question that relates to a matter not relevant to the suit or proceeding, except insofar as it affects the credit of the witness by injuring his character. The court shall have regard to certain considerations, such as the importance of the imputation made against the witness's character and the importance of his evidence. No such question ought to be asked unless the person asking it has reasonable grounds for thinking that the imputation is well-founded. If the court is of the opinion that any such question was asked without reasonable grounds, it may report the circumstances of the case to the High Court or other authority to which the barrister, pleader, vakil, or attorney is subject in the exercise of his profession.

Section 151 permits the court to forbid any questions or inquiries which it regards as indecent or scandalous, unless they relate to facts in issue or to matters necessary to be known in order to determine whether or not the facts in issue existed. The court shall forbid any question which appears to it to be intended to insult or annoy, or which, though proper in itself, appears to the court needlessly offensive in form. Evidence that tends to contradict answers to questions testing veracity is generally not admissible, but if a witness answers falsely, he may be charged with giving false evidence.

The Act consists of 20 sections divided into three chapters: Preliminary, Constitution of Bar Councils, and Miscellaneous.

In the Preliminary chapter, Section 1 provides the short title, extent, and application of the Act, while Section 2 explains the interpretation of terms used in the Act. The term "advocate" refers to an advocate entered in the roll of advocates of a High Court under the provisions of this Act; "Advocate-General" includes, where there is no Advocate-General, the Government Advocate and, where there is no Advocate-General or Government Advocate, such officer as the State Government may declare to be the Advocate-General for the purposes of this Act; "High Court" means a High Court to which this Act applies; and "prescribed" means prescribed by rules made under this Act.

The Constitution of Bar Councils chapter includes Sections 3 to 7. Section 3 provides for the constitution and incorporation of Bar Councils, while Section 4 explains the composition of Bar Councils. Every Bar Council shall consist of fifteen members, of whom one shall be the Advocate-General, four shall be persons nominated by the High Court, and ten shall be elected by the advocates of the High Court from amongst their number. Of the elected members of every Bar Council, not less than five shall be persons who have for not less than ten years been entitled as of right to practise in the High Court for which the Bar Council has been constituted.

Section 5 contains special provisions regarding the constitution of the first Bar Councils, while Section 5A provides for the Ad hoc Bar Council for the Gujarat High Court. Section 6 allows for the making of rules regarding the constitution and procedure of Bar Councils, while Section 7 permits the Bar Council to make bye-laws for the appointment of ministerial officers and servants, and the appointment and constitution of Committees of the Council, the procedure of such Committees, and the determination of the powers or duties of the Council which may be delegated to such Committees.

The Miscellaneous chapter includes Sections 8 to 20. Section 8 provides for the enrolment of advocates, while Section 9 explains the qualifications and admission of advocates. The Bar Council may, with the previous sanction of the High Court, make rules to regulate the admission of persons to be advocates of the High Court. Section 10 to 13, which dealt with punishment of advocate for misconduct, tribunal of Bar Council, procedure in inquiries, and powers of the Tribunal and Courts in inquiries, respectively, have been repealed by the Advocates Act, 1961.

Section 14 provides for the right of advocates to practice, while Section 15 allows the Bar Council to make rules consistent with this Act to provide for and regulate any of the following matters, namely: the rights and duties of the advocates of the High Court and their discipline and professional conduct; the conditions subject to which advocates of other High Courts may be permitted to practise in the High Court; the giving of facilities for legal education and training and the holding and conduct of examinations by the Bar Council; the charging of fees payable to the Bar Council in respect of the enjoyment of educational facilities provided, or of the right to appear at examinations held, by the Bar Council; the investment and management of the funds of the Bar Council; and any other matter in respect of which the High Court may require rules to be made under this section.

The Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, is a law that applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, and Sikhs by religion, as well as any person who is domiciled in India and not governed by Muslim, Christian, Parsi, or Jewish law. This Act is supplemental to the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, and applies to Hindus domiciled in India who are outside the country.
