Natural guardians of a Hindu minor, in respect of the minor's person as well as in respect of the minor’s property, are the father, and after him, the mother. However, the custody of a minor who has not completed the age of five years shall ordinarily be with the mother. The natural guardianship of an adopted son who is a minor passes, on adoption, to the adoptive father and after him to the adoptive mother. The natural guardian has the power to do all acts that are necessary or reasonable and proper for the benefit of the minor or for the realization, protection, or benefit of the minor's estate, but the guardian cannot bind the minor by a personal covenant. The natural guardian shall not, without the previous permission of the court, mortgage or charge, or transfer by sale, gift, exchange, or otherwise, any part of the immovable property of the minor or lease any part of such property for a term exceeding five years or for a term extending more than one year beyond the date on which the minor will attain majority. Any disposal of immovable property by a natural guardian, in contravention of sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), is voidable at the instance of the minor or any person claiming under him. No court shall grant permission to the natural guardian to do any of the acts mentioned in sub-section (2) except in case of necessity or for an evident advantage to the minor. The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, shall apply to and in respect of an application for obtaining the permission of the court under sub-section (2) in all respects as if it were an application for obtaining the permission of the court under section 29 of that Act. A Hindu father entitled to act as the natural guardian of his minor legitimate children may, by will, appoint a guardian for any of them in respect of the minor’s person or in respect of the minor’s property or in respect of both. An appointment made under sub-section (1) shall have no effect if the father predeceases the mother, but shall revive if the mother dies without appointing, by will, any person as guardian. A Hindu widow entitled to act as the natural guardian of her minor legitimate children, and a Hindu mother entitled to act as the natural guardian of her minor legitimate children by reason of the fact that the father has become disentitled to act as such, may, by will, appoint a guardian for any of them in respect of the minor’s person or in respect of the minor’s property or in respect of both. A Hindu mother entitled to act as the natural guardian of her minor illegitimate children may; by will, appoint a guardian for any of them in respect of the minor’s person or in respect of the minor's property or in respect of both. The guardian so appointed by will has the right to act as the minor’s guardian after the death of the minor’s father or mother, as the case may be, and to exercise all the rights of a natural guardian under this Act to such extent and subject to such restrictions, if any, as are specified in this Act and in the will. The right of the guardian so appointed by will shall, where the minor is a girl, cease on her marriage. A minor shall be incompetent to act as guardian of the property of any minor. After the commencement of this Act, no person shall be entitled to dispose of, or deal with, the property of a Hindu minor merely on the ground of his or her being the de facto guardian of the minor. The Indian Code of Civil Procedure covers the rules and regulations for the execution of decrees and orders by courts in India. The code outlines the powers of the court to impound movable property, allow the decree appealed from to be executed, stay the execution of the decree appealed from, place a party seeking assistance under conditions or give directions, increase security found inadequate, and enforce orders of the Supreme Court. The document outlines the rules for reviewing decrees and orders passed by courts in India. According to Order XLVII Rule 1, an application for review can be made without previous notice to the opposite party, allowing them to appear and be heard in support of the decree or order being reviewed. However, such an application cannot be granted on the ground of discovery of new matter or evidence that was not within the applicant's knowledge or could not be adduced by them when the decree or order was passed or made, without strict proof of such allegation.

Rule 5 of Order XLVII states that where the Judge or Judges who passed the decree or made the order being reviewed are still attached to the court when the application for review is presented, they shall hear the application, and no other Judge or Judges of the court shall hear the same. If the application is rejected, it cannot be appealed, but an order granting an application may be objected to at once by an appeal from the order granting the application or in an appeal from the decree or order finally passed or made in the suit.

If the application has been rejected due to the applicant's failure to appear, they may apply for an order to have the rejected application restored to the file, provided they can prove that they were prevented by a sufficient cause from appearing when the application was called on for hearing. The court may then order it to be restored to the file upon such terms as it thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for hearing the same.

When an application for review is granted, a note shall be made in the register, and the court may at once re-hear the case or make such order in regard to the re-hearing as it thinks fit. No application to review an order made on an application for a review or a decree or order passed or made on a review shall be entertained.

The Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, is a law that outlines the procedure for investigating the misbehavior or incapacity of a judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court in India. The Act defines key terms such as "Chairman," "Committee," "Judge," "prescribed," and "Speaker."

Under the Act, if a motion for the removal of a judge is signed by a certain number of members in either the House of the People or the Council of States, the Speaker or Chairman may constitute a Committee to investigate the grounds for removal. This Committee will consist of three members, including one chosen from among the Chief Justice and other Judges of the Supreme Court, one chosen from among the Chief Justices of the High Courts, and one distinguished jurist.

The Committee will frame definite charges against the Judge and communicate them, along with a statement of the grounds for each charge. The Judge will be given a reasonable opportunity to present a written statement of defence. If the Judge is alleged to be unable to discharge the duties of his office efficiently due to physical or mental incapacity, the Committee may arrange for a medical examination of the Judge.

The Committee will have the powers of a civil court while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Committee will submit its report to the Speaker or Chairman, or both, stating its findings on each of the charges separately with observations on the whole case. The report will be laid before the House of the People and the Council of States.

If the report of the Committee contains a finding that the Judge is not guilty of any misbehavior or does not suffer from any incapacity, then no further steps will be taken in either House of Parliament. If the report contains a finding that the Judge is guilty of misbehavior or suffers from incapacity, then the motion for removal, along with the report of the Committee, will be taken up for consideration by the House or Houses of Parliament. If the motion is adopted by each House of Parliament, an address praying for the removal of the Judge will be presented to the President by each House of Parliament in the same session in which the motion has been adopted.

The Act also provides for the constitution of a Joint Committee of both Houses of Parliament to make rules to carry out the purposes of this Act. These rules will be subject to the approval and confirmation of the Speaker and Chairman and will be published in the Official Gazette.

The Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, adds a new article 21A to the Constitution, which guarantees free and compulsory education to all children between the ages of six and fourteen. This amendment is significant as it makes education a fundamental right for children in India.

Furthermore, the Act substitutes a new article 45 for the existing one, which now mandates the State to provide early childhood care and education to all children until they complete the age of six years. This provision emphasizes the importance of early childhood education in preparing children for formal schooling.

Lastly, the Act amends article 51A of the Constitution by adding a new clause (k), which imposes a duty on parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children or wards between the ages of six and fourteen. This provision seeks to ensure that parents and guardians play an active role in their children's education and are aware of their responsibility towards their education.

Overall, the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, is a significant step towards strengthening the educational system in India, ensuring that all children have access to quality education and are provided with a safe and supportive learning environment.

The National Council for Teacher Education Act, 1993, establishes a National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE) to regulate and maintain the standards of teacher education in India. The NCTE is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal, and is headquartered in Delhi with regional offices in other parts of India. The NCTE consists of a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, Member-Secretary, and other Members appointed by the Central Government. The term of office for the Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, and Member-Secretary is four years or until they reach the age of sixty, whichever is earlier. The NCTE is responsible for ensuring planned and coordinated development of teacher education, determining and maintaining standards for teacher education, and making recommendations to the Central and State Governments, Universities, and recognized institutions in the field of teacher education. The NCTE may also co-opt up to three persons for specific purposes, and may appoint officers and other employees as necessary. The NCTE is authorized to inspect recognized institutions to ensure compliance with the provisions of the Act, and may withdraw recognition of a recognized institution if it contravenes any of the provisions of the Act or any rules, regulations, orders, or conditions subject to which recognition was granted. Any person aggrieved by an order of the NCTE may prefer an appeal to the Council within the prescribed period. The Council shall have its own fund, and shall prepare a budget and annual report for each financial year. The accounts of the Council shall be audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India. The Central Government may supersede the Council if it is unable to perform its duties, has persistently made default in performing its duties, has exceeded or abused its powers, or has wilfully or without sufficient cause failed to comply with any direction issued by the Central Government. The Central Government may make rules to carry out the provisions of the Act, and the NCTE may make regulations not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. Every rule and every regulation made under the Act shall be laid before each House of Parliament. The Central Government may also make orders to remove any difficulties in giving effect to the provisions of the Act.

Section 70 outlines the appointment and remuneration of auditors for a multi-State co-operative society. Every multi-State co-operative society is required to appoint an auditor or auditors to hold office from the conclusion of the annual general meeting until the conclusion of the next annual general meeting. The remuneration of the auditors may be fixed by the board or the Central Registrar, as the case may be, and subject to that, shall be fixed by the multi-State co-operative society in general meeting or in such manner as the multi-State co-operative society in general meeting may determine.
The document outlines provisions related to the appointment, qualifications, disqualifications, powers, duties, and rights of auditors for multi-State co-operative societies in India. 

Under Section 69, a multi-State co-operative society is required to appoint an auditor within 30 days of its registration, and the auditor's term lasts for five years. The auditor can be removed before their term ends by passing a special resolution in a general meeting, with a notice period of at least 14 days.

Section 70 specifies the qualifications for auditors, who must be chartered accountants under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949. A body corporate, an officer or employee of the multi-State co-operative society, or a person who is a member, or who is in the employment, of an officer or employee or the multi-State co-operative society cannot be appointed as an auditor. A person who is indebted to the multi-State co-operative society or who has given any guarantee or provided any security in connection with the indebtedness of any third person to the multi-State co-operative society for an amount exceeding one thousand rupees is also disqualified.

Under Section 71, a special notice is required for a resolution at an annual general meeting appointing as auditor a person other than a retiring auditor, or providing expressly that a retiring auditor shall not be reappointed. The retiring auditor must be informed of such a resolution and given an opportunity to make representations in writing, which must be notified to members of the multi-State co-operative society.

Section 72 outlines the powers and duties of auditors, who have the right to access all books, accounts, and vouchers of the multi-State co-operative society and are entitled to require information and explanations from officers or employees. The auditor must inquire into certain matters, such as the proper securing of loans and advances, transactions represented merely by book entries, personal expenses charged to revenue account, and the allotment of shares for cash.

The auditor must prepare a report on the accounts examined, which must state whether the accounts give the required information and present a true and fair view of the state of the multi-State co-operative society's affairs and profit or loss for the financial year. The report must also state whether the auditor has received all necessary information and explanations, whether proper books of account have been kept, and whether the balance-sheet and profit and loss account dealt with by the report are in agreement with the books of account and returns.

Under Section 74, only the person appointed as an auditor of the multi-State co-operative society can sign the auditor's report or sign or authenticate any other document of the multi-State co-operative society required by law to be signed or authenticated by the auditor. The Indian Constitution, in Article 19, guarantees several fundamental freedoms to every citizen of India. These freedoms are not absolute and have certain restraints and exceptions. The six fundamental freedoms are:

1. Freedom of Speech and Expression (Article 19(1)(a)): This includes the freedom to express oneself through speech, writing, printing, visual representations, or any other means. Reasonable restrictions can be imposed on this right for the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign nations, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offense, or the sovereignty and integrity of Parliament.

3. Freedom to Form Associations or Unions (Article 19(1)(c)): Citizens have the freedom to form social, cultural, economic, or political associations or unions. Reasonable restrictions can be imposed on this right in the interests of public order, morality, or the sovereignty and integrity of India.
4. Freedom to Move Freely Throughout the Territory of India (Article 19(1)(d)): Citizens have the liberty to move within the country, reside in any part of India, and settle in any place of their choice. Part I, titled "SUITS RELATING TO LAND," applies to specific local areas, and its provisions come into force in those areas on dates determined by the State Government. Part II, titled "OTHER SUITS," applies to suits other than those referred to in the Court-fees Act, 1870, section 7, paragraphs v, vi, and ix, and paragraph x, clause (d). Where court-fees are payable ad valorem under the Court-fees Act, 1870, the value as determinable for the computation of court-fees and the value for purposes of jurisdiction shall be the same. When the subject-matter of suits of any class does not admit of being satisfactorily valued, the High Court may direct that such suits shall, for the purposes of the Court-fees Act, 1870, and this Act, be treated as if their subject-matter were of such value as the High Court thinks fit to specify in this behalf.

Part III, titled "SUPPLEMENTAL PROVISIONS," lays down the procedure for dealing with objections regarding the over-valuation or under-valuation of a suit or appeal. The objection must be taken in the Court of first instance at or before the hearing at which issues are first framed and recorded, or in the lower Appellate Court in the memorandum of appeal to that Court. The Appellate Court may entertain the objection if it is satisfied that the suit or appeal was over-valued or under-valued and that the over-valuation or under-valuation thereof has prejudicially affected the disposal of the suit or appeal on its merits. The provisions of this section shall apply to a Court exercising revisional jurisdiction under section 622 of the Code of Civil Procedure or other enactment for the time being in force.

The Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen. A contingent contract cannot be enforced by law unless and until the event on which it is contingent has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event does not happen can be enforced when the happening of that event becomes impossible, and not before. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if a specified uncertain event happens within a fixed time become void if, at the expiration of the time fixed, such event has not happened, or if, before the time fixed, such event becomes impossible. Contingent agreements to do or not to do anything, if an impossible event happens, are void, whether the impossibility of the event is known or not to the parties to the agreement at the time when it is made. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law. Promises bind the representatives of the promisors in case of the death of such promisors before performance, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If a promisor has made an offer of performance to the promisee, and the offer has not been accepted, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance, nor does he thereby lose his rights under the contract. Every such offer must fulfill certain conditions, such as being unconditional, made at a proper time and place, and under such circumstances that the person to whom it is made may have a reasonable opportunity of ascertaining that the person by whom it is made is able and willing there and then to do the whole of what he is bound by his promise to do. The sale of tangible immoveable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or in the case of a reversion or other intangible thing, can only be made by a registered instrument. In the case of tangible immoveable property of a value less than one hundred rupees, such transfer may be made either by a registered instrument or by delivery of the property. Delivery of tangible immoveable property takes place when the seller places the buyer, or such person as he directs, in possession of the property. A contract for the sale of immoveable property is a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between the parties, but it does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on such property.

The section gives the High Court or the District Court the power to transfer or withdraw any suit, appeal, or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same. This power can be exercised on the application of any of the parties or of its own motion without notice.

The section also provides for the transfer of a suit, appeal, or other proceeding pending in any Court subordinate to the High Court or District Court to any Court subordinate to the same High Court or District Court and competent to try or dispose of the same. This power can be exercised by the High Court or District Court on its own motion or on the application of any of the parties after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desired to be heard.

Where any suit or proceeding has been transferred or withdrawn under sub-section (1), the Court which is thereafter to try or dispose of such suit or proceeding may, subject to any special directions in the case of an order of transfer, either retry it or proceed from the point at which it was transferred or withdrawn.

Section 25: Power of Supreme Court to transfer suits, etc.

Section 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for the transfer of suits, appeals, and other proceedings by the Supreme Court. The section empowers the Supreme Court, on the application of a party and after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desire to be heard, to direct that any suit, appeal, or other proceeding be transferred from a High Court or other Civil Court in one State to a High Court or other Civil Court in any other State.

Section 221 deals with cases where it is doubtful what offence has been committed. Section 222 states that when an offense proved includes the commission of another offense, the accused may be convicted of the latter offense also.

Section 223 deals with the consolidation of charges. According to this section, when a person is accused of more offenses than one of the same kind, not being offenses of the same section, the Magistrate may, with the consent of the accused, try the offenses together, or frame charges for the offenses separately, and deal with them separately.

Section 224 deals with the trial of persons accused jointly. According to this section, persons accused jointly of the same offense may be tried together.

Section 225 deals with the issue of separate warrants in cases of joint offense. According to this section, when two or more persons are accused of the same offense, the Court may issue one warrant directing them to appear before it or issue separate warrants for each of them.

Section 226 deals with the issue of process in cases of joint offense. According to this section, when two or more persons are accused of the same offense, the Court may issue process against them separately or jointly.

Section 227 deals with the discharge of accused persons. According to this section, if, upon considering the police report and the documents sent with it under section 173 and making such examination, if any, as he thinks necessary, the Judge or Magistrate considers that there is not sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, he shall discharge the accused, and record his reasons for so doing.

Section 228 deals with the framing of charge. According to this section, if, after such consideration and examination, the Judge or Magistrate is of opinion that there is ground for presuming that the accused has committed an offense which, prima facie, comes within the cognizance of the Court, he shall frame a charge against the accused.

Section 232 deals with the trial of warrant cases. According to this section, in warrant cases, the trial shall be commenced on the day on which the accused is brought before the Court, unless the Court, for reasons to be recorded, orders the adjournment of the trial.

Section 305 outlines the procedure when a corporation or registered society is an accused. The corporation may appoint a representative for the purpose of the inquiry or trial, and any requirement of this Code that anything shall be done in the presence of the accused shall be construed as a requirement that thing shall be done in the presence of the representative or read or stated or explained to the representative. If a question arises as to whether any person appearing as the representative of a corporation in an inquiry or trial before a Court is or is not such representative, the question shall be determined by the Court.

Section 306 deals with the tender of pardon to an accomplice. The Chief Judicial Magistrate, a Metropolitan Magistrate, or a Magistrate of the first class may tender a pardon to any person supposed to have been directly or indirectly concerned in or privy to an offence on condition of his making a full and true disclosure of the whole of the circumstances within his knowledge relative to the offence and to every other person concerned, whether as principal or abettor, in the commission thereof. The section applies to any offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session or by the Court of a Special Judge appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952, or any offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to seven years or with a more severe sentence. Every Magistrate who tenders a pardon under sub-section (1) shall record his reasons for doing so and whether the tender was accepted by the person to whom it was made. Every person accepting a tender of pardon made under sub-section (1) shall be examined as a witness in the Court of the Magistrate taking cognizance of the offence and in the subsequent trial, if any, and shall, unless he is already on bail, be detained in custody until the termination of the trial.

Under section 306, a Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence can tender a pardon to any person who is supposed to have been directly or indirectly concerned in, or privy to, the offence. If the person accepts the pardon and is subsequently examined, the Magistrate shall commit the case for trial to the Court of Session or a Special Judge appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952, or make over the case to the Chief Judicial Magistrate for trial.

Section 307 outlines the power of the Court to direct a tender of pardon at any time after commitment of a case but before judgment is passed. The purpose of this provision is to obtain the evidence of any person who is supposed to have been directly or indirectly concerned in, or privy to, the offence. If the person who has accepted the tender of pardon does not comply with the conditions on which it was made, they may be tried for the offence in respect of which the pardon was tendered or for any other offence of which they appear to have been guilty in connection with the same matter.

Under section 310, any Judge or Magistrate may visit and inspect any place in which an offence is alleged to have been committed or any other place in which it is necessary to view for the purpose of properly appreciating the evidence given at the inquiry or trial. The Magistrate shall record a memorandum of any relevant facts observed at such inspection, which shall form part of the record of the case.

Finally, section 311 provides that any Court may summon any person as a witness or examine any person in attendance, or recall and re-examine any person already examined, if his evidence appears to be essential to the just decision of the case. This power can be exercised at any stage of any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under the Code.
Summary:

This document discusses various provisions related to criminal law in India. Section 263 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) outlines the power of the court to dispense with the personal attendance of the accused in a summons case. It also allows for the dispensation of the accused's examination under clause (b) in such cases. No oath is to be administered to the accused when they are examined under this section, and they cannot be punished for refusing to answer questions or giving false answers. The answers given by the accused can be taken into consideration during the inquiry or trial and used as evidence in any other related offenses.

Under Part II, Chapter II on specific performance of contracts, the Act states that specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14, and section 16. The Act also states that specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favor of a person who has obtained substituted performance of the contract under section 20 or who has become incapable of performing, or violates any essential term of, the contract that remains to be performed, or acts in fraud of the contract, or wilfully acts at variance with or in subversion of the relation intended to be established by the contract. The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the laws related to bailments, which are defined as the delivery of goods by one person (the bailor) to another person (the bailee) for a specific purpose. The bailee is responsible for taking care of the goods and returning them to the bailor, or delivering them according to the bailor's directions, once the purpose of the bailment has been fulfilled. The bailor is responsible to the bailee for any loss that the bailee may sustain if the bailment is not legally valid or if the bailor is not entitled to receive back the goods. If several joint owners of goods bail them, the bailee may deliver them back to, or according to the directions of, one joint owner without the consent of all, in the absence of any agreement to the contrary. If the bailor has no title to the goods, and the bailee, in good faith, delivers them back to, or according to the directions of, the bailor, the bailee is not responsible to the owner in respect of such delivery. THE INDIAN TREASURE-TROVE ACT, 1878, is an Act that amends the law relating to treasure-trove. The Act extends to the whole of India except the territories that were formerly part of Part B States.

The Act is divided into three chapters: PRELIMINARY, PROCEDURE ON FINDING TREASURE, and PENALTIES.

The PRELIMINARY chapter defines the terms used in the Act. Treasure is defined as anything of any value hidden in the soil or anything affixed thereto. The Collector is defined as any Revenue Officer in independent charge of a district or any officer appointed by the State Government to perform the functions of a Collector under this Act. The owner is defined as the person entitled to treasure in a land or thing affixed thereto.

The PROCEDURE ON FINDING TREASURE chapter outlines the steps to be taken when treasure is found. The finder of treasure exceeding ten rupees in amount or value must give notice in writing to the Collector as soon as practicable. The notice must include the nature and amount or approximate value of the treasure, the place it was found, and the date of the finding. The finder must either deposit the treasure in the nearest Government treasury or give the Collector security to produce the treasure at a specified time and place.

The Collector must publish a notification in a manner prescribed by the State Government, requiring all persons claiming the treasure or any part thereof to appear personally or by agent before the Collector on a specified date. The Collector must also serve a special notice in writing on the person in possession of the place where the treasure was found.

Any person having a right to the treasure or any part thereof and not appearing as required by the notification shall forfeit such right.

The Collector must enquire as to the person by whom, the place in which, and the circumstances under which, the treasure was found and as far as possible the person by whom, and the circumstances under which, the treasure was hidden.

If the Collector sees reason to believe that the treasure was hidden within one hundred years before the date of the finding by a person appearing as required by the notification, he may make an order adjourning the hearing of the case for a sufficient period to allow of a suit being instituted in the Civil Court by the claimant to establish his right.

If the Collector sees no reason to believe that the treasure was so hidden, or if no suit is instituted within a specified period, or if such suit is instituted and the plaintiff's claim is finally rejected, the Collector may declare the treasure to be ownerless.

Any person aggrieved by a declaration made under this section may appeal within two months from the date thereof to the Chief Controlling Revenue Authority.

When a declaration has been made in respect of any treasure under section 9, such treasure shall, in accordance with the provisions hereinafter contained, either be delivered to the finder thereof or be divided between him and the owner of the place in which it has been found in manner hereinafter provided.

The PENALTIES chapter outlines the penalties for failing to give notice, making a false declaration, or altering or attempting to alter the treasure so as to conceal its identity. The share of such treasure, or the money in lieu thereof to which the offender would otherwise be entitled, shall vest in Government, and he shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.

If the owner of the place in which any treasure is found abets any offence under this Act, the share of such treasure, or the money in lieu thereof to which he would otherwise be entitled, shall vest in Government, and he shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is an Act of the Parliament of India that consolidates and amends the law relating to domestic arbitration, international commercial arbitration, and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards. It also defines the law relating to conciliation and matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The Act is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985) and the UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules (1980). The Act applies to the whole of India and came into force on a date appointed by the Central Government. The Act is divided into two parts: Part I - Arbitration and Part II - Conciliation. Part I of the Act contains general provisions, arbitration agreement, composition and jurisdiction of arbitral tribunal, conduct of arbitral proceedings, making of arbitral award and terms of settlement, recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards, and appeals. Part II of the Act deals with conciliation, including provisions for the commencement of conciliation proceedings, the conduct of the conciliation proceedings, the termination of conciliation proceedings, and the effects of conciliation agreements. The Act provides for extensive judicial intervention in arbitration proceedings, but also allows for parties to agree to derogate from certain provisions of the Act. The Act applies to every arbitration under any other enactment for the time being in force, as if the arbitration were pursuant to an arbitration agreement and as if that other enactment were an arbitration agreement. However, the provisions of this Part are inconsistent with that other enactment or with any rules made thereunder. The Act also provides for administrative assistance in the conduct of arbitral proceedings.
Summary:

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is a law in India that governs domestic and international commercial arbitration and conciliation. The Act applies to any arbitration agreement, whether it is in the form of an arbitration clause in a contract or a separate agreement.

Section 7 defines an arbitration agreement as a written agreement between two or more parties to submit to arbitration all or certain disputes that have arisen or may arise between them in respect of a defined legal relationship, whether contractual or not.

Section 8 empowers a judicial authority to refer parties to arbitration where there is an arbitration agreement, provided that a party to the agreement or any person claiming through or under him applies for it not later than the date of submitting his first statement on the substance of the dispute.

Section 9 allows a party to apply to a court for the appointment of a guardian for a minor or person of unsound mind for the purposes of arbitral proceedings, or for an interim measure of protection in respect of certain matters, such as the preservation, interim custody or sale of goods, securing the amount in dispute, and interim injunction or the appointment of a receiver.

Section 10 provides that the parties are free to determine the number of arbitrators, provided that such number shall not be an even number. Failing the determination, the arbitral tribunal shall consist of a sole arbitrator.

Section 11 states that a person of any nationality may be an arbitrator, unless otherwise agreed by the parties. The parties are free to agree on a procedure for appointing the arbitrator or arbitrators. If there is no agreement, in an arbitration with three arbitrators, each party shall appoint one arbitrator, and the two appointed arbitrators shall appoint the third arbitrator who shall act as the presiding arbitrator.
Summary:
Chapter VII of the Act deals with recourse against arbitral awards. An arbitral award may be set aside by the court only if the party making the application establishes that a party was under some incapacity, the arbitration agreement is not valid under the law to which the parties have subjected it or, failing any indication thereon, under the law for the time being in force, the party making the application was not given proper notice of the appointment of an arbitrator or of the arbitral proceedings or was otherwise unable to present his case, the arbitral award deals with a dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration, or it contains decisions on matters beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration, the composition of the arbitral tribunal or the arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties, unless such agreement was in conflict with a provision of this Part from which the parties cannot derogate, or, failing such agreement, was not in accordance with this Part, the subject-matter of the dispute is not capable of settlement by arbitration under the law for the time being in force, or the arbitral award is in conflict with the public policy of India.

Chapter VIII of the Act deals with the finality and enforcement of arbitral awards. Subject to this Part, an arbitral award shall be final and binding on the parties and persons claiming under them respectively. Where the time for making an application to set aside the arbitral award under section 34 has expired, then, subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), such award shall be enforced in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), in the same manner as if it were a decree of the court. Where an application to set aside the arbitral award has been filed in the Court under section 34, the filing of such an application shall not by itself render that award unenforceable, unless the Court grants an order of stay of the operation of the said arbitral award in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (3), on a separate application made for that purpose. Upon filing of an application under sub-section (2) for stay of the operation of the arbitral award, the Court may, subject to such conditions as it may deem fit, grant stay of the operation of such award for reasons to be recorded in writing.

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides a comprehensive framework for the resolution of disputes through arbitration and conciliation. The Act lays down the rules and procedures for the appointment of arbitrators, the conduct of arbitral proceedings, and the enforcement of arbitral awards. The Act also provides for the termination of arbitral proceedings, recourse against arbitral awards, and the finality and enforcement of arbitral awards. The Act seeks to ensure that the arbitration process is fair, efficient, and effective, and that arbitral awards are enforceable and binding on the parties.
Summary:

Chapter IX of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1996 deals with appeals. An appeal can be made from the following orders: (a) refusing to refer the parties to arbitration under section 8, (b) granting or refusing to grant any measure under section 9, and (c) setting aside or refusing to set aside an arbitral award under section 34. Additionally, an appeal can also be made to a court from an order of the arbitral tribunal accepting the plea referred to in sub-section (2) or sub-section (3) of section 16 or granting or refusing to grant an interim measure under section 17. No second appeal shall lie from an order passed in appeal under this section, but nothing in this section shall affect or take away any right to appeal to the Supreme Court.

Summary:
The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, is an act that amends and codifies the law relating to marriage among Hindus. It applies to any person who is a Hindu by religion in any of its forms or developments, including a Virashaiva, a Lingayat or a follower of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj, as well as to any person who is a Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion, and to any other person domiciled in the territories to which this Act extends who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew by religion. The Act defines various terms related to Hindu marriages, including "custom," "district court," "full blood," "half blood," "uterine blood," "prescribed," "sapinda relationship," and "degrees of prohibited relationship." It also specifies the conditions for a Hindu marriage, including the requirement that neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage, that both parties are capable of giving a valid consent to the marriage, that the bridegroom has completed the age of 21 years and the bride the age of 18 years, and that the parties are not within the degrees of prohibited relationship or sapindas of each other, unless the custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two. The Act also provides for the registration of Hindu marriages, the restitution of conjugal rights, judicial separation, and divorce, and specifies the grounds for nullity and voidable marriages. It also regulates the jurisdiction and procedure for proceedings under the Act.
Section 52 states that Chapter II of this Part shall not apply in relation to foreign awards to which this Chapter applies.

Chapter II of the Act deals with Geneva Convention Awards and defines a foreign award as an arbitral award made in a country that is a party to the Geneva Convention. Section 54 allows a judicial authority to refer the parties to arbitration if the arbitration agreement is valid and capable of being carried into effect.

Section 55 states that any foreign award which would be enforceable under this Chapter shall be treated as binding for all purposes on the persons as between whom it was made and may accordingly be relied on by any of those persons by way of defence, set off or otherwise in any legal proceedings in India.

Summary:

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Part II, governs the enforcement of foreign awards in India. A foreign award can be enforced if it fulfills certain conditions, such as being made in pursuance of a valid submission to arbitration, having a capable subject matter, being made by the arbitral tribunal provided for in the submission or constituted in the agreed manner, having become final in the country of origin, and not being contrary to the public policy or law of India. If these conditions are met, the award shall be deemed to be a decree of the Court. An appeal lies from the order refusing to enforce a foreign award to the court authorized by law to hear appeals from such order. Part III of the Act governs conciliation proceedings. The party initiating conciliation sends a written invitation to the other party to conciliate under this Part, and conciliation proceedings commence when the other party accepts the invitation. The parties may agree on the number of conciliators, and the appointment of conciliators may be made directly by the parties or with the assistance of a suitable institution or person. The conciliator is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, or the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The conciliator assists the parties in an independent and impartial manner in their attempt to reach an amicable settlement of their dispute, and may make proposals for a settlement of the dispute. In order to facilitate the conduct of the conciliation proceedings, the parties or the conciliator with the consent of the parties may arrange for administrative assistance by a suitable institution or person.
Summary:

The document summarizes the Indian Conciliation Act of 1996, which provides a legal framework for the resolution of disputes through conciliation. The Act outlines the role and responsibilities of the conciliator, including the ability to invite parties to meet or communicate with them, determine the location of meetings, and disclose factual information to parties. The Act also emphasizes the importance of cooperation between parties and the conciliator, as well as the ability for parties to submit suggestions for settlement.

The Act also details the process for reaching a settlement agreement, which includes the formulation of terms by the conciliator, observation by the parties, and the potential for reformation of the terms. Once an agreement is reached, it is final and binding on the parties and any persons claiming under them. The settlement agreement has the same status and effect as an arbitral award on agreed terms.

Confidentiality is a key aspect of the conciliation process, with all matters relating to the proceedings required to be kept confidential, except where disclosure is necessary for implementation and enforcement. The conciliation proceedings may be terminated by the signing of the settlement agreement, a declaration by the conciliator, a declaration by the parties, or a declaration by one party to the other and the conciliator.

During the conciliation proceedings, parties are prohibited from initiating arbitral or judicial proceedings except in certain circumstances. The conciliator is also prohibited from acting as an arbitrator or representative in any related proceedings. The Act also specifies that views expressed, suggestions made, admissions, proposals, and willingness to accept proposals made by the conciliator cannot be used as evidence in any related proceedings.

question_text: Which section under the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 deals with the settlement of disputes outside the court
context:
The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, is a procedural law that governs the filing, hearing, and disposal of civil suits in India. It was enacted in 1908 and has been amended several times since then. The Code applies to the whole of India except for the state of Nagaland and the tribal areas, and the application of the Code to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, and certain agencies in Andhra Pradesh is subject to the application of any rule or regulation for the time being in force in those areas.

The Code defines various legal terms used in civil proceedings, such as "decree," "decree-holder," "district," "foreign Court," "foreign judgment," "Government Pleader," "High Court," "Judge," "judgment," "judgment-debtor," "legal representative," "mesne profits," "movable property," "order," "pleader," "prescribed," "public officer," "rules," "share in a corporation," and "signed."

Under the Code, the District Court is subordinate to the High Court, and every Civil Court of a grade inferior to that of a District Court and every Court of Small Causes is subordinate to the High Court and District Court. The Code also provides for the subordination of Revenue Courts, which are governed by the provisions of this Code in those matters of procedure upon which any special enactment applicable to them is silent.

The Code lays down the pecuniary jurisdiction of Civil Courts, which means that Civil Courts have jurisdiction over suits the amount or value of the subject-matter of which does not exceed the pecuniary limits of their ordinary jurisdiction. The Code also provides for the application of the Code to Revenue Courts, which may be excluded from the application of certain portions of the Code by notification in the Official Gazette by the State Government.

The Code provides for the stay of suits, which means that no Court shall proceed with the trial of any suit in which the matter in issue is also directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title where such suit is pending in the same or any other Court in India having jurisdiction to grant the relief claimed, or in any Court beyond the limits of India established or continued by the Central Government and having like jurisdiction, or before the Supreme Court.

The Code also provides for the doctrine of res judicata, which means that no Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court.

The Code provides for the bar to further suit, which means that where a plaintiff is precluded by rules from instituting a further suit in respect of any particular cause of action, he shall not be entitled to institute a suit in respect of such cause of action in any Court to which this Code applies.

The Code provides for the conclusiveness of foreign judgments, which means that a foreign judgment shall be conclusive as to any matter thereby directly adjudicated upon between the same parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title except in certain circumstances.

The Code provides for the institution of suits, which means that every suit shall be instituted in the Court of the lowest grade competent to try it. The Code also provides for the place of suing, which means that suits for the recovery of immovable property with or without rent or profits, for the partition of immovable property, for foreclosure, sale or redemption in the case of a mortgage of or charge upon immovable property, for the determination of any other right to or interest in immovable property, for compensation for wrong to immovable property, for the recovery of movable property actually under distraint or attachment, shall be instituted in the Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the property is situate.

The Code provides for the transfer of suits, which means that where a suit may be instituted in any one of two or more Courts and is instituted in one of such Courts, any defendant, after notice to the other parties, may, at the earliest possible opportunity and in all cases where issues are settled, at or before such settlement, apply to have the suit transferred to another Court, and the Court to which such application is made, after considering the objections of the other parties (if any), shall determine in which of the several Courts having jurisdiction the suit shall proceed.
Under Section 18, where it is alleged to be uncertain within the local limits of the jurisdiction of which of two or more Courts, any immovable property is situate, any one of those Courts may, if satisfied that there is ground for the alleged uncertainty, record a statement to that effect and thereupon proceed to entertain and dispose of any suit relating to that property.

Under Section 19, where a suit is for compensation for wrong done to the person or to movable property, if the wrong was done within the local limits of the jurisdiction of one Court and the defendant resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, within the local limits of the jurisdiction of another Court, the suit may be instituted at the option of the plaintiff in either of the said Courts.

Under Section 20, subject to the limitations aforesaid, every suit shall be instituted in a Court within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the defendant, or each of the defendants where there are more than one, at the time of the commencement of the suit, actually and voluntarily resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain.

Under Section 21, no objection as to the place of suing shall be allowed by any Appellate or Revisional Court unless such objection was taken in the Court of first instance at the earliest possible opportunity and in all cases where issues are settled at or before such settlement, and unless there has been a consequent failure of justice.

Under Section 21A, no suit shall lie challenging the validity of a decree passed in a former suit between the same parties, or between the parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, on any ground based on an objection as to the place of suing.

Under Section 22, where a suit may be instituted in any one of two or more Courts and is instituted in one of such Courts, any defendant, after notice to the other parties, may, at the earliest possible opportunity and in all cases where issues are settled at or before such settlement, apply to have the suit transferred to another Court, and the Court to which such application is made, after considering the objections of the other parties (if any), shall determine in which of the several Courts having jurisdiction the suit shall proceed.

Under Section 23, an application under Section 22 shall be made to the Appellate Court where the several Courts having jurisdiction are subordinate to the same Appellate Court. Where such Courts are not subordinate to the same Appellate Court, the application shall be made to the Court to which they are subordinate.
In this summary, we will explain the key provisions of Sections 24 and 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which deal with the power of transfer and withdrawal of suits, appeals, and other proceedings.

Section 24: General power of transfer and withdrawal

Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for the transfer and withdrawal of suits, appeals, and other proceedings. The section gives the High Court or the District Court the power to transfer or withdraw any suit, appeal, or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same. This power can be exercised on the application of any of the parties or of its own motion without notice.

The section also provides for the transfer of a suit, appeal, or other proceeding pending in any Court subordinate to the High Court or District Court to any Court subordinate to the same High Court or District Court and competent to try or dispose of the same. This power can be exercised by the High Court or District Court on its own motion or on the application of any of the parties after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desired to be heard.

Where any suit or proceeding has been transferred or withdrawn under sub-section (1), the Court which is thereafter to try or dispose of such suit or proceeding may, subject to any special directions in the case of an order of transfer, either retry it or proceed from the point at which it was transferred or withdrawn.

Section 25: Power of Supreme Court to transfer suits, etc.

Section 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for the transfer of suits, appeals, and other proceedings by the Supreme Court. The section empowers the Supreme Court, on the application of a party and after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desire to be heard, to direct that any suit, appeal, or other proceeding be transferred from a High Court or other Civil Court in one State to a High Court or other Civil Court in any other State.

Summary:

THE EQUAL REMUNERATION ACT, 1976 (ACT NO. 25 OF 1976) came into force on the 11th of February, 1976, with the main objective of providing for the payment of equal remuneration to men and women workers and for the prevention of discrimination against women in matters of employment. The Act applies to the whole of India and has overriding effect over any other law or instrument that is inconsistent with its provisions.

Chapter I of the Act deals with preliminary matters and defines key terms used throughout the Act. The term "appropriate Government" refers to the Central Government in cases where the employment is carried out by or under the authority of the Central Government, a railway administration, a banking company, a mine, oilfield, or major port, or any corporation established by or under a Central Act. In all other cases, the "appropriate Government" refers to the State Government. The term "employer" is defined as any person who employs one or more workers in an establishment or employment in which this Act has come into force. "Man" and "woman" are defined as male and female human beings, respectively, of any age. "Remuneration" includes basic wage or salary and any additional emoluments payable in cash or kind to a person employed in respect of employment or work done in such employment. "Same work or work of a similar nature" means work in respect of which the skill, effort, and responsibility required are the same when performed under similar working conditions by a man or a woman.

Chapter II of the Act focuses on the payment of remuneration at equal rates to men and women workers and other matters. Section 4 states that no employer shall pay to any worker remuneration at rates less favorable than those at which remuneration is paid by him to workers of the opposite sex in the same establishment or employment for performing the same work or work of a similar nature. Section 5 prohibits discrimination in recruitment and other conditions of service, such as promotions, training, or transfer, based on sex. However, this provision does not affect any priority or reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, ex-servicemen, retrenched employees, or any other class or category of persons in the matter of recruitment to the posts in an establishment or employment.

Chapter III of the Act contains miscellaneous provisions. Section 8 mandates employers to maintain registers and other documents in relation to the workers employed by them. Section 9 empowers the appropriate Government to appoint Inspectors for the purpose of making investigations as to whether the provisions of this Act or the rules made thereunder are being complied with by employers. Section 10 lays down penalties for non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, including failure to maintain registers or other documents, making recruitment in contravention of the provisions of the Act, making payment of remuneration at unequal rates, and making discrimination between men and women workers.

The Act also contains provisions relating to offences by companies, cognizance and trial of offences, power to make rules, power of Central Government to give directions, act not to apply in certain special cases, power to make declaration, power to remove difficulties, and repeal and saving.

THE WORKING JOURNALISTS (FIXATION OF RATES OF WAGES) ACT, 1958, is an Act to provide for the fixation of rates of wages in respect of working journalists and for matters connected therewith. The Act defines key terms such as "Committee," "prescribed," "Wage Board," "Wage Board decision," "Wages," "Working Journalists Act," and "words and expressions."

The Act establishes a Committee to fix rates of wages in respect of working journalists in the light of the Judgment of the Supreme Court, dated the 19th day of March, 1958, relating to the Wage Board decision, and in the light of all other relevant circumstances. The Committee's functions include calling upon newspaper establishments and working journalists and other persons interested in the Wage Board decision to make representations, examining materials placed before the Wage Board and further materials obtained under this Act, and making recommendations to the Central Government for the fixation of rates of wages in respect of working journalists.

The Act grants the Committee the power to exercise all or any of the powers which an industrial tribunal, constituted under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, exercises for the adjudication of an industrial dispute referred to it and to regulate its own procedure. The Committee may also examine accounts or documents or obtain statements from any person, and the authorised officer may exercise all or any of the powers which an industrial tribunal may exercise under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

The Central Government may enforce the recommendations of the Committee by making an order in terms of the recommendations or subject to such modifications as it thinks fit. The order shall come into operation on the date of publication or on such date, whether prospectively or retrospectively, as may be specified in the order.

Every working journalist shall be entitled to be paid by his employer wages at a rate which shall in no case be less than the rate of wages specified in the order. If any question arises as to the amount due under this Act to a working journalist from his employer, the State Government may refer the question to any Labour Court constituted by it under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, or under any corresponding law relating to investigation and settlement of industrial disputes in force in the State.

The Act includes provisions for the authentication of orders, letters, etc., of the Committee and for the recovery of money due to working journalists. The Act also specifies that the provisions of this Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith in the terms of any award, agreement, contract of service, whether made before or after the commencement of this Act. The Act also includes provisions for penalties for non-compliance.

The Central Government may make rules to carry out the purposes of this Act, and every rule made under this Act shall be laid before each House of Parliament. The Act repeals and saves certain provisions of the Repealing and Amending Act, 1960.

Article 254 deals with requirements as to recommendations and previous sanctions to be regarded as matters of procedure only. No Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of a State and no provision in any such Act, shall be invalid by reason only that some recommendation or previous sanction required by this Constitution was not given, if assent to that Act was given-(a)where the recommendation required was that of the Governor, either by the Governor or by the President; (b) where the recommendation required was that of the Rajpramukh, either by the Rajpramukh or by the President; (c) where the recommendation or previous sanction required was that of the President, by the President.

Article 255 deals with obligation of States and the Union. The executive power of every State shall be so exercised as to ensure compliance with the laws made by Parliament and any existing laws which apply in that State, and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of such directions to a State as may appear to the Government of India to be necessary for that purpose.

Article 256 deals with control of the Union over States in certain cases. The executive power of every State shall be so exercised as not to impede or prejudice the exercise of the executive power of the Union, and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of such directions to a State as may appear to the Government of India to be necessary for that purpose. The executive power of the Union shall also extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the construction and maintenance of means of communication declared in the direction to be of national or military importance: Provided that nothing in this clause shall be taken as restricting the power of Parliament to declare highways or waterways to be national highways or national waterways so declared or the power of the Union to construct and maintain means of communication as part of its functions with respect to naval, military and air force works. The executive power of the Union shall also extend to the giving of directions to a State as to the measures to be taken for the protection of the railways within the State. Where in carrying out any direction given to a State under clause (2) as to the construction or maintenance of any means of communication or under clause (3) as to the measures to be taken for the protection of any railway, costs have been incurred in excess of those which would have been incurred in the discharge of the normal duties of the State if such direction had not been given, there shall be paid by the Government of India to the State such sum as may be agreed, or, in default of agreement, as may be determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India, in respect of the extra costs so incurred by the State.

Article 257 deals with assistance to States by deployment of armed forces or other forces of the Union. Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the Parliament may by law provide for the establishment of any additional courts for the better administration of laws made by Parliament or of any existing laws with respect to a matter enumerated in the Union List.

Article 258 deals with power of the Union to confer powers, etc., on States in certain cases. Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may, with the consent of the Governor of a State, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the Union extends. A law made by Parliament which applies in any State may, notwithstanding that it relates to a matter with respect to which the Legislature of the State has no power to make laws, confer powers and impose duties, or authorize the conferring of powers and the imposition of duties, upon the State or officers and authorities thereof. Where by virtue of this article powers and duties have been conferred or imposed upon a State or officers or authorities thereof, there shall be paid by the Government of India to the State such sum as may be agreed, or, in default of agreement, as may be determined by an arbitrator appointed by the Chief Justice of India, in respect of any extra costs of administration incurred by the State in connection with the exercise of those powers and duties.

Article 259 deals with power of the States to entrust functions to the Union. Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the Governor of a State may, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust either conditionally or unconditionally to that Government or to its officers functions in relation to any matter to which the executive power of the State extends.

Summary:

The Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, is a law that outlines the procedure for investigating the misbehavior or incapacity of a judge of the Supreme Court or of a High Court in India. The Act defines key terms such as "Chairman," "Committee," "Judge," "prescribed," and "Speaker."

Under the Act, if a motion for the removal of a judge is signed by a certain number of members in either the House of the People or the Council of States, the Speaker or Chairman may constitute a Committee to investigate the grounds for removal. This Committee will consist of three members, including one chosen from among the Chief Justice and other Judges of the Supreme Court, one chosen from among the Chief Justices of the High Courts, and one distinguished jurist.

The Committee will frame definite charges against the Judge and communicate them, along with a statement of the grounds for each charge. The Judge will be given a reasonable opportunity to present a written statement of defence. If the Judge is alleged to be unable to discharge the duties of his office efficiently due to physical or mental incapacity, the Committee may arrange for a medical examination of the Judge.

The Committee will have the powers of a civil court while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Committee will submit its report to the Speaker or Chairman, or both, stating its findings on each of the charges separately with observations on the whole case. The report will be laid before the House of the People and the Council of States.

If the report of the Committee contains a finding that the Judge is not guilty of any misbehavior or does not suffer from any incapacity, then no further steps will be taken in either House of Parliament. If the report contains a finding that the Judge is guilty of misbehavior or suffers from incapacity, then the motion for removal, along with the report of the Committee, will be taken up for consideration by the House or Houses of Parliament. If the motion is adopted by each House of Parliament, an address praying for the removal of the Judge will be presented to the President by each House of Parliament in the same session in which the motion has been adopted.

The Act also provides for the constitution of a Joint Committee of both Houses of Parliament to make rules to carry out the purposes of this Act. These rules will be subject to the approval and confirmation of the Speaker and Chairman and will be published in the Official Gazette.

The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, defines various terms related to labor laws and disputes in India. Key terms defined in the Act include:

* "Strike" - a cessation of work by a body of persons employed in an industry acting in combination.
* "Lock-out" - the temporary closing of a place of employment or the suspension of work by an employer.
* "Retrenchment" - the termination of the service of a workman by the employer for any reason other than as a punishment for misconduct.
* "Wages" - all remuneration capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would be payable to a workman in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment.
* "Workman" - any person employed in an industry to do any manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward.

The Act also specifies the powers and functions of various authorities, such as Labour Courts and Industrial Tribunals, in resolving industrial disputes. Additionally, the Act includes provisions for the conciliation and settlement of disputes, as well as provisions for the prevention and regulation of strikes and lock-outs.

State amendments to the Act include changes to the definition of "workman" to include any person employed in an industrial establishment for the promotion of sales, as well as provisions for the adjudication of disputes between an individual workman and his employer.

In summary, the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, provides a legal framework for the resolution of disputes between employers and employees in industrial establishments in India. The Act defines key terms related to labor laws and disputes, specifies the powers and functions of various authorities, and includes provisions for the conciliation and settlement of disputes. State amendments to the Act provide additional protections for workmen and individual disputes.

The Act specifies the qualifications required for appointment as the presiding officer of a Tribunal, including being a Judge of a High Court, having been a District Judge or an Additional District Judge for at least three years, or being an officer of Indian Legal Service in Grade III with three years' experience in the grade. Section 94 states that where a bequest is made to the "representatives" or "legal representatives" or "personal representatives" or "executors or administrators" of a particular person, and the class so designated forms the direct and independent object of the bequest, the property bequeathed shall be distributed as if it had belonged to such person and he had died intestate in respect of it. No appeal shall lie against any decision or order given or made by the Tribunal.

Whenever an application is made to a Tribunal for the determination of any dispute, question or other matter relating to a waqf or waqf property, it shall hold its proceedings as expeditiously as possible and shall as soon as practicable, on the conclusion of the hearing of such matter give its decision in writing and furnish a copy of such decision to each of the parties to the dispute.

The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the consequences of breaching a contract in Chapter VI, specifically in Section 73. According to this section, when a contract is broken, the party who suffers as a result is entitled to receive compensation from the party who breached the contract for any loss or damage caused by the breach. This compensation is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The same compensation is also applicable when an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged.

The section further explains that in estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

A avails himself of those opportunities, but is put to trouble and expense in doing so. A is entitled to receive compensation from B in respect of such trouble and expense.

Overall, this section of the Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the compensation that the party who suffers from a breach of contract is entitled to receive from the party who breached the contract. The compensation is for any loss or damage caused by the breach, and it is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account while estimating the loss or damage.

THE CIVIL LIABILITY FOR NUCLEAR DAMAGE ACT, 2010

This Act establishes a no-fault liability regime for nuclear damage, with the operator being liable for compensation to victims. The Act applies to nuclear incidents occurring in or over the maritime areas beyond the territorial waters of India, in the exclusive economic zone of India, on board or by a ship or aircraft registered in India, or on or by an artificial island, installation, or structure under the jurisdiction of India. The operator is liable for nuclear damage caused by a nuclear incident occurring in or involving nuclear material coming from the nuclear installation. The liability of the operator is strict and based on the principle of no-fault liability.

The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board is required to notify a nuclear incident within 15 days of its occurrence. The operator is liable for nuclear damage caused by a nuclear incident directly due to a grave natural disaster or an act of armed conflict, hostility, civil war, insurrection, or terrorism. The operator is not liable for nuclear damage caused to the nuclear installation itself, to property on the same site used in connection with the installation, or to the means of transport upon which the nuclear material involved was carried at the time of the nuclear incident.

The maximum amount of liability for each nuclear incident is the rupee equivalent of three hundred million Special Drawing Rights or such higher amount as the Central Government may specify by notification. The liability of an operator for each nuclear incident is rupees one thousand five hundred crores in respect of nuclear reactors having thermal power equal to or above ten MW, rupees three hundred crores in respect of spent fuel reprocessing plants, and rupees one hundred crores in respect of the research reactors having thermal power below ten MW, fuel cycle facilities other than spent fuel reprocessing plants, and transportation of nuclear materials. The Central Government may review the amount of operator's liability from time to time and specify a higher amount.

The Central Government may establish a fund called the Nuclear Liability Fund to meet part of its liability under clause (a) or clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 7. The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the consequences of breaching a contract in Chapter VI, specifically in Section 73. According to this section, when a contract is broken, the party who suffers as a result is entitled to receive compensation from the party who breached the contract for any loss or damage caused by the breach. This compensation is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The same compensation is also applicable when an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged.

The section further explains that in estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Illustrations are provided to further explain the application of this section. For example, if A contracts to sell and deliver 50 maunds of saltpetre to B, at a certain price to be paid on delivery, and A breaks his promise, B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the sum, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which B might have obtained 50 maunds of saltpetre of like quality at the time when the saltpetre ought to have been delivered.

Another illustration explains that if A hires B‟s ship to go to Bombay, and there take on board, on the first of January, a cargo, which A is to provide, and to bring it to Calcutta, the freight to be paid when earned.
