A avails himself of those opportunities, but is put to trouble and expense in doing so. A is entitled to receive compensation from B in respect of such trouble and expense.

Overall, this section of the Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the compensation that the party who suffers from a breach of contract is entitled to receive from the party who breached the contract. The compensation is for any loss or damage caused by the breach, and it is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The lessee has the following obligations:

1. If an accession is made to the property during the lease term, it is deemed to be comprised in the lease.
2. If a material part of the property is wholly destroyed or rendered substantially and permanently unfit for its intended use due to fire, tempest, flood, violence of an army or mob, or other irresistible force, the lease becomes void at the lessee's option, provided the injury was not caused by the lessee's wrongful act or default.
3. If the lessor neglects to make repairs, the lessee may make them and deduct the expense from the rent or recover it from the lessor.
4. If the lessor neglects to make a payment recoverable from the lessee or against the property, the lessee may make the payment and deduct it from the rent or recover it from the lessor.
5. The lessee may remove all things attached to the earth at any time while in possession but must leave the property in the same state as received.
6. When a lease of uncertain duration determines, the lessee is entitled to all crops and free ingress and egress to gather and carry them.
7. The lessee may transfer the whole or any part of their interest in the property, and any transferee may again transfer it. However, the lessee remains subject to the lease's liabilities.
8. The lessee is bound to disclose any fact as to the nature or extent of the interest being taken that materially increases its value and of which the lessee is aware but the lessor is not.
9. The lessee is bound to pay or tender the premium or rent at the proper time and place.
10. The lessee is bound to keep and restore the property in good condition, subject to reasonable wear and tear, and allow the lessor and their agents to enter and inspect the property.
11. The lessee must give notice of any proceeding to recover the property, encroachment, or interference with the lessor's rights concerning the property.
12. The lessee may use the property and its products as a person of ordinary prudence would, but must not use it for a purpose other than intended or commit any act destructive or permanently injurious to the property.
13. The lessee must not correct any permanent structure without the lessor's consent, except for agricultural purposes.

If the lessor transfers the property leased or any part of their interest, the transferee possesses all the rights and, if the lessee so elects, is subject to all the liabilities of the lessor as to the property or part transferred so long as they own it. However, the lessor does not cease to be subject to any of the liabilities imposed upon them by the lease unless the lessee elects to treat the transferee as the person liable to them.

2. By the happening of an event on which the time is limited.
3. By the termination of the lessor's interest in the property.
4. By the vesting of the interests of the lessee and the lessor in the whole of the property in one person in the same right.
5. By express surrender.
6. By implied surrender.
7. By forfeiture.
8. On the expiration of a notice to determine the lease, quit, or to quit, or of intention to quit, the property leased, duly given by one party to the other.

The Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen. A contingent contract cannot be enforced by law unless and until the event on which it is contingent has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event does not happen can be enforced when the happening of that event becomes impossible, and not before. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if a specified uncertain event happens within a fixed time become void if, at the expiration of the time fixed, such event has not happened, or if, before the time fixed, such event becomes impossible. Contingent agreements to do or not to do anything, if an impossible event happens, are void, whether the impossibility of the event is known or not to the parties to the agreement at the time when it is made. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law. Promises bind the representatives of the promisors in case of the death of such promisors before performance, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If a promisor has made an offer of performance to the promisee, and the offer has not been accepted, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance, nor does he thereby lose his rights under the contract. Every such offer must fulfill certain conditions, such as being unconditional, made at a proper time and place, and under such circumstances that the person to whom it is made may have a reasonable opportunity of ascertaining that the person by whom it is made is able and willing there and then to do the whole of what he is bound by his promise to do. If the offer is an offer to deliver anything to the promisee, the promisee must have a reasonable opportunity of seeing that the thing offered is the thing which the promisor is bound by his promise to deliver.

The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, defines various terms related to labor laws and disputes in India. Key terms defined in the Act include:

* "Industrial establishment" - any establishment in which industrial activity is carried on.
* "Industrial dispute" - any dispute or difference between employers and employees in an industrial establishment.
* "Strike" - a cessation of work by a body of persons employed in an industry acting in combination.
* "Lock-out" - the temporary closing of a place of employment or the suspension of work by an employer.
* "Retrenchment" - the termination of the service of a workman by the employer for any reason other than as a punishment for misconduct.
* "Wages" - all remuneration capable of being expressed in terms of money, which would be payable to a workman in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment.
* "Workman" - any person employed in an industry to do any manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward.

The Act also specifies the powers and functions of various authorities, such as Labour Courts and Industrial Tribunals, in resolving industrial disputes. Additionally, the Act includes provisions for the conciliation and settlement of disputes, as well as provisions for the prevention and regulation of strikes and lock-outs.

The confirming officer has the power to direct that the offender not be committed to prison or force custody until the orders of the specified authority or officer have been obtained.
* Suspension of Sentences: Where a sentence is suspended, the offender shall be released from custody. The period during which the sentence is under suspension shall be reckoned as part of the term of such sentence. The authority or officer specified in section 130 may order that the offender be committed to undergo the unexpired portion of the sentence or that the sentence be remitted.
* Reconsideration of Case after Suspension: The case may be reconsidered by the authority or officer specified in section 130, or by any officer not below the rank of a Deputy Inspector-General duly authorized by the authority or officer specified in section 130. If the conduct of the offender since his conviction has been such as to justify a remission of the sentence, the matter shall be referred to the authority or officer specified in section 130.
* Fresh Sentence after Suspension: If an offender is sentenced for any other offence while a sentence on him is suspended, the sentences shall run concurrently if both sentences are suspended. If the further sentence is for a period of three months or more and is not suspended, the offender shall be committed to prison or force custody for the unexpired portion of the previous sentence, but both sentences shall run concurrently. If the further sentence is for a period of less than three months and is not suspended, the offender shall be committed on that sentence only, and the previous sentence shall continue to be suspended.
* Powers of Suspension: The powers conferred by sections 130 and 134 shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of, the power of mitigation, remission and commutation.
* Effect of Suspension and Remission on Dismissal: If the punishment of dismissal has been awarded by a Security Force Court and such other sentence is suspended under section 130, then, such dismissal shall not take effect until so ordered by the authority or officer specified in section 130. * Powers and Duties Conferrable and Imposable on Members of the Force: The Central Government may direct that any member of the Force may exercise or discharge certain powers or duties under specific Acts for the purpose of prevention of offences or apprehending offenders. * Power to Make Rules: The Central Government may make rules for the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions of this Act. These rules may provide for the constitution, governance, command and discipline of the Force, enrolment of persons to the Force, conditions of service, rank, precedence, powers of command and authority of the officers, removal, retirement, release or discharge from the service of persons subject to this Act, and any other matter necessary for the proper implementation of this Act.

The Specific Relief Act, 1963 (Act No. 47 of 1963) is an Act that defines and amends the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief. The Act is divided into three parts. Part I is the preliminary part, which includes the short title, extent, commencement, definitions, savings, and specific relief to be granted only for enforcing individual civil rights and not for enforcing penal laws. Part II is the specific relief part, which includes Chapter I on recovering possession of property, Chapter II on specific performance of contracts, Chapter III on rectification of instruments, Chapter IV on rescission of contracts, Chapter V on cancellation of instruments, Chapter VI on declaratory decrees, Chapter VII on injunctions generally, and Chapter VIII on perpetual injunctions. Under Part II, Chapter II on specific performance of contracts, the Act states that specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14, and section 16. The court may, in its discretion, direct rectification of the instrument so as to express that intention, so far as this can be done without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value.

The Act also states that the court may refuse to rescind the contract if the plaintiff has expressly or impliedly ratified the contract, or if owing to the change of circumstances which has taken place since the making of the contract, the parties cannot be substantially restored to the position in which they stood when the contract was made, or if third parties have, during the subsistence of the contract, acquired rights in good faith without notice and for value, or if only a part of the contract is sought to be rescinded and such part is not severable from the rest of the contract.

Under Part II, Chapter V on cancellation of instruments, the Act states that any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, and who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable, and the court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled.

The Married Women’s Property Act, 1874, is a law in India that aims to clarify and amend the law related to certain married women, primarily focusing on their wages, earnings, and insurances. The Act is applicable to the whole of India, except for the state of Jammu and Kashmir, and it does not apply to any married woman who professed Hindu, Muhammadan, Buddhist, Sikh, or Jain religion at the time of her marriage, nor to her husband who professed any of those religions at the time of marriage. The State Government has the power to exempt any race, sect, or tribe or part of a race, sect, or tribe from the operation of the Act.

The Act consists of five chapters. Chapter I, Preliminary, includes the short title and extent of the application of the Act. Chapter II, Married Women’s Wages and Earnings, states that the wages and earnings of any married woman acquired or gained by her after the passing of this Act, in any employment, occupation, or trade carried on by her and not by her husband, and all savings from and investments of such wages, earnings and property, shall be deemed to be her separate property. Chapter III, Insurances by Wives and Husbands, explains that any married woman may effect a policy of insurance on her own behalf and independently of her husband, and the same and all benefits thereof, if expressed on the face of it to be so effected, shall enure as her separate property. Chapter IV, Legal Proceedings by and against Married Women, allows a married woman to maintain a suit in her own name for the recovery of property of any description which, by force of the said Indian Succession Act, 1865, or of this Act, is her separate property, and she shall have, in her own name, the same remedies, both civil and criminal, against all persons, for the protection and security of such property, as if she were unmarried. Chapter V, Husband’s Liability for Wife’s Debts, states that a husband married after the thirty-first day of December, 1865, shall not by reason only of such marriage be liable to the debts of his wife contracted before marriage, but the wife shall be liable to be sued for, and shall, to the extent of her separate property, be liable to satisfy such debts as if he had continued unmarried.

This Act has been extended to and brought into force in Dadra and Nagar Haveli by Regulation 6 of 1963, and it is made applicable to the Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir and the Union territory of Ladakh. The Act has also been amended several times, including by Act 61 of 1959, Act 13 of 1923, Act 21 of 1929, Act 18 of 1927, and Act 12 of 1891.

context:
* Section 172: Award of compensatory costs in certain cases. question_text: The question is, whether A owes B rupees 10,000. Which of the following statements are relevant under Evidence Act;
options:
A) The facts that A asked C to lend him money, 
 B) D said to C in A's presence and hearing— "I advise you not to trust A, for he owes B 10,000 rupees," 
 C) A went away without making any answer 
 D) All of the above
context:
The Indian Evidence Act, 1872, governs the rules of evidence in India. This document summarizes various sections of the Act related to the examination and cross-examination of witnesses, leading questions, evidence as to matters in writing, and questions related to the character of the witness.

Under Section 137, a witness can be cross-examined on any matter relevant to the case, even if it was not mentioned during the examination-in-chief. The re-examination should be directed to explaining matters referred to in cross-examination. Leading questions, which suggest the answer the person asking it wishes or expects to receive, are not allowed in examination-in-chief or re-examination without the permission of the court. However, they may be asked in cross-examination.

Section 144 allows a witness to give oral evidence of statements made by other persons about the contents of documents if such statements are in themselves relevant facts. Section 145 permits a witness to be cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing or reduced into writing, relevant to matters in question, without the writing being shown to him.

Section 146 outlines the questions that can be asked during cross-examination, including those that test the veracity of the witness, discover who they are and what is their position in life, or to shake their credit by injuring their character. However, in a prosecution for certain offences under the Indian Penal Code, it is not permissible to adduce evidence or to put questions in the cross-examination of the victim as to their general immoral character or previous sexual experience.

The court has the discretion to decide whether a witness should be compelled to answer a question that relates to a matter not relevant to the suit or proceeding, except insofar as it affects the credit of the witness by injuring his character. The court shall have regard to certain considerations, such as the importance of the imputation made against the witness's character and the importance of his evidence. No such question ought to be asked unless the person asking it has reasonable grounds for thinking that the imputation is well-founded. If the court is of the opinion that any such question was asked without reasonable grounds, it may report the circumstances of the case to the High Court or other authority to which the barrister, pleader, vakil, or attorney is subject in the exercise of his profession.

Section 151 permits the court to forbid any questions or inquiries which it regards as indecent or scandalous, unless they relate to facts in issue or to matters necessary to be known in order to determine whether or not the facts in issue existed. The court shall forbid any question which appears to it to be intended to insult or annoy, or which, though proper in itself, appears to the court needlessly offensive in form. Evidence that tends to contradict answers to questions testing veracity is generally not admissible, but if a witness answers falsely, he may be charged with giving false evidence.
Summary:

The Indian Evidence Act, 1872, governs the admission and proof of evidence in legal proceedings in India. This document summarizes various sections of the Act related to the questioning of witnesses, impeaching the credit of witnesses, corroborating evidence, and the production and use of documents.

Section 145 permits a witness to be contradicted on a fact which affects their credit. This means that if a witness makes a statement that is inconsistent with a fact that affects their credibility, they can be questioned about it. For example, if a witness denies being at a certain location on a particular day, they can be contradicted with evidence that they were, in fact, at that location on that day.

Section 154 allows the person who calls a witness to put questions to them that could be asked in cross-examination by the adverse party. This is to ensure that the witness's testimony is fully explored and that any inconsistencies or biases are brought to light.

Section 155 outlines the ways in which the credit of a witness can be impeached. This can be done by evidence of persons who testify that they believe the witness to be unworthy of credit, proof that the witness has been bribed or has accepted a bribe, or proof of former statements inconsistent with any part of their evidence.

Section 156 allows a witness to be questioned about any other circumstances that they observed at or near the time or place at which a relevant fact occurred, if the Court is of the opinion that such circumstances, if proved, would corroborate the testimony of the witness as to the relevant fact.

Section 157 permits the testimony of a witness to be corroborated by any former statement made by such witness relating to the same fact, at or about the time when the fact took place, or before any authority legally competent to investigate the fact.
Section 39 states that when any statement of which evidence is given forms part of a longer statement, or of a conversation or part of an isolated document, or is contained in a document which forms part of a book, or is contained in part of electronic record or of a connected series of letters or papers, evidence shall be given of so much and no more of the statement, conversation, document, electronic record, book or series of letters or papers as the court considers necessary in that particular case to the full understanding of the nature and effect of the statement, and of the circumstances under which it was made.

Section 40 states that the existence of any judgment, order or decree which by law prevents any court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial, is a relevant fact when the question is whether such court ought to take cognizance of such suit or to hold such trial.

Section 41 states that a final judgment, order or decree of a competent court, in the exercise of probate, matrimonial, admiralty or insolvency jurisdiction, which confers upon or takes away from any person any legal character, or which declares any person to be entitled to any such character, or to be entitled to any specific thing, not as against any specified person but absolutely, is relevant when the existence of any such legal character, or the title of any such person to any such thing, is relevant. Such judgment, order or decree is conclusive proof that any legal character which it confers accrued at the time when such judgment, order or decree came into operation, and that anything to which it declares any person to be so entitled was the property of that person at the time from which such judgment, order or decree declares that it had been or should be his property.

Section 42 states that judgments, orders or decrees other than those mentioned in section 41 are relevant if they relate to matters of a public nature relevant to the enquiry, but such judgments, orders or decrees are not conclusive proof of that which they state.

Section 43 states that judgments, orders or decrees, other than those mentioned in sections 40, 41, and 42, are irrelevant, unless the existence of such judgment, order or decree is a fact in issue, or is relevant under some other provision of this Act.

Section 44 states that any party to a suit or other proceeding may show that any judgment, order, or decree which is relevant under section 40, 41, or 42, and which has been proved by the adverse party, was delivered by a court not competent to deliver it, or was obtained by fraud or collusion.

Section 45 states that when the court has to form an opinion upon a point of foreign law or of science, or art, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, the opinions upon that point of persons specially skilled in such foreign law, science, or art, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, are relevant facts.

Section 46 states that facts bearing upon the question whether an expert is competent to express an opinion, and facts calculated to affect the weight of his opinion, are relevant, whether they are or are not themselves proved by other evidence.

Section 47 states that opinions of third persons, when uncommunicated to the person for whose use the opinion is given, are not relevant, unless the court has or the person to whom the opinion is given has special means of knowledge as to the accuracy of such opinions.
Summary:

Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) explains the procedure for giving information regarding the commission of a cognizable offence. In cases where the offence is committed against a woman under certain sections of the Indian Penal Code, the information must be recorded by a woman police officer or any woman officer. If the person against whom the offence is alleged to have been committed is temporarily or permanently mentally or physically disabled, the information shall be recorded by a police officer at the residence of the person seeking to report such offence or at a convenient place of such person’s choice, in the presence of an interpreter or a special educator, as the case may be.

Section 155 of the CrPC deals with information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases. When information is given to an officer in charge of a police station of the commission of a non-cognizable offence, he shall enter or cause to be entered the substance of the information in a book to be kept by such officer. No police officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate having power to try such case or commit the case for trial.

Section 156 of the CrPC provides for police officer’s power to investigate cognizable cases. Any officer in charge of a police station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case which a Court having jurisdiction over the local area within the limits of such station would have power to inquire into or try under the provisions of Chapter XIII.

Section 157 of the CrPC explains the procedure for investigation. If an officer in charge of a police station has reason to suspect the commission of an offence which he is empowered under section 156 to investigate, he shall forthwith send a report of the same to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of such offence upon a police report and shall proceed in person or shall depute one of his subordinate officers to proceed to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case.

Section 158 of the CrPC deals with report how submitted. Every report sent to a Magistrate under section 157 shall, if the State Government so directs, be submitted through such superior officer of police as the State Government appoints in that behalf.

Section 159 of the CrPC provides for the Magistrate’s power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry.

Section 160 of the CrPC deals with police officer’s power to require attendance of witnesses. The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the consequences of breaching a contract in Chapter VI, specifically in Section 73. According to this section, when a contract is broken, the party who suffers as a result is entitled to receive compensation from the party who breached the contract for any loss or damage caused by the breach. This compensation is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The same compensation is also applicable when an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged.

The section further explains that in estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Illustrations are provided to further explain the application of this section. A avails himself of those opportunities, but is put to trouble and expense in doing so. A is entitled to receive compensation from B in respect of such trouble and expense.

Overall, this section of the Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the compensation that the party who suffers from a breach of contract is entitled to receive from the party who breached the contract. The compensation is for any loss or damage caused by the breach, and it is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account while estimating the loss or damage.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the act of a partner which is done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind carried on by the firm, binds the firm. The authority of a partner to bind the firm conferred by this section is called his "implied authority".

In order to bind a firm, an act or instrument done or executed by a partner or other person on behalf of the firm shall be done or executed in the firm name, or in any other manner expressing or implying an intention to bind the firm.

An admission or representation made by a partner concerning the affairs of the firm is evidence against the firm, if it is made in the ordinary course of business.

Notice to a partner who habitually acts in the business of the firm of any matter relating to the affairs of the firm operates as notice to the firm, except in the case of a fraud on the firm committed by or with the consent of that partner.

Every partner is liable, jointly with all the other partners and also severally, for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner.

Where, by the wrongful act or omission of a partner acting in the ordinary course of the business of a firm, or with the authority of his partners, loss or injury is caused to any third party, or any penalty is incurred, the firm is liable therefor to the same extent as the partner.

Where a partner acting within his apparent authority receives money or property from a third party and misapplies it, or where a firm in the course of its business receives money or property from a third party, and the money or property is misapplied by any of the partners while it is in the custody of the firm, the firm is liable to make good the loss.

Anyone who by words spoken or written or by conduct represents himself, or knowingly permits himself to be represented, to be a partner in a firm, is liable as a partner in that firm to anyone who has on the faith of any such representation given credit to the firm, whether the person representing himself or represented to be a partner does or does not know that the representation has reached the person so giving credit.

A person who is a minor according to the law to which he is subject may not be a partner in a firm, but, with the consent of all the partners for the time being, he may be admitted to the benefits of partnership.

In summary, the Patents Act, 1970 is an Act that governs the grant and enforcement of patents in India. The Act sets out the requirements for obtaining a patent, the grounds for refusal of a patent, and the procedures for appeal and opposition to the grant of a patent. According to Section 5(1) of the Patents Act, 1970, any person claiming to be the true and first inventor of an invention, an assignee of such a person, or the legal representative of a deceased person who was entitled to make an application for a patent can file an application. The application must be made in the prescribed form and filed in the patent office. This amendment can include an amendment of the priority date of a claim. After the grant of a patent, the patentee can still amend the specification in any proceeding before the Appellate Board or High Court for the revocation of a patent, subject to certain provisions and terms.

If the patent is decided to be invalid, the specification can be amended under this section instead of revoking the patent.

Section 59 outlines the supplementary provisions as to amendment of an application or specification. No amendment of an application for a patent or a complete specification or any document relating thereto shall be made except by way of disclaimer, correction, or explanation. The amendment must be for the purpose of incorporation of actual fact, and no amendment of a complete specification shall be allowed if it would claim or describe matter not in substance disclosed or shown in the specification before the amendment.

Under Section 61, if the Controller is prima facie satisfied that the failure to pay the renewal fee was unintentional and that there has been no undue delay in the making of the application, he shall publish the application in the prescribed manner. Section 62 outlines the rights of patentees of lapsed patents which have been restored. Section 63 allows for the surrender of patents. A patentee may offer to surrender his patent by giving notice in the prescribed manner to the Controller. Any person interested may, within the prescribed period, give notice to the Controller of opposition to the surrender. If the Controller is satisfied after hearing the patentee and any opponent that the patent may properly be surrendered, he may accept the offer and revoke the patent.

context:
The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 introduces the goods and services tax (GST) in India. This tax aims to replace various indirect taxes levied by the Union and State Governments and create a common national market for goods and services. The GST will be levied on all transactions involving the supply of goods or services or both, except those explicitly excluded.

The Act proposes to subsume various Central indirect taxes, such as Central Excise Duty, Additional Excises Duties, Excise Duty on medicinal and toilet preparations, Service Tax, Countervailing Duty, Special Additional Duty of Customs, and Central Surcharges and Cesses related to the supply of goods and services. Similarly, State Value Added Tax/Sales Tax, Entertainment Tax, Central Sales Tax, Octroi and Entry tax, Purchase Tax, Luxury tax, Taxes on lottery, betting and gambling, and State cesses and surcharges related to supply of goods and services will also be subsumed.

The Act also introduces Integrated Goods and Services Tax on inter-State transactions of goods and services. An additional tax of up to 1% on the supply of goods in the course of inter-State trade or commerce will be levied for a period of two years, collected by the Government of India, and assigned to the States from where the supply originates.

The Act confers concurrent powers upon Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws governing goods and services tax, covering all goods and services, except alcoholic liquor for human consumption. Petroleum and petroleum products will not be subject to the levy of Goods and Services Tax till a date notified on the recommendation of the Goods and Services Tax Council.

The Act provides compensation to the States for loss of revenue arising on account of implementing the Goods and Services Tax for a period that may extend to five years. A Goods and Services Tax Council is created to examine issues relating to goods and services tax and make recommendations to the Union and the States on parameters like rates, exemption list, and threshold limits. The Council will function under the Chairmanship of the Union Finance Minister and will have the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance as a member, along with the Minister in-charge of Finance or Taxation or any other Minister nominated by each State Government. The Council's decisions will be taken by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting.

The Act provides transitional provisions to address any inconsistency arising with respect to any law relating to tax on goods or services or on both in force in any State on the commencement of the provisions of the Constitution as amended by this Act within a period of one year.

Summary:

The Indian Contract Act, 1872, is a legal act that defines and amends certain parts of the law relating to contracts in India. The act is divided into chapters, with Chapter 1 focusing on the communication, acceptance, and revocation of proposals. The communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made, while the communication of an acceptance is complete when it is put in a course of transmission to the proposer. A proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete, but not afterwards, while an acceptance may be revoked at any time before the communication of the acceptance is complete. The act also defines what constitutes a sound mind for the purpose of making a contract and states that consent is said to be free when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake.
Summary:
The document outlines various aspects of Indian contract law, focusing on the concepts of coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, and mistake. Coercion is defined as the committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code or the unlawful detaining or threatening to detain any property to the prejudice of any person, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement. Undue influence is defined as a contract induced by the relations between the parties, where one party is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage. Fraud is defined as any act committed by a party to a contract, or with his connivance, or by his agent, with the intent to deceive another party. Misrepresentation is defined as the positive assertion, in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it, of that which is not true, though he believes it to be true, or any breach of duty which gains an advantage by misleading another to his prejudice. A contract is voidable if consent is caused by coercion, fraud, or misrepresentation. If consent was caused by misrepresentation or by silence, fraudulent within the meaning of section 17, the contract is not voidable if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. In the case of undue influence, the agreement is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused, and any such contract may be set aside either absolutely or, if the party who was entitled to avoid it has received any benefit thereunder, upon such terms and conditions as to the Court may seem just. Lastly, where both the parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void. An erroneous opinion as to the value of the thing which forms the subject-matter of the agreement is not to be deemed a mistake as to a matter of fact.

Subject to contract between the partners, if a partner derives any profits for himself from any transaction of the firm, or from the use of the property or business connection of the firm or the firm name, he shall account for that profit and pay it to the firm; if a partner carries on any business of the same nature as and competing with that of the firm, he shall account for and pay to the firm all profits made by him in that business.

Subject to contract between the partners, where a change occurs in the constitution of a firm, the mutual rights and duties of the partners in the reconstituted firm remain the same as they were immediately before the change, as far as may be; where a firm constituted for a fixed term continues to carry on business after the expiry of that term, the mutual rights and duties of the partners remain the same as they were before the expiry, so far as they may be consistent with the incidents of partnership at will; and where a firm constituted to carry out one or more adventures or undertakings carries out other adventures or undertakings, the mutual rights and duties of the partners in respect of the other adventures or undertakings are the same as those in respect of the original adventures or undertakings.

Subject to contract between the partners, a partner is the agent of the firm for the purposes of the business of the firm.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the act of a partner which is done to carry on, in the usual way, business of the kind carried on by the firm, binds the firm. The authority of a partner to bind the firm conferred by this section is called his "implied authority".

The partners in a firm may, by contract between the partners, extend or restrict the implied authority of any partner. Notwithstanding any such restriction, any act done by a partner on behalf of the firm which falls within his implied authority binds the firm, unless the person with whom he is dealing knows of the restriction or does not know or believe that partner to be a partner.

A Partner has authority, in an emergency, to do all such acts for the purpose of protecting the firm from loss as would be done by a person of ordinary prudence, in his own case, acting under similar circumstances, and such acts bind the firm.

In order to bind a firm, an act or instrument done or executed by a partner or other person on behalf of the firm shall be done or executed in the firm name, or in any other manner expressing or implying an intention to bind the firm.

An admission or representation made by a partner concerning the affairs of the firm is evidence against the firm, if it is made in the ordinary course of business.

Notice to a partner who habitually acts in the business of the firm of any matter relating to the affairs of the firm operates as notice to the firm, except in the case of a fraud on the firm committed by or with the consent of that partner.

Every partner is liable, jointly with all the other partners and also severally, for all acts of the firm done while he is a partner.

Where, by the wrongful act or omission of a partner acting in the ordinary course of the business of a firm, or with the authority of his partners, loss or injury is caused to any third party, or any penalty is incurred, the firm is liable therefor to the same extent as the partner.

Where a partner acting within his apparent authority receives money or property from a third party and misapplies it, or where a firm in the course of its business receives money or property from a third party, and the money or property is misapplied by any of the partners while it is in the custody of the firm, the firm is liable to make good the loss.

Anyone who by words spoken or written or by conduct represents himself, or knowingly permits himself to be represented, to be a partner in a firm, is liable as a partner in that firm to anyone who has on the faith of any such representation given credit to the firm, whether the person representing himself or represented to be a partner does or does not know that the representation has reached the person so giving credit.

A person who is a minor according to the law to which he is subject may not be a partner in a firm, but, with the consent of all the partners for the time being, he may be admitted to the benefits of partnership.

Where any person has been admitted as a minor to the benefits of partnership in a firm, the burden of proving the fact that such person had no knowledge of such admission until a particular date after the expiry of six months of his attaining majority shall lie on the persons asserting that fact.

This document contains a list of sections from the Indian Penal Code, which is a criminal code in India. The sections listed here cover various offences related to causing harm to others, either physically or mentally. The offences include causing hurt, grievous hurt, or death, as well as endangering the life or personal safety of others. Some sections also cover specific circumstances, such as causing harm to deter a public servant from performing their duty, or causing harm to extort property or to compel someone to do something illegal. Each section includes a description of the offence, the punishment for committing the offence, and any relevant explanations or exceptions.

One of the sections, Section 326A, deals specifically with the offence of causing harm by throwing or attempting to throw acid. This section includes a definition of "acid" as any substance with acidic or corrosive character or burning nature that is capable of causing bodily injury leading to scars or disfigurement or temporary or permanent disability. The punishment for this offence is imprisonment for a term of not less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and a fine that is just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses of the treatment of the victim. The fine imposed under this section shall be paid to the victim.

Another section, Section 326B, deals with the offence of voluntarily throwing or attempting to throw acid with the intention of causing permanent or partial damage or deformity or burns or maiming or disfigurement or disability or grievous hurt to the person. The punishment for this offence is imprisonment for a term of not less than five years but which may extend to seven years, and a fine.

Section 330 and 331 deals with voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession or to compel restoration of property. The punishment for this offence is imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Section 332 and 333 deals with voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty. Article 3 of the Constitution allows Parliament to form a new State by separating territory from any State or by uniting two or more States or parts of States or by uniting any territory to a part of any State. It can increase, diminish, or alter the boundaries or name of any State, provided that no Bill for the purpose shall be introduced in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President and after the expression of views by the State Legislature, if the proposal affects the area, boundaries, or name of any of the States.

The Constitution (Fifth Amendment) Act, 1955, modified Article 3 to provide a time limit within which the State has to express their views on State reorganization laws. If they do not express their views within the specified time, the Bill may be passed by Parliament. The meaning of "Other Authorities" under Article 12 has been interpreted by Indian courts to include any authority created by a statute on which powers are conferred to carry out governmental or quasi-governmental functions and functioning within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.

The 'Doctrine of Eclipse' asserts that all pre-constitutional laws which are against the fundamental rights of the Indian Constitution will become dormant and not dead. They will remain dormant as long as the state does not amend the law and its infringing nature.

The Bye-Laws made by the Cooperative Societies are also not part of the definition of Law. The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the consequences of breaching a contract in Chapter VI, specifically in Section 73. According to this section, when a contract is broken, the party who suffers as a result is entitled to receive compensation from the party who breached the contract for any loss or damage caused by the breach. This compensation is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The same compensation is also applicable when an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged.

The section further explains that in estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Illustrations are provided to further explain the application of this section. For example, if A contracts to sell and deliver 50 maunds of saltpetre to B, at a certain price to be paid on delivery, and A breaks his promise, B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the sum, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which B might have obtained 50 maunds of saltpetre of like quality at the time when the saltpetre ought to have been delivered.

Another illustration explains that if A hires B‟s ship to go to Bombay, and there take on board, on the first of January, a cargo, which A is to provide, and to bring it to Calcutta, the freight to be paid when earned. Overall, this section of the Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the compensation that the party who suffers from a breach of contract is entitled to receive from the party who breached the contract. The compensation is for any loss or damage caused by the breach, and it is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account while estimating the loss or damage.

The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the legal framework for contracts in India. This summary focuses on the sections of the Act related to agency, specifically sections 187-204.

An agent is a person who is authorized to act on behalf of another person, known as the principal. An agency can be created either expressly or impliedly, and the agent is required to act in the best interests of the principal. The agent's authority can be either general or special, and the extent of the agent's authority is determined by the terms of the agency agreement. An agent has the authority to do everything necessary to carry out the purpose of the agency, including acts that are usually done in the course of conducting such business. In an emergency, an agent has the authority to take any reasonable action to protect the principal from loss.

An agent cannot delegate his authority to another person unless it is customary in the trade or necessary due to the nature of the agency. If an agent employs a sub-agent without authority, the agent is responsible for the sub-agent's acts both to the principal and to third parties. However, if a sub-agent is properly appointed, the principal is represented by the sub-agent, and is bound by and responsible for the sub-agent's acts.

An agent can ratify unauthorized acts done on behalf of the principal, and such ratification has the same effect as if the acts had been performed with authority. However, a person cannot validly ratify an unauthorized act if his knowledge of the facts is materially defective.

The principal can revoke the agent's authority at any time before the authority has been exercised, except in cases where the agent has an interest in the subject matter of the agency. If the agent has an interest in the property that is the subject of the agency, the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of such interest. The principal cannot revoke the authority given to his agent after the authority has been partly exercised, except in cases where a power of revocation has been reserved in the agency agreement.

In summary, the Indian Contract Act of 1872 provides a legal framework for contracts in India, including the creation, authority, and termination of agency relationships. The Act recognizes the importance of agency relationships in commercial transactions and provides clear rules for their creation, operation, and termination.

The agent is also required to act with reasonable diligence and use the skill that they possess. Additionally, the agent is bound to render proper accounts to the principal on demand.

The principal, on the other hand, is required to make compensation to the agent for any previous revocation or renunciation of the agency without sufficient cause, if there is an express or implied contract that the agency should be continued for any period of time. The principal must also give reasonable notice of such revocation or renunciation, otherwise the damage thereby resulting to the principal or the agent must be made good to the one by the other.

This document is divided into several parts, with Part 0 being the preliminary section that includes the short title, commencement, and extent of the Act. The Act extends to the whole of India, except for the State of Nagaland and the tribal areas, unless extended by the State Government with supplemental, incidental, or consequential modifications.

Part 0 also includes definitions of various legal terms used throughout the Act. For example, "decree" is defined as the formal expression of an adjudication that conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit. It may be preliminary or final, and does not include any adjudication from which an appeal lies or any order of dismissal for default. A "decree-holder" is any person in whose favor a decree has been passed or an order capable of execution has been made.

Part 1 of the Act deals with the jurisdiction and powers of civil courts. Section 9 states that every suit shall be instituted in the court of the lowest grade competent to try it. Part 2 of the Act deals with written statements, setting out the defendant's version of the case. Part 5 of the Act deals with the execution of decrees and orders. Section 36 states that the court shall execute a decree or order for the payment of money forthwith. Section 37 provides that the court may, in its discretion, order the payment of the amount in installments.

The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the consequences of breaching a contract in Chapter VI, specifically in Section 73. According to this section, when a contract is broken, the party who suffers as a result is entitled to receive compensation from the party who breached the contract for any loss or damage caused by the breach. This compensation is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The same compensation is also applicable when an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged.

The section further explains that in estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Illustrations are provided to further explain the application of this section. For example, if A contracts to sell and deliver 50 maunds of saltpetre to B, at a certain price to be paid on delivery, and A breaks his promise, B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the sum, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which B might have obtained 50 maunds of saltpetre of like quality at the time when the saltpetre ought to have been delivered.

Another illustration explains that if A hires B‟s ship to go to Bombay, and there take on board, on the first of January, a cargo, which A is to provide, and to bring it to Calcutta, the freight to be paid when earned. B’s ship does not go to Bombay, but A has opportunities of procuring suitable conveyance for the cargo upon terms as advantageous as those on which he had chartered the ship. A avails himself of those opportunities, but is put to trouble and expense in doing so. A is entitled to receive compensation from B in respect of such trouble and expense.

Overall, this section of the Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the compensation that the party who suffers from a breach of contract is entitled to receive from the party who breached the contract. The compensation is for any loss or damage caused by the breach, and it is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account while estimating the loss or damage.

The Act applies to the whole of India and has overriding effect over any other law or instrument that is inconsistent with its provisions.

Chapter I of the Act deals with preliminary matters and defines key terms used throughout the Act. The term "employer" is defined as any person who employs one or more workers in an establishment or employment in which this Act has come into force. "Same work or work of a similar nature" means work in respect of which the skill, effort, and responsibility required are the same when performed under similar working conditions by a man or a woman.

THE SOCIETIES REGISTRATION ACT, 1860, is an Act to provide for the registration of literary, scientific, and charitable societies. The Act defines societies as those formed by a memorandum of association and registration, with a minimum of seven members associated for any literary, scientific, or charitable purpose, or for any purpose described in section 20 of the Act.

The memorandum of association must contain the name of the society, the objects of the society, and the names, addresses, and occupations of the governors, council, directors, committee, or other governing body. A copy of the rules and regulations of the society, certified to be a correct copy by not less than three of the members of the governing body, must also be filed with the memorandum of association.

Upon such memorandum and certified copy being filed, the Registrar shall certify under his hand that the society is registered under this Act. The registration fee is fifty rupees, or such smaller fee as the State Government may, from time to time, direct.

Every society registered under this Act may sue or be sued in the name of the president, chairman, or principal secretary, or trustees, as shall be determined by the rules and regulations of the society. No suit or proceeding in any Civil Court shall abate or discontinue by reason of the person, by or against whom such suit or proceedings shall have been brought or continued, dying or ceasing to fill the character in the name whereof he shall have sued or been sued.

The property, movable and immovable, belonging to a society registered under this Act, if not vested in trustees, shall be deemed to be vested, for the time being, in the governing body of such society.

If a judgment shall be recovered against the person or officer named on behalf of the society, such judgment shall not be put in force against the property, movable or immovable, or against the body of such person or officer, but against the property of the society.

The Act enables societies to alter, extend or abridge their purposes, and to amalgamate with any other society, subject to the provisions of the Act. The governing body may submit the proposition to the members of the society in a written or printed report, and may convene a special meeting for the consideration thereof according to the regulations of the society. No such proposition shall be carried into effect unless such report shall have been delivered or sent by post to every member of the society ten days previous to the special meeting convened by the governing body for the consideration thereof, nor unless such proposition shall have been agreed to by the votes of three-fifths of the members delivered in person or by proxy, and confirmed by the votes of three-fifths of the members present at a second special meeting convened by the governing body at an interval of one month after the former meeting.

Anymember of the society who shall steal, purloin or embezzle any money or other property, or wilfully and maliciously destroy or injure any property of such society, or shall forge any deed, bond, security for money, receipt, or other instrument, whereby the funds of the society may be exposed to loss, shall be subject to the same prosecution, and, if convicted, shall be liable to be punished in like manner, as any person not a member would be subject and liable to in respect of the like offence.

The Act provides for the dissolution of societies and the adjustment of their affairs. Upon a dissolution, no member to receive profit. If upon the dissolution of any society registered under this Act there shall remain after the satisfaction of all its debts and liabilities any property whatsoever, the same shall not be paid to or distributed among the members of the said society or any of them, but shall be given to some other society, to be determined by the votes of not less than three-fifths of the members present personally or by proxy at the time of the dissolution, or, in default thereof, by such Court as aforesaid.

For the purposes of this Act, a member of a society shall be a person who, having been admitted therein according to the rules and regulations thereof, shall have paid a subscription, or shall have signed the roll or list of members thereof, and shall not have resigned in accordance with such rules and regulations.

The governing body of the society shall be the governors, council, directors, committee, trustees or other body to whom by the rules and regulations of the society the management of its affairs is entrusted.

The Act also lays down the procedure for filing and disposing of complaints and appeals, and the powers and functions of the consumer dispute redressal agencies. The Act also empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act, and the State Governments to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act in relation to the State Commissions and District Fora. An easement is extinguished when either the dominant or the servient heritage is completely destroyed.

An easement is extinguished when it totally ceases to be enjoyed as such for an unbroken period of twenty years.

When an easement is extinguished, the rights (if any) accessory thereto are also extinguished.

This Act is supplemental to the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, and applies to Hindus domiciled in India who are outside the country. Natural guardians of a Hindu minor, in respect of the minor's person as well as in respect of the minor’s property, are the father, and after him, the mother. However, the custody of a minor who has not completed the age of five years shall ordinarily be with the mother. The natural guardianship of an adopted son who is a minor passes, on adoption, to the adoptive father and after him to the adoptive mother. The natural guardian has the power to do all acts that are necessary or reasonable and proper for the benefit of the minor or for the realization, protection, or benefit of the minor's estate, but the guardian cannot bind the minor by a personal covenant. The natural guardian shall not, without the previous permission of the court, mortgage or charge, or transfer by sale, gift, exchange, or otherwise, any part of the immovable property of the minor or lease any part of such property for a term exceeding five years or for a term extending more than one year beyond the date on which the minor will attain majority. Any disposal of immovable property by a natural guardian, in contravention of sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), is voidable at the instance of the minor or any person claiming under him. No court shall grant permission to the natural guardian to do any of the acts mentioned in sub-section (2) except in case of necessity or for an evident advantage to the minor. An appointment made under sub-section (1) shall have no effect if the father predeceases the mother, but shall revive if the mother dies without appointing, by will, any person as guardian. A Hindu widow entitled to act as the natural guardian of her minor legitimate children, and a Hindu mother entitled to act as the natural guardian of her minor legitimate children by reason of the fact that the father has become disentitled to act as such, may, by will, appoint a guardian for any of them in respect of the minor’s person or in respect of the minor’s property or in respect of both. A Hindu mother entitled to act as the natural guardian of her minor illegitimate children may; by will, appoint a guardian for any of them in respect of the minor’s person or in respect of the minor's property or in respect of both. The Indian Evidence Act of 1872 outlines the rules for the admission of evidence in legal proceedings in India. The Act defines an admission as a statement made by a party or their agent that suggests any inference as to a fact in issue or a relevant fact. Admissions can be made orally, in writing, or electronically. Admissions made by parties to a proceeding, or their agents, are admissible as evidence. Admissions made by parties in a representative capacity, such as a suitor, are admissible if made while they held that character. Admissions made by parties interested in the subject matter or persons from whom they have derived their interest are admissible if made during the continuance of their interest. Statements made by persons whose position or liability must be proved in the suit are admissions if made while they occupy that position or are subject to that liability. Statements made by persons to whom a party has expressly referred for information are also admissions. Admissions can be proved by or on behalf of the person making them in certain circumstances, such as if the statement is of a nature that would be relevant if the person were dead, or if it is relevant otherwise than as an admission. Oral admissions as to the contents of a document are not relevant unless the party proposing to prove them shows that they are entitled to give secondary evidence of the contents of the document or if the genuineness of the document is in question. In civil cases, no admission is relevant if it is made on the condition that evidence of it is not to be given or if the parties agreed that evidence of it should not be given. Confessions caused by inducement, threat, or promise are irrelevant in criminal proceedings. Confessions made to a police officer cannot be proved as against a person accused of an offense. Confessions made while a person is in the custody of a police officer, unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, are not admissible as evidence against them. However, if a fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of an offense, so much of such information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered may be proved. A confession made after the removal of the impression caused by any such inducement, threat, or promise is relevant. A confession is not rendered inadmissible merely because it was made under a promise of secrecy or in consequence of a deception practiced on the accused.
The Indian Evidence Act of 1872 outlines the rules for the admissibility of evidence in courts of law in India. In this summary, we will focus on Sections 27-33 of the Act, which deal with statements made by persons who cannot be called as witnesses.

Under Section 27, confessions made to a police officer are not admissible as evidence against the person making the confession. This provision is meant to protect individuals from being coerced into confessing to a crime by the police.

Summary:
The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is an Act of the Parliament of India that consolidates and amends the law relating to domestic arbitration, international commercial arbitration, and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards. It also defines the law relating to conciliation and matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The Act is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985) and the UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules (1980). The Act applies to the whole of India and came into force on a date appointed by the Central Government. The Act is divided into two parts: Part I - Arbitration and Part II - Conciliation. Part I of the Act contains general provisions, arbitration agreement, composition and jurisdiction of arbitral tribunal, conduct of arbitral proceedings, making of arbitral award and terms of settlement, recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards, and appeals. Part II of the Act deals with conciliation, including provisions for the commencement of conciliation proceedings, the conduct of the conciliation proceedings, the termination of conciliation proceedings, and the effects of conciliation agreements. The Act provides for extensive judicial intervention in arbitration proceedings, but also allows for parties to agree to derogate from certain provisions of the Act. The Act applies to every arbitration under any other enactment for the time being in force, as if the arbitration were pursuant to an arbitration agreement and as if that other enactment were an arbitration agreement. However, the provisions of this Part are inconsistent with that other enactment or with any rules made thereunder. The Act also provides for administrative assistance in the conduct of arbitral proceedings.
Summary:

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is a law in India that governs domestic and international commercial arbitration and conciliation. The Act applies to any arbitration agreement, whether it is in the form of an arbitration clause in a contract or a separate agreement.

Section 7 defines an arbitration agreement as a written agreement between two or more parties to submit to arbitration all or certain disputes that have arisen or may arise between them in respect of a defined legal relationship, whether contractual or not.

Section 8 empowers a judicial authority to refer parties to arbitration where there is an arbitration agreement, provided that a party to the agreement or any person claiming through or under him applies for it not later than the date of submitting his first statement on the substance of the dispute.

Section 9 allows a party to apply to a court for the appointment of a guardian for a minor or person of unsound mind for the purposes of arbitral proceedings, or for an interim measure of protection in respect of certain matters, such as the preservation, interim custody or sale of goods, securing the amount in dispute, and interim injunction or the appointment of a receiver.

Section 10 provides that the parties are free to determine the number of arbitrators, provided that such number shall not be an even number. Failing the determination, the arbitral tribunal shall consist of a sole arbitrator.

Section 11 states that a person of any nationality may be an arbitrator, unless otherwise agreed by the parties. The parties are free to agree on a procedure for appointing the arbitrator or arbitrators. If there is no agreement, in an arbitration with three arbitrators, each party shall appoint one arbitrator, and the two appointed arbitrators shall appoint the third arbitrator who shall act as the presiding arbitrator.

The First Schedule of the Act contains the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards. The Convention applies to the recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards made in a State other than the State where recognition and enforcement are sought and arising out of differences between persons, whether physical or legal. The Convention also applies to arbitral awards not considered as domestic awards in the State where recognition and enforcement are sought.

The Convention requires Contracting States to recognize an agreement in writing under which the parties undertake to submit to arbitration all or any differences that have arisen or may arise between them in respect of a defined legal relationship. The court of a Contracting State, when seized of an action in a matter in respect of which the parties have made an agreement within the meaning of this article, shall refer the parties to arbitration, unless it finds that the agreement is null and void.

Each Contracting State shall recognize arbitral awards as binding and enforce them in accordance with the rules of procedure of the territory where the award is relied upon, under the conditions laid down in the Convention. The party applying for recognition and enforcement of the award shall supply the duly authenticated original award or a duly certified copy thereof and the original agreement referred to in article II or a duly certified copy thereof. If the award or agreement is not made in an official language of the country in which the award is relied upon, the party applying for recognition and enforcement of the award shall produce a translation of these documents into such language.

Recognition and enforcement of the award may be refused at the request of the party against whom it is invoked only if that party furnishes proof that the parties to the agreement were, under the law applicable to them, under some incapacity, or the agreement is not valid under the law to which the parties have subjected it, or if the party against whom the award is invoked was not given proper notice of the appointment of the arbitrator or of the arbitration proceedings, or if the composition of the arbitral authority or the arbitral procedure was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties. Recognition and enforcement may also be refused if the competent authority in the country where recognition and enforcement is sought finds that the subject-matter of the difference is not capable of settlement by arbitration under the law of that country or that the recognition or enforcement of the award would be contrary to the public policy of that country.
