context:
Article 291 of the Indian Constitution, which dealt with the payment of privy purses to former rulers of princely states, was repealed by the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971. The former article guaranteed specific rights and privileges to rulers of princely states and ensured that princes would receive tax-free privy purses, equivalent to one-fourth of the money they earned earlier. The executive power of the Union extends to borrowing upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of India within limits fixed by Parliament by law and to the giving of guarantees within such limits, if any, as may be so fixed. The executive power of a State extends to borrowing within the territory of India upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of the State within such limits, if any, as may from time to time be fixed by the Legislature of such State by law and to the giving of guarantees within such limits, if any, as may be so fixed. The Government of India may make loans to any State or give guarantees in respect of loans raised by any State, and any sums required for the purpose of making such loans shall be charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. A State may not raise any loan if there is still outstanding any part of a loan which has been made to the State by the Government of India or by its predecessor Government, or in respect of which a guarantee has been given by the Government of India or by its predecessor Government. As from the commencement of this Constitution, all property and assets which were vested in His Majesty for the purposes of the Government of the Dominion of India and all property and assets which were vested in His Majesty for the purposes of the Government of each Governor's Province shall vest respectively in the Union and the corresponding State. All rights, liabilities and obligations of the Government of the Dominion of India and of the Government of each Governor's Province, whether arising out of any contract or otherwise, shall be the rights, liabilities and obligations respectively of the Government of India and the Government of each corresponding State. The executive power of the Union and of each State shall extend to the carrying on of any trade or business and to the acquisition, holding and disposal of property and the making of contracts for any purpose. All contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State shall be expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor of the State, as the case may be, and all such contracts and all assurances of property made in the exercise of that power shall be executed on behalf of the President or the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise. Neither the President nor the Governor shall be personally liable in respect of any contract or assurance made or executed for the purposes of this Constitution, or for the purposes of any enactment relating to the Government of India heretofore in force, nor shall any person making or executing any such contract or assurance on behalf of any of them be personally liable in respect thereof. Article 297 of the Constitution deals with the vesting of property accruing by escheat or lapse or as bona vacantia in the Union or a State. The Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, added the words “or the continental shelf” after the words “territorial waters” in Article 297. The Constitution (Fortieth Amendment) Act, 1976, gave the Parliament the power to periodically define India's territorial seas, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone (EEZ), and maritime zones.
Summary:

The document summarizes various provisions related to Indian laws, specifically focusing on the Constitution of India.

Firstly, the Constitution outlines the names under which the Government of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued. It also specifies that any legal proceedings pending at the commencement of the Constitution will continue with the Union of India or the corresponding State as parties.

Secondly, the Constitution guarantees the protection of property rights, stating that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law. However, the Constitution (Forty-Fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, repealed Article 19 (1) (f) and took out Article 31(1) has been taken out of Part III and made a separate Article 300A in Chapter IV of Part XII. This amendment may have taken away the scope of speedy remedy under Article 32 for the violation of Right to Property because it is no more a Fundamental Right. Making it a legal right under the Constitution serves two purposes: Firstly, it gives emphasis to the value of socialism included in the preamble and secondly, in doing so, it conformed to the doctrine of basic structure of the Constitution.
The third provision is Article 222, which deals with the transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another. The President may, on the recommendation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission, transfer a Judge from one High Court to any other High Court. When a Judge has been or is so transferred, he shall, during the period he serves, after the commencement of the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, as a Judge of the other High Court, be entitled to receive in addition to his salary such compensatory allowance as may be determined by Parliament by law and, until so determined, such compensatory allowance as the President may by order fix.

The fourth provision is Article 223, which deals with the appointment of acting Chief Justice. When the office of Chief Justice of a High Court is vacant or when any such Chief Justice is, by reason of absence or otherwise, unable to perform the duties of his office, the duties of the office shall be performed by such one of the other Judges of the court as the President may appoint for the purposes.

The fifth provision is Article 224, which deals with the appointment of additional and acting Judges. If by reason of any temporary increase in the business of High Court or by reason of arrears of work therein, it appears to the President that the number of the Judges of that Court should be for the time being increased, the President may, in consultation with the National Judicial Appointments Commission, appoint duly qualified persons to be additional Judges of the Court for such period not exceeding two years as he may specify.

The sixth provision is Article 224A, which deals with the appointment of retired Judges at sittings of High Courts. Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, the National Judicial Appointments Commission on a reference made to it by the Chief Justice of a High Court for any State, may with the previous consent of the President, request any person who has held the office of Judge of that Court or of any other High Court to sit and act as a Judge of the High Court for that State, and every such person so requested shall, while so sitting and acting, be entitled to such allowances as the President may by order determine and have all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of, but shall not otherwise be deemed to be, a Judge of that High Court: Provided that nothing in this article shall be deemed to require any such person as aforesaid to sit and act as a Judge of that High Court unless he consents so to do.

The seventh provision is Article 225, which deals with the jurisdiction of existing High Courts. Subject to the provisions of this Constitution and to the provisions of any law of the appropriate Legislature made by virtue of powers conferred on that Legislature by this Constitution, the jurisdiction of, and the law administered in, any existing High Court, and the respective powers of the Judges thereof in relation to the administration of justice in the Court, including any power to make rules of Court and to regulate the sittings of the court and of members thereof sitting alone or in Division Courts, shall be the same as immediately before the commencement of this Constitution: Provided that any restriction to which the exercise of original jurisdiction by any of the High Courts with respect to any matter concerning the revenue or concerning any act ordered or done in the collection thereof was subject immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall no longer apply to the exercise of such jurisdiction.

The eighth provision is Article 226, which deals with the power of High Courts to issue certain writs. Notwithstanding anything in article 32 every High Court shall have powers, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercise jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.

This document pertains to Chapter XXI of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) of India, which deals with Summary Trials, and Chapter XXIA, which deals with Plea Bargaining.

Summary Trials:

1. Under Section 260, a Chief Judicial Magistrate, Metropolitan Magistrate, or a Magistrate of the first class specially empowered by the High Court can try summarily certain offenses. These include offenses punishable with imprisonment for less than two years, theft (where the value of the property stolen does not exceed INR 2,000), receiving or retaining stolen property (where the value of the property does not exceed INR 2,000), assisting in the concealment or disposal of stolen property (where the value of such property does not exceed INR 2,000), offenses under sections 454 and 456 of the Indian Penal Code, insult with intent to provoke a breach of the peace, and criminal intimidation (punishable with imprisonment for up to two years).

2. Under Section 261, the High Court may confer on any Magistrate invested with the powers of a Magistrate of the second class the power to try summarily any offence punishable only with fine or with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months.

3. In summary trials, the procedure specified in the CrPC for the trial of summons-cases is followed, except as mentioned in Section 262. No sentence of imprisonment for a term exceeding three months can be passed in the case of any conviction under this Chapter.

4. Under Section 263, the Magistrate shall enter specific particulars in every case tried summarily. These include the serial number of the case, the date of the commission of the offense, the date of the report or complaint, the name of the complainant, the name, parentage, and residence of the accused, the offence complained of and the offence (if any) proved, the plea of the accused and his examination (if any), the finding, the sentence or other final order, and the date on which proceedings terminated.

5. Under Section 264, in every case tried summarily in which the accused does not plead guilty, the Magistrate shall record the substance of the evidence and a judgment containing a brief statement of the reasons for the finding.

6. Under Section 265, every such record and judgment shall be written in the language of the Court.

Section 91 states that whenever, in the course of a trial by a Security Force Court, it appears to the court that the examination of a witness is necessary for the ends of justice, and that the attendance of such witness cannot be procured without an amount of delay, expense or inconvenience which, in the circumstances of the case, would be unreasonable, such court may address the Chief Law Officer in order that a commission to take the evidence of such witness may be issued. The Magistrate or officer to whom the commission is issued shall proceed to the place where the witness is, or shall summon the witness before him and shall take down his evidence in the same manner, and may for this purpose exercise the same powers, as in the trials of warrant-cases under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.

The Act, which applies to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir, defines gains of learning as all acquisitions of property made substantially by means of learning, whether such acquisitions were made before or after the commencement of the Act. Learning is defined as education and training of every kind that enables a person to pursue a trade, industry, profession, or avocation in life.

Under this Act, gains of learning cannot be held not to be the exclusive and separate property of the acquirer merely because the acquirer's learning was imparted to him by a family member, with the aid of the joint funds of the family, or if the acquirer or his family was maintained or supported by the joint funds of the family while he was acquiring his learning.

Additionally, any remedy or proceeding pending in a Court at the commencement of the Act may be enforced, instituted, or continued as if the Act had not been passed.

For instance, Works Committees must consist of representatives of employers and workmen and promote measures for securing and preserving amity and good relations between the employer and workmen. Conciliation Officers are appointed to mediate in and promote the settlement of industrial disputes. Labour Courts are responsible for the adjudication of industrial disputes relating to any matter specified in the Second Schedule and for performing other functions assigned to them under the Act. The Act specifies the qualifications required for appointment as the presiding officer of a Tribunal, including being a Judge of a High Court, having been a District Judge or an Additional District Judge for at least three years, or being an officer of Indian Legal Service in Grade III with three years' experience in the grade. The Act also allows for the appointment of two persons as assessors to advise the Tribunal in the proceeding before it.

The Act includes state amendments, such as those from Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka, which modify the provisions related to the qualifications required for appointment as the presiding officer of a Tribunal. The Act defines "appropriate Government" as the Central Government in relation to certain industries and the State Government in relation to other industrial disputes. "Award" means a determination of an industrial dispute or a question relating thereto by a Labour Court, Industrial Tribunal, or National Industrial Tribunal, including an arbitration award made under section 10A. "Executive," in relation to a trade union, means the body, by whatever name called, to which the management of the affairs of the trade union is entrusted. "Industrial establishment or undertaking" means an establishment or undertaking in which any industry is carried on. "Insurance company" means an insurance company as defined in the Insurance Act, 1938, having branches or other establishments in more than one State. "Labour court" means a Labour Court constituted under this Act. "Prescribed" means prescribed by rules made under this Act. "Tribunal" means an Industrial Tribunal constituted under this Act. and any other allowance, which is variable and is linked to any factors other than the factors mentioned above. "Workman" means any person (including an apprentice) employed in any industry to do any manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, whether the terms of employment be expressed or implied, and for the purposes of any proceeding under this Act in relation to an industrial dispute, includes any such person who has been dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection with, or as a consequence of, that dispute, or who is on the date of the commencement of the proceeding, a workman within the meaning of this clause in relation to that dispute.

The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 54, defines "sale" as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised. The sale of tangible immoveable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or in the case of a reversion or other intangible thing, can only be made by a registered instrument. In the case of tangible immoveable property of a value less than one hundred rupees, such transfer may be made either by a registered instrument or by delivery of the property. Delivery of tangible immoveable property takes place when the seller places the buyer, or such person as he directs, in possession of the property. A contract for the sale of immoveable property is a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between the parties, but it does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on such property.

The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 55, outlines the rights and liabilities of the buyer and seller in the absence of a contract to the contrary. The seller is bound to disclose to the buyer any material defect in the property or in the seller’s title thereto of which the seller is, and the buyer is not, aware, and which the buyer could not with ordinary care discover. The seller is also bound to produce to the buyer on his request for examination all documents of title relating to the property which are in the seller's possession or power, to answer to the best of his information all relevant questions put to him by the buyer in respect to the property or the title thereto, and on payment or tender of the amount due in respect of the price, to execute a proper conveyance of the property when the buyer tenders it to him for execution at a proper time and place. The Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970, is a law in India that expands the appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in criminal matters. The Act allows an appeal to the Supreme Court from any final judgment, order, or sentence in a criminal proceeding of a High Court in the territory of India if the High Court has reversed an order of acquittal of an accused person and sentenced him to imprisonment for life or to imprisonment for a period of not less than ten years, or if the High Court has withdrawn a case from any court subordinate to its authority and has in such trial convicted the accused person and sentenced him to imprisonment for life or to imprisonment for a period of not less than ten years. This Act does not apply to the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The Act was enacted on August 9, 1970.

question_text: Which of the following is true of rules framed by the Supreme Court with reference to appeals to it?
options:
A) They are a special law within Section 4 of the code of civil procedure 
 B) They must take precedence over Section. 114 or Order. 47 
 C) Both (A) and (B) 
 D) None of these
context:
Rule 41 allows for the appointment of a Collector as a receiver of property in certain cases where the property is land paying revenue to the Government, or land of which the revenue has been assigned or redeemed, and the court considers that the interests of those concerned will be promoted by the management of the Collector.

Order XLI, Rule 1 outlines the form of appeal and what must accompany a memorandum of appeal, including a copy of the judgment. It also provides that where two or more suits have been tried together and a common judgment has been delivered therefor and two or more appeals are filed against any decree covered by that judgment, whether by the same appellant or by different appellants, the Appellate Court may dispense with the filing of more than one copy of the judgment.

Rule 2 states that the memorandum of appeal shall set forth, concisely and under distinct heads, the grounds of objection to the decree appealed from without any argument or narrative; and such grounds shall be numbered consecutively.

Rule 3 states that where the appeal is against a decree for payment of money, the appellant shall, within such time as the Appellate Court may allow, deposit the amount disputed in the appeal or furnish such security in respect thereof as the Court may think fit.

Rule 5 states that an appeal shall not operate as a stay of proceedings under a decree or order appealed from except so far as the Appellate Court may order, nor shall execution of a decree be stayed by reason only of an appeal having been preferred from the decree; but the Appellate Court may for sufficient cause order stay of execution of such decree.

Rule 6A states that where an application is made for stay of execution of an appealable decree before the expiration of the time allowed for appealing therefrom, the Court which passed the decree may on sufficient cause being shown order the execution to be stayed.

Rule 6B states that no order for stay of execution shall be made under sub-rule (1) or sub-rule (2) of rule 6 unless the Court making it is satisfied that substantial loss may result to the party applying for stay of execution unless the order is made, that the application has been made without unreasonable delay, and that security has been given by the applicant for the due performance of such decree or order as may ultimately be binding upon him.

Rule 6C states that the Court may make an ex parte order for stay of execution pending the hearing of the application.

Rule 6D states that notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing sub-rules, where the appellant fails to make the deposit or furnish the security specified in sub-rule (3) of rule 1, the Court shall not make an order staying the execution of the decree.

Rule 6E states that where an order is made for the execution of a decree from which an appeal is pending, the Court which passed the decree shall, on sufficient cause being shown by the appellant, require security to be taken for the restitution of any property which may be or has been taken in execution of the decree or for the payment of the value of such property and for the due performance of the decree or order of the Appellate Court, or the Appellate Court may for like cause direct the Court which passed the decree to take such security.

Rule 6F states that where an order has been made for the sale of immovable property in execution of a decree, and an appeal is pending from such decree, the sale shall, on the application of the judgment-debtor to the Court which made the order, be stayed on such terms as to giving security or otherwise as the Court thinks fit until the appeal is disposed of.

Rule 7 states that no security shall be required from the Government or a public officer in certain cases.

Rule 8 states that the powers conferred by rules 5 and 6 shall be exercisable where an appeal may be or has been preferred not from the decree but from an order made in execution of such decree.

Rule 9 states that the Court from whose decree an appeal lies shall entertain the memorandum of appeal and shall endorse thereon the date of presentation and shall register the appeal in a book of appeal kept for that purpose.

Rule 10 states that the Appellate Court may require the appellant to furnish security for costs.
The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Part VII, Appeals, deals with appeals from original decrees and appeals from appellate decrees. Section 96 outlines the general rule that an appeal shall lie from every decree passed by any court exercising original jurisdiction to the court authorized to hear appeals from the decisions of such court. The section also specifies that an appeal may lie from an original decree passed ex parte and that no appeal shall lie from a decree passed by the court with the consent of parties. Section 97 states that where a party aggrieved by a preliminary decree passed after the commencement of the code does not appeal from such decree, he shall be precluded from disputing its correctness in any appeal which may be preferred from the final decree. Section 98 outlines the decision-making process when an appeal is heard by a bench of two or more judges. The section states that the appeal shall be decided in accordance with the opinion of such judges or of the majority (if any) of such judges and provides for the hearing of the appeal on a point of law where the judges composing the bench differ in opinion. Section 99 states that no decree shall be reversed or substantially varied, nor shall any case be remanded, in appeal on account of any misjoinder or non-joinder of parties or causes of action or any error, defect or irregularity in any proceedings in the suit, not affecting the merits of the case or the jurisdiction of the court. Section 99A states that no order under section 47 shall be reversed or substantially varied, on account of any error, defect or irregularity in any proceeding relating to such order, unless such error, defect or irregularity has prejudicially affected the decision of the case.

The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 100 lays out the rules for second appeals. The section states that an appeal shall lie to the High Court from every decree passed in appeal by any court subordinate to the High Court if the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law. The section also outlines the procedure for filing and hearing a second appeal, including the requirement for the memorandum of appeal to precisely state the substantial question of law involved in the appeal and the power of the High Court to formulate the question. The section also provides that the appeal shall be heard on the question so formulated and the respondent shall, at the hearing of the appeal, be allowed to argue that the case does not involve such question. The section also includes a state amendment that allows for a second appeal on the ground of a conflicting finding of fact by the lower appellate court.

The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 100A states that where any appeal from an original or appellate decree or order is heard and decided by a Single Judge of a High Court, no further appeal shall lie from the judgment and decree of such Single Judge.

The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 101 states that no second appeal shall lie except on the ground mentioned in section 100.

The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Section 102 states that no second appeal shall lie from any decree when the subject matter of the original suit is for recovery of money not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees.

The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is an Act to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumer councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers’ disputes and for matters connected therewith. The Act establishes three tiers of consumer dispute redressal agencies, namely, the District Forum, the State Commission, and the National Commission. The District Forum has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed does not exceed rupees twenty lakhs. The State Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed exceeds rupees twenty lakhs but does not exceed rupees one crore, and appeals against the orders of any District Forum within the State. The National Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed exceeds rupees one crore, and appeals against the orders of any State Commission. The Act also provides for the appointment of members to these forums, their qualifications, terms of office, salaries and allowances, resignation, removal, and other terms and conditions of service. The Act also lays down the procedure for filing and disposing of complaints and appeals, and the powers and functions of the consumer dispute redressal agencies. The Act also provides for penalties for non-compliance with the orders of the consumer dispute redressal agencies, and protection of action taken in good faith. The Act also empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act, and the State Governments to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act in relation to the State Commissions and District Fora. The Act also empowers the National Commission to make regulations not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

context:
Under Section 9, the Bar Council of India is responsible for constituting disciplinary committees to investigate and punish misconduct by advocates. These committees can meet at any time and place, and must observe rules of procedure prescribed by the Bar Council of India.

Section 10B outlines the disqualification of members of a Bar Council. A member can be disqualified if they are absent without sufficient excuse from three consecutive meetings, if their name is removed from the roll of advocates, or if they are otherwise disqualified under any rule made by the Bar Council of India.

Section 11 allows every Bar Council to appoint a secretary, an accountant, and such other persons on its staff as it deems necessary. The secretary and accountant must possess qualifications prescribed by the Bar Council of India.

Under Section 12, every Bar Council must maintain books of accounts and other books in the form and manner prescribed. The accounts of a Bar Council must be audited by auditors qualified to act as auditors of companies under the Companies Act, 1956. The audited accounts must be sent to the Bar Council of India and published in the official Gazette.

Section 13 states that no act done by a Bar Council or any committee thereof shall be called in question on the ground merely of the existence of any vacancy in, or any defect in the constitution of, the Council or committee.

Section 14 states that no election of a member to a Bar Council shall be called in question on the ground merely that due notice thereof has not been given to any person entitled to vote thereat, if notice of the date has, not less than thirty days before that date, been published in the Official Gazette.

Finally, Section 15 gives the Bar Council the power to make rules to carry out the purposes of this Chapter. These rules may provide for the election of members of the Bar Council, the manner of election of the Chairman and Vice-Chairman, the filling of casual vacancies, the powers and duties of the Chairman and Vice-Chairman, the constitution of funds, the summoning and holding of meetings, the conduct of business, the qualifications and conditions of service of the secretary, the accountant and other employees, the maintenance of books of accounts, the appointment of auditors, and the management and investment of the funds of the Bar Council. No rules made under this section by a State Bar Council shall have effect unless they have been approved by the Bar Council of India.

The Bar Council of India has the authority to transfer the name of a person from one State Bar Council roll to another, without requiring any fee. This transfer does not affect the seniority of the person in the new roll. Every State Bar Council must send an authenticated copy of their roll of advocates to the Bar Council of India and inform them of any alterations or additions made. Certain advocates have the right of pre-audience over others, including the Attorney-General of India, the Solicitor-General of India, the Additional Solicitor-General of India, the Advocate-General of any State, and senior advocates. A vakil or pleader who is a law graduate can be admitted as an advocate on a State roll if they make an application within two years of the appointed day and fulfill the specified conditions. Certain individuals who have been a vakil, pleader, mukhtar, or advocate for at least three years, or were entitled to practice law before December 1, 1961, or were an advocate of a High Court in Burma before April 1, 1937, or are entitled to be enrolled as an advocate under a rule made by the Bar Council of India, can also be admitted as an advocate on a State roll if they make an application and fulfill the specified conditions. No person can be admitted as an advocate on a State roll if they have been convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude, an offence under the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955, or if they have been dismissed or removed from employment or office under the State.

Section 24 outlines the disqualifications for enrolment as an advocate, including being of unsound mind, having been convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude, or being found guilty of misconduct in the opinion of the Bar Council of India. Under Chapter XVII, Section 165, persons not subject to naval law who fail to attend as a witness before a court-martial or disciplinary court, refuse to take an oath or make an affirmation, refuse to answer questions, refuse to produce or deliver up a document, or are guilty of contempt of court can be punished with imprisonment for up to two years, a fine, or both. Section 167 states that every governor, gaoler, and keeper of any prison, gaol, or house of correction or of any naval detention quarters, and every person having the charge of command of any place, ship, or vessel for imprisonment, who shall refuse or neglect to receive or confine, remove, discharge, or deliver up any offender against the provisions of this Act, shall incur a penalty not exceeding one thousand rupees. Chapter XVIII outlines the appointment of the Judge Advocate General of the Navy and his subordinate officers. The Judge Advocate General of the Navy must be a citizen of India and have for at least ten years held a judicial office in the territory of India, or have for at least ten years been an advocate of a High Court. The Deputy Judge Advocate General of the Navy must be a citizen of India and have for at least seven years held a judicial office in the territory of India, or have for at least seven years been an advocate of a High Court. Summary:

The Indian Naval Discipline Act of 1934 outlines the responsibilities of the Judge Advocate General of the Navy and their functions in their absence. The Act also includes provisions for the disposal of the private property of persons in the Navy who have died, gone missing, or been declared dead.

Under Section 170, in the absence of the Judge Advocate General of the Navy, their functions are to be performed by a designated judge advocate in their department.

Chapter XIX of the Act, titled "Disposal of the Private Property of Persons Deceased, Missing, Etc.," includes Sections 171-178, which detail the procedures for disposing of the property of deceased sailors and officers.

Under Section 171, on the death of a sailor while subject to naval law, the commanding officer of the ship to which the sailor belonged is responsible for securing all movable property belonging to the deceased, drawing the pay and allowances due to the deceased, and collecting any moneys left by the deceased in banking companies or other institutions. The commanding officer may sell or convert the deceased's property into money to secure the payment of ship and service debts and other debts in the ship or quarters, and any surplus property is to be delivered to the deceased's representative.

Under Section 172, the provisions of Section 171 also apply to the disposal of the property of an officer who dies while subject to naval law, with the following modifications: the functions of the commanding officer are to be performed by a Committee of Adjustment, and the surplus, if any, after the payment of debts and expenses is to be paid to the person prescribed in this behalf.

Under Section 173, if doubt or difference arises as to what are the ship or service debts and the debts in ship or quarters of a deceased officer or sailor, or as to the amount payable in respect thereof, the decision of the prescribed person shall be final and binding on all persons for all purposes.

Under Section 174, the commanding officer or the Committee of Adjustment, as the case may be, shall have the same rights and powers as if they had taken out representation to the estate of the deceased for the purpose of exercising their duties under Section 171 or 172.

Under Section 175, the Central Government may direct that the estate of a deceased sailor or officer be handed over to the Administrator-General of a State for administration. The Administrator-General shall administer the estate in accordance with the provisions of the Administrator-General's Act, 1913, and shall pay the surplus, if any, to the heirs of the deceased or, if no heir is traceable, to the person prescribed in this behalf.

The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act No. 3 of 1930), is an Indian law that defines and amends the law relating to the sale of goods. The Act has 7 chapters and 66 sections, including provisions related to the formation of the contract, transfer of property, performance of the contract, rights of unpaid seller against the goods, suits for breach of the contract, and miscellaneous provisions. The Act also includes definitions of various legal terms related to the sale of goods, such as buyer, delivery, goods, insolvency, mercantile agent, price, property, quality of goods, seller, and specific goods. The Act applies to the whole of India, except the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The Act defines the rights and obligations of buyers and sellers in a sales contract, and provides remedies for breach of contract. The Act also recognizes the concept of implied terms and conditions, which can be negated or varied by express agreement or the course of dealing between the parties. The Act also provides for the calculation of interest and special damages in certain cases.
Section 63 allows the promisee to dispense with or remit performance of the promise, extend the time for performance, or accept any satisfaction which they think fit. If the debtor is incapable of entering into a contract or anyone they are legally bound to support is supplied with necessaries suited to their condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person (Section 68).

A person who is interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is entitled to be reimbursed by the other (Section 69). Where a person lawfully does anything for another person or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered (Section 70).

A person who finds goods belonging to another and takes them into his custody is subject to the same responsibility as a bailee (Section 71). A person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must restore it to the person from whom it was received or make compensation for it (Section 72).

The Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the consequences of breaching a contract in Chapter VI, specifically in Section 73. According to this section, when a contract is broken, the party who suffers as a result is entitled to receive compensation from the party who breached the contract for any loss or damage caused by the breach. This compensation is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The same compensation is also applicable when an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged.

The section further explains that in estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Illustrations are provided to further explain the application of this section. For example, if A contracts to sell and deliver 50 maunds of saltpetre to B, at a certain price to be paid on delivery, and A breaks his promise, B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the sum, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which B might have obtained 50 maunds of saltpetre of like quality at the time when the saltpetre ought to have been delivered.

Another illustration explains that if A hires B‟s ship to go to Bombay, and there take on board, on the first of January, a cargo, which A is to provide, and to bring it to Calcutta, the freight to be paid when earned. B’s ship does not go to Bombay, but A has opportunities of procuring suitable conveyance for the cargo upon terms as advantageous as those on which he had chartered the ship. A avails himself of those opportunities, but is put to trouble and expense in doing so. A is entitled to receive compensation from B in respect of such trouble and expense.

Overall, this section of the Indian Contract Act of 1872 outlines the compensation that the party who suffers from a breach of contract is entitled to receive from the party who breached the contract. The compensation is for any loss or damage caused by the breach, and it is not to be given for any remote or indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. The means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account while estimating the loss or damage.

The Indian Penal Code includes provisions for punishing abetment, or the act of instigating, aiding, or attempting to aid another person in committing an offense. According to Section 107, a person is considered an abettor if they intentionally aid or instigate another person in committing an offense, or if they intentionally engage in a conspiracy to commit an offense. The punishment for abetment is generally the same as the punishment for the offense committed, as stated in Section 109. However, if the person abetted commits the offense with a different intention or knowledge than the abettor, the abettor will be punished with the punishment for the offense that would have been committed if the act had been done with the intention or knowledge of the abettor, as stated in Section 110. If a different act is committed than the one that was abetted, the abettor is liable for the act committed, as long as it was a probable consequence of the abetment and committed under the influence of the instigation, aid, or conspiracy that constituted the abetment, as stated in Section 111. If the act abetted is committed in addition to another act that constitutes a distinct offense, the abettor is liable for punishment for each offense, as stated in Section 112. The abettor is also liable for any effect caused by the act abetted that is different from the one intended, as long as they knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect, as stated in Section 113. If the abettor is present when the offense is committed, they are deemed to have committed the offense, as stated in Section 114. If the offense is not committed, but an act causing harm is done in consequence of the abetment, the abettor is liable to punishment, as stated in Section 115. If the offense is punishable with imprisonment, the abettor is punishable with one-fourth of the longest term provided for that offense, or with such fine as is provided for that offense, or with both, as stated in Section 116. If the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant, and the abettor knew that the act abetted was likely to cause harm, the abettor is liable to punishment with one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for that offense, and also to fine, as stated in Section 116. If a person abets the commission of an offense by the public generally or by any number or class of persons exceeding ten, they shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, as stated in Section 117. If a person conceals by any act or illegal omission, or by the use of encryption or any other information hiding tool, the existence of a design to commit an offense punishable with death or imprisonment for life, they shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or, if the offense be not committed, with imprisonment of either description, for a term which may extend to three years, as stated in Section 118. Section 121 defines the offense of waging war against the Government of India and provides that any person who wages war against the Government of India, attempts to wage such war, or abets the waging of such war shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine. Section 121A defines the offense of conspiracy to commit offenses punishable by section 121 and provides that any person who conspires to commit any of the offenses punishable by section 121 shall be punished with imprisonment for life or imprisonment of either description which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine.

Section 122 defines the offense of collecting arms, etc., with the intention of waging war against the Government of India and provides that any person who collects men, arms, or ammunition or otherwise prepares to wage war with the intention of either waging or being prepared to wage war against the Government of India shall be punished with imprisonment for life or imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years and shall also be liable to fine.

Section 123 defines the offense of concealing with intent to facilitate a design to wage war and provides that any person who, by any act or illegal omission, conceals the existence of a design to wage war against the Government of India, intending by such concealment to facilitate, or knowing it to be likely that such concealment will facilitate, the waging of such war, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years and shall also be liable to fine.

Section 124 defines the offense of assaulting the President, Governor, etc., with the intent to compel or restrain the exercise of any lawful power and provides that any person who assaults or wrongfully restrains, or attempts wrongfully to restrain, or overawes, by means of criminal force or the show of criminal force, or attempts so to overawe, the President of India or the Governor of any State, with the intention of inducing or compelling such President or Governor to exercise or refrain from exercising in any manner any of the lawful powers of such President or Governor, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine.

Section 124A defines the offense of sedition and provides that any person who, by words, either spoken or written, or by signs, or by visible representation, or otherwise, brings or attempts to bring into hatred or contempt, or excites or attempts to excite disaffection towards, the Government established by law in India, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, to which fine may be added, or with imprisonment which may extend to three years, to which fine may be added, or with fine.

Section 125 defines the offense of waging war against any Asiatic power in alliance with the Government of India and provides that any person who wages war against the Government of any Asiatic Power in alliance or at peace with the Government of India, or attempts to wage such war, or abets the waging of such war, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, to which fine may be added, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, to which fine may be added, or with fine.

Section 126 defines the offense of committing depredation on territories of a power at peace with the Government of India and provides that any person who commits depredation, or makes preparations to commit depredation, on the territories of any Power in alliance or at peace with the Government of India, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine and to forfeiture of any property used or intended to be used in committing such depredation, or acquired by such depredation.

Section 127 defines the offense of receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 125 and 126 and provides that any person who receives any property knowing the same to have been taken in the commission of any of the offenses mentioned in sections 125 and 126, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine and to forfeiture of the property so received.

THE TERRITORIAL WATERS, CONTINENTAL SHELF, EXCLUSIVE ECONOMIC ZONE AND OTHER MARITIME ZONES ACT, 1976

The Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 (Act No. 80 of 1976) came into force on August 25, 1976. The Act defines the limits and extent of India's territorial waters, contiguous zone, continental shelf, and exclusive economic zone. It also outlines the rights and jurisdiction of India in these maritime zones, and the regulations for the exploration, exploitation, conservation, and management of natural resources in these zones.

The Act defines "limit" as the limit of territorial waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone, or any other maritime zone of India, including the mainland and individual or composite group of islands constituting part of the territory of India.

Section 3 of the Act defines the sovereignty of India over its territorial waters, which extends up to a limit of 12 nautical miles from the nearest point of the appropriate baseline. The Central Government has the power to alter this limit by notification in the Official Gazette, subject to the approval of both Houses of Parliament.

Section 4 of the Act outlines the right of innocent passage of foreign ships through India's territorial waters, subject to certain conditions and restrictions. Foreign warships, including submarines and other underwater vehicles, must give prior notice to the Central Government and navigate on the surface while passing through such waters. The Central Government has the power to suspend the entry of foreign ships into certain areas of the territorial waters in the interests of the peace, good order, or security of India or any part thereof.

Section 5 of the Act defines the contiguous zone of India, which extends beyond and adjacent to the territorial waters up to a limit of 24 nautical miles from the nearest point of the baseline. The Central Government has the power to alter this limit by notification in the Official Gazette, subject to the approval of both Houses of Parliament. The Central Government has the power to exercise certain powers and take measures in or in relation to the contiguous zone with respect to security, immigration, sanitation, customs, and other fiscal matters.

Section 6 of the Act defines the continental shelf of India, which comprises the seabed and subsoil of the submarine areas that extend beyond the limit of its territorial waters throughout the natural prolongation of its land territory to the outer edge of the continental margin or to a distance of 200 nautical miles from the baseline. India has full and exclusive sovereign rights in respect of its continental shelf, including sovereign rights for the purposes of exploration, exploitation, conservation, and management of all resources, exclusive rights and jurisdiction for the construction, maintenance, or operation of artificial islands, off-shore terminals, installations, and other structures and devices, exclusive jurisdiction to authorize, regulate, and control scientific research, and exclusive jurisdiction to preserve and protect the marine environment and to prevent and control marine pollution. No person, including a foreign government, shall explore the continental shelf or exploit its resources or carry out any search or excavation or conduct any research within the continental shelf or drill therein or construct, maintain, or operate any artificial island, off-shore terminal, installation, or other structure or device therein for any purpose whatsoever, except under and in accordance with the terms of a licence or a letter of authority granted by the Central Government.

context:
The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 introduces the goods and services tax (GST) in India. This tax aims to replace various indirect taxes levied by the Union and State Governments and create a common national market for goods and services. The GST will be levied on all transactions involving the supply of goods or services or both, except those explicitly excluded.

The Act proposes to subsume various Central indirect taxes, such as Central Excise Duty, Additional Excises Duties, Excise Duty on medicinal and toilet preparations, Service Tax, Countervailing Duty, Special Additional Duty of Customs, and Central Surcharges and Cesses related to the supply of goods and services. Similarly, State Value Added Tax/Sales Tax, Entertainment Tax, Central Sales Tax, Octroi and Entry tax, Purchase Tax, Luxury tax, Taxes on lottery, betting and gambling, and State cesses and surcharges related to supply of goods and services will also be subsumed.

The Act also introduces Integrated Goods and Services Tax on inter-State transactions of goods and services. An additional tax of up to 1% on the supply of goods in the course of inter-State trade or commerce will be levied for a period of two years, collected by the Government of India, and assigned to the States from where the supply originates.

The Act confers concurrent powers upon Parliament and State Legislatures to make laws governing goods and services tax, covering all goods and services, except alcoholic liquor for human consumption. Petroleum and petroleum products will not be subject to the levy of Goods and Services Tax till a date notified on the recommendation of the Goods and Services Tax Council.

The Act provides compensation to the States for loss of revenue arising on account of implementing the Goods and Services Tax for a period that may extend to five years. A Goods and Services Tax Council is created to examine issues relating to goods and services tax and make recommendations to the Union and the States on parameters like rates, exemption list, and threshold limits. The Council will function under the Chairmanship of the Union Finance Minister and will have the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance as a member, along with the Minister in-charge of Finance or Taxation or any other Minister nominated by each State Government. The Council's decisions will be taken by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting.

The Act provides transitional provisions to address any inconsistency arising with respect to any law relating to tax on goods or services or on both in force in any State on the commencement of the provisions of the Constitution as amended by this Act within a period of one year.

The Act has 28 sections divided into six chapters.

Chapter I, Preliminary, defines the short title, extent, and commencement of the Act and provides definitions for various terms used in the Act.

Chapter II, Establishment of Mints, empowers the Government to establish and abolish Mints, and authorizes the minting of coins by any organization or Government of any foreign country, within or beyond the limits of India.

The Act also contains a Schedule that amends the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

The Act aims to provide a specialized forum for adjudicating commercial disputes and to ensure speedy and efficient disposal of such disputes. It also seeks to promote ease of doing business in India by reducing the time and cost of litigation in commercial matters.

4. Section 6: Notwithstanding that a child marriage has been annulled by a decree of nullity under section 3, every child begotten or conceived of such marriage before the decree is made, whether born before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be deemed to be a legitimate child for all purposes.

Section 40 states that the existence of any judgment, order or decree which by law prevents any court from taking cognizance of a suit or holding a trial, is a relevant fact when the question is whether such court ought to take cognizance of such suit or to hold such trial.

In this summary, we will explain the key provisions of Sections 24 and 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which deal with the power of transfer and withdrawal of suits, appeals, and other proceedings.

Section 24: General power of transfer and withdrawal

Section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for the transfer and withdrawal of suits, appeals, and other proceedings. The section gives the High Court or the District Court the power to transfer or withdraw any suit, appeal, or other proceeding pending before it for trial or disposal to any Court subordinate to it and competent to try or dispose of the same. This power can be exercised on the application of any of the parties or of its own motion without notice.

The section also provides for the transfer of a suit, appeal, or other proceeding pending in any Court subordinate to the High Court or District Court to any Court subordinate to the same High Court or District Court and competent to try or dispose of the same. This power can be exercised by the High Court or District Court on its own motion or on the application of any of the parties after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desired to be heard.

Where any suit or proceeding has been transferred or withdrawn under sub-section (1), the Court which is thereafter to try or dispose of such suit or proceeding may, subject to any special directions in the case of an order of transfer, either retry it or proceed from the point at which it was transferred or withdrawn.

Section 25: Power of Supreme Court to transfer suits, etc.

Section 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for the transfer of suits, appeals, and other proceedings by the Supreme Court. The section empowers the Supreme Court, on the application of a party and after notice to the parties and after hearing such of them as desire to be heard, to direct that any suit, appeal, or other proceeding be transferred from a High Court or other Civil Court in one State to a High Court or other Civil Court in any other State.

The Charge chapter in the Indian Code of Criminal Procedure outlines the rules for formulating charges against accused individuals. A charge must state the offence with which the accused is charged, and if the law that creates the offence gives it a specific name, the offence may be described in the charge by that name only. If the law does not give the offence a specific name, so much of the definition of the offence must be stated as to give the accused notice of the matter with which they are charged. The law and section of the law against which the offence is said to have been committed must be mentioned in the charge. The charge must be written in the language of the Court. If the accused is liable to enhanced punishment or a different kind of punishment for a subsequent offence due to a previous conviction, the fact, date, and place of the previous conviction must be stated in the charge. The charge shall contain such particulars as to the time and place of the alleged offence, and the person (if any) against whom, or the thing (if any) in respect of which, it was committed, as are reasonably sufficient to give the accused notice of the matter with which they are charged. When the nature of the case is such that the particulars mentioned in sections 211 and 212 do not give the accused sufficient notice of the matter with which they are charged, the charge shall also contain such particulars of the manner in which the alleged offence was committed as will be sufficient for that purpose. In every charge, words used in describing an offence shall be deemed to have been used in the sense attached to them respectively by the law under which such offence is punishable. No error in stating either the offence or the particulars required to be stated in the charge, and no omission to state the offence or those particulars, shall be regarded at any stage of the case as material, unless the accused was in fact misled by such error or omission, and it has occasioned a failure of justice. Any Court may alter or add to any charge at any time before judgment is pronounced. If the alteration or addition to a charge is such that proceeding immediately with the trial is not likely, in the opinion of the Court, to prejudice the accused in his defence or the prosecutor in the conduct of the case, the Court may, in its discretion, after such alteration or addition has been made, proceed with the trial as if the altered or added charge had been the original charge. If the alteration or addition is such that proceeding immediately with the trial is likely, in the opinion of the Court, to prejudice the accused or the prosecutor as aforesaid, the Court may either direct a new trial or adjourn the trial for such period as may be necessary. If the offence stated in the altered or added charge is one for the prosecution of which previous sanction is necessary, the case shall not be proceeded with until such sanction is obtained, unless sanction has been already obtained for a prosecution on the same facts as those on which the altered or added charge is founded. Whenever a charge is altered or added to by the Court after the commencement of the trial, the prosecutor and the accused shall be allowed—to recall or re-summon and cross-examine any witness who has been examined.

It also defines the law relating to conciliation and matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. The Act is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985) and the UNCITRAL Conciliation Rules (1980). The Act applies to the whole of India and came into force on a date appointed by the Central Government. The Act is divided into two parts: Part I - Arbitration and Part II - Conciliation. Part I of the Act contains general provisions, arbitration agreement, composition and jurisdiction of arbitral tribunal, conduct of arbitral proceedings, making of arbitral award and terms of settlement, recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards, and appeals. Part II of the Act deals with conciliation, including provisions for the commencement of conciliation proceedings, the conduct of the conciliation proceedings, the termination of conciliation proceedings, and the effects of conciliation agreements. The Act provides for extensive judicial intervention in arbitration proceedings, but also allows for parties to agree to derogate from certain provisions of the Act. The Act applies to every arbitration under any other enactment for the time being in force, as if the arbitration were pursuant to an arbitration agreement and as if that other enactment were an arbitration agreement. The Act defines dowry as any property or valuable security given or agreed to be given either directly or indirectly by one party to a marriage to the other party to the marriage or by the parents of either party to a marriage or by any other person to either party to the marriage or to any other person at or before or after the marriage. The Act specifies that dower or mahr in the case of persons to whom the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) applies is not considered dowry. The Act imposes penalties for giving or taking dowry, demanding dowry, and for advertising for the purpose of giving or taking dowry. The Act also states that any agreement for the giving or taking of dowry is void, and that dowry received by any person other than the woman in connection with whose marriage it is given shall be transferred to the woman within three months after the date of marriage or after the date of its receipt, or if the dowry was received when the woman was a minor, within three months after she has attained the age of eighteen years. Failure to transfer such property within the specified time limit is punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than six months, but which may extend to two years or with fine which shall not be less than five thousand rupees, but which may extend to ten thousand rupees. The Act also specifies that cognizance of offences under this Act can only be taken upon its own knowledge or a police report of the facts which constitute such offence, or a complaint by the person aggrieved by the offence or a parent or other relative of such person, or by any recognized welfare institution or organization. The Act also states that the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 shall apply to offences under this Act as if they were cognizable offences for the purposes of investigation of such offences and for the purposes of matters other than matters referred to in section 42 of that Code and the arrest of a person without a warrant or without an order of a Magistrate. Every offence under this Act is non-bailable and non-compoundable.
The Act also provides for the solemnization of marriage after the issue of the certificate. After the issue of the certificate by the Minister, marriage may be solemnized between the persons therein described according to such form or ceremony as the Minister thinks fit to adopt.

The Act also provides for the registration of marriages solemnized under Part V. After the solemnization of any marriage under this Part, the Marriage Registrar present at such solemnization shall forthwith register the marriage in duplicate; that is to say, in a marriage-register-book, according to the form of the Fourth Schedule hereto annexed, and also in a certificate attached to the marriage-register-book as a counterfoil.

The Act also provides for the registration of marriages between Indian Christians. The registration of marriages between Indian Christians under this Part shall be made in conformity with the rules laid down in section 37 (so far as they are applicable), and not otherwise.

The Act also provides for penalties for false oath, declaration, notice, or certificate for procuring marriage, forbidding, by false personation, the issue of a certificate by a Marriage Registrar, solemnizing marriage without due authority, solemnizing marriage out of proper time or without witnesses, solemnizing marriage with a minor within fourteen days after notice or without authority of Court or without sending copy of notice, issuing a certificate authorizedly forbidden, and solemnizing marriage authorizedly forbidden.

The Act also provides for the limitation of prosecutions under the Act and miscellaneous provisions. Every prosecution for every offence punishable under this Act shall be commenced within two years after the offence is committed. The Act also provides for the correction of errors, searches and copies of entries, certified copies of entry in marriage register, etc., to be evidence, certificates of certain marriages to be sent to Central Government, state government to prescribe fees, power to make rules, power to prescribe fees and rules for Indian States, power to declare who shall be District Judge, powers and functions exercisable as regards Indian States, saving of Consular marriages, non-validation of marriages within prohibited degrees, and repeal of enactments.

The Act also contains Schedules for forms and fees.

Summary:
The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is an Act to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumer councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers’ disputes and for matters connected therewith. The Act establishes three tiers of consumer dispute redressal agencies, namely, the District Forum, the State Commission, and the National Commission. The District Forum has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed does not exceed rupees twenty lakhs. The State Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed exceeds rupees twenty lakhs but does not exceed rupees one crore, and appeals against the orders of any District Forum within the State. The National Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation, if any, claimed exceeds rupees one crore, and appeals against the orders of any State Commission. The Act also provides for the appointment of members to these forums, their qualifications, terms of office, salaries and allowances, resignation, removal, and other terms and conditions of service. The Act also lays down the procedure for filing and disposing of complaints and appeals, and the powers and functions of the consumer dispute redressal agencies. The Act also provides for penalties for non-compliance with the orders of the consumer dispute redressal agencies, and protection of action taken in good faith. The Act also empowers the Central Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act, and the State Governments to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act in relation to the State Commissions and District Fora. The Act also empowers the National Commission to make regulations not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act for carrying out the provisions of the Act.

Section 21 states that a contract is not void due to a mistake in law, but a mistake in a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact. Section 22 states that a contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by a mistake of one party as to a matter of fact. Section 23 outlines the lawfulness of the consideration or object of an agreement, which is unlawful if it is forbidden by law, defeats the provisions of any law, is fraudulent, involves injury to the person or property of another, or is immoral or opposed to public policy. Section 24 states that if any part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any one or any part of any one of several considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void. Section 25 states that an agreement made without consideration is void, unless it is expressed in writing and registered, or is a promise to compensate for something done, or is a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation law. Section 26 states that every agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person, other than a minor, is void. Section 27 states that every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void. Section 28 states that every agreement, by which any party thereto is restricted absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any contract, by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or which limits the time within which he may thus enforce his rights, is void to that extent. The Indian Contract Act, 1872, defines a contingent contract as a contract to do or not to do something, if some event, collateral to such contract, does or does not happen. A contingent contract cannot be enforced by law unless and until the event on which it is contingent has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event does not happen can be enforced when the happening of that event becomes impossible, and not before. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if a specified uncertain event happens within a fixed time become void if, at the expiration of the time fixed, such event has not happened, or if, before the time fixed, such event becomes impossible. Contingent agreements to do or not to do anything, if an impossible event happens, are void, whether the impossibility of the event is known or not to the parties to the agreement at the time when it is made. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law. Promises bind the representatives of the promisors in case of the death of such promisors before performance, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If a promisor has made an offer of performance to the promisee, and the offer has not been accepted, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance, nor does he thereby lose his rights under the contract. Every such offer must fulfill certain conditions, such as being unconditional, made at a proper time and place, and under such circumstances that the person to whom it is made may have a reasonable opportunity of ascertaining that the person by whom it is made is able and willing there and then to do the whole of what he is bound by his promise to do. If the offer is an offer to deliver anything to the promisee, the promisee must have a reasonable opportunity of seeing that the thing offered is the thing which the promisor is bound by his promise to deliver.

The terms defined in Section 133 include "estate", "homestead", "intermediary", "tenant", and "tenure holder". An "estate" refers to lands included under one entry in any of the general registers of revenue-paying and revenue-free lands, and includes revenue-free lands not entered in any register, a part of or a share in an estate, and land used for agricultural purposes. A "homestead" means a dwelling house together with any courtyard, compound, garden, or outhouse and includes any outbuildings used for purposes connected with agriculture and any family graveyard, library, office, guest house, grainstore, latrines, boundary walls, tanks, wells, or places of worship appertaining to such dwelling house. An "intermediary" means a person who holds in an estate the right, title, or interest of a talukdar and includes a person who holds land either revenue-free or at a concessional rate and a tenure holder.
